title: Every MHEV rear diff case cast lock-ready; pack cars receive a clip-in lock module
description: [MHEV] Deletes the second MHEV rear differential housing pattern, its fixtures, PPAP and a separate axle part-number family. Every housing is cast and machined lock-ready; road cars pay a small premium for the extra machining and a blanking ring. Baseline: the MHEV rear axle uses two EN-GJS-600-3 differential housings. The plain one goes to 70% of MHEV production; the off-road pack version (30% of MHEV, 18% of fleet) is its own casting with a dog-face boss, coil pilot and outer spline, and has its own pattern, fixtures, gauges, PPAP and sub-line. Proposal: cast and machine every MHEV housing lock-ready (+0.4 min, +0.12 kg). Road cars get a stamped blanking ring and plug; pack cars get a 0.9 kg pre-tested lock module (dog ring, armature, coil) clipped on at the axle line with one circlip. Why it works: ring-gear torque is the same on both versions, so the housing is already strong enough for the locked case. Check: rear axle 1,600 kg × 9.81 × µ 0.9 × 0.40 m ≈ 5,650 Nm at the wheels, ÷ 3.73 final drive ≈ 1,515 Nm at the pinion; the case itself carries the full ≈ 5,650 Nm ring-gear torque, inside the ≈ 9,300 Nm (2,500 Nm gearbox output × 3.73) the plain housing is already rated to. Benchmark: Ineos Grenadier sells Eaton front and rear locks as an option on most trims and as standard on Trialmaster, which shows locking is naturally an add-on to one common axle.

title: Centre lock by fully clamping the transfer-case clutch; separate centre dog lock deleted
description: [MHEV] Removes the centre dog lock (dog ring, coil, armature, position sensor, harness branch and its machining) from the two-speed transfer case. The existing wet multi-plate centre clutch gets two more plates so that its full clamp holds the static lock torque. Baseline: the MHEV two-speed transfer case (off-road pack, 18% of fleet) has a planetary centre differential with a wet multi-plate clutch for torque bias, plus a separate electromagnetic dog for 100% centre lock. Proposal: delete the dog. Raise the clutch from 8 to 10 plates (20 friction faces) and add a Lock command that drives the existing ball-ramp actuator to full clamp. Why it works: in lock mode the clutch does not slip, so it generates no heat; it only has to hold torque. Lock torque check: the worst case is all front-axle traction through the centre: 1,500 kg × 9.81 × µ 0.9 × 0.40 m ≈ 5,300 Nm at the front wheels, ÷ 3.73 final drive ≈ 1,420 Nm at the transfer output. Clutch capacity T = n·µ·F·rm = 20 × 0.11 × 18 kN × 0.075 m ≈ 2,970 Nm, a 2.1× margin. Above that the clutch slips briefly under a rock-drop shock, acting as a torque limiter for the front shafts. The ball-ramp is spring-opened, so loss of power unlocks the centre, which is the safe state. Benchmark: Ineos Grenadier uses a Tremec two-speed case with a built-in lockable centre diff and 2.5:1 low range; we keep the lock function but deliver it through the clutch.

title: Tri-motor BEV: two-motor axle synchronises wheel speeds, so its dog clutch is deleted
description: [800V BEV] On the tri-motor trim each rear wheel already has its own motor, yet the programme carried over the rear dog clutch from the dual-motor gear train. Deleting it removes the dog ring, coil, driver, harness and their tests. Baseline: the tri-motor BEV (4% of fleet) has a twin-motor rear unit, but still carries a rear dog clutch with coil, driver and lead, inherited from the dual-motor gear train. Proposal: delete it. In lock mode both rear inverters follow one common wheel-speed command, a virtual lock: each wheel is held at the same speed, so an unloaded wheel cannot flare and the loaded one gets the torque it can use. The front mechanical lock stays, because a single front machine drives through an open differential. Why it works: a virtual lock only has to supply the grip of each wheel on its own. Worst case, one rear wheel airborne and weight thrown diagonally onto the other: 1,100 kg × 9.81 × µ 0.9 × 0.40 m ≈ 3,880 Nm; a 380 Nm machine through 11.5:1 delivers 4,370 Nm, 13% above it. An inverter fault means lost drive on that wheel, not a lost fail-safe: friction brakes and steering are untouched. Benchmark: the Tesla Cybertruck gives the dual-motor truck front and rear lockers, while the tri-motor Cyberbeast pairs a front mechanical lock with a virtual rear lock from its two rear motors.

title: Locker function test runs on the ESC roller dyno with a split-speed routine
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Avoids a dedicated locker end-of-line station (lift, hand rotation of wheels, operator check) for the new line and cuts 2.5 minutes of labour per pack car. The existing roller dyno that already tests brakes and ESC runs left and right rollers at different speeds to prove each locker. Baseline: every off-road pack car (30% of fleet) goes to a separate locker station: the car is lifted, an operator rotates one wheel with a hand-held drive while the locker is commanded, and engagement is confirmed by sensor and feel, about 2.5 minutes per car. A new station for the platform line costs about €1.4M. Proposal: add a split-speed routine to the roller dyno that already tests brakes, ABS and ESC. With the axle in lock mode the left roller is driven at 3 km/h and the right roller is braked; a locked axle passes more than 300 Nm across, an open axle only friction (about 30 Nm). The test takes about 40 s per axle and the result is stored with the VIN. Why it works: the roller dyno already has independent left and right motors and torque measurement for brake tests, so the only addition is a torque transducer upgrade and software. Benchmark: Tesla Cybertruck mechanical lockers were fitted at the factory and only enabled later by an OTA update, which shows the locker command path is fully electronic and can be exercised by a test routine.

title: Two-tier off-road pack: brake-based traction standard, rear e-locker only in Extreme tier
description: [MHEV] Splits the MHEV off-road pack into Trail and Extreme tiers. Trail cars use the ESC to brake a spinning rear wheel (brake-based cross-axle traction) instead of a rear e-locker; Extreme keeps the locker. The rear locker, its driver and harness are deleted on two-thirds of pack cars. Baseline: every MHEV off-road pack car (18% of fleet) has a rear e-locker. Proposal: Trail tier (12% of fleet) uses brake-based cross-axle traction plus the centre lock; Extreme tier (6%) keeps the rear e-locker. Why it works: to move torque across an open rear diff, the spinning wheel must be braked with a torque equal to what the grounded wheel uses. Rear caliper check: 12 MPa × 1,590 mm² piston × µ 0.40 × 2 faces × 0.14 m effective radius ≈ 2,140 Nm per wheel, enough to pass about 2,100 Nm to the grounded wheel. Heat check for a 30 s brake-held climb at 5 km/h: 2,000 Nm × 3.5 rad/s ≈ 7 kW, × 30 s = 210 kJ; on a 7.5 kg disc that is 210,000 / (7.5 × 460) ≈ 61 K. A true locker still wins on long rock sections, which is why Extreme keeps it. This is a declared capability split, not a hidden downgrade. Benchmark: the 2024 Land Rover Defender X lists braking-based torque vectoring alongside an electronic active differential, which shows brake-based traction is used alongside a mechanical device in this segment, not instead of one.

title: MHEV e-locker coils wound for 48 V; 12 V relay and heavy feed deleted
description: [MHEV] Rewinds the e-locker coils for 48 V so the same ampere-turns need one quarter of the current. The 15 A relay in the rear junction box disappears, the feed drops from 1.0 to 0.35 mm², and the connector shrinks to a 0.64 mm terminal system. Baseline: MHEV rear and front e-lockers (rear on all MHEV pack cars, front on 60% of them) use 12 V coils drawing 4.5 A inrush and 2.5 A hold, switched by a 15 A relay in the rear junction box through about 12 m of 1.0 mm² feed and return. Proposal: wind each coil with four times the turns of 0.28 mm wire, giving the same 1,100 ampere-turns and the same copper mass, fed at 48 V from a smart high-side switch in the existing 48 V distribution module. Inrush falls to 1.1 A and the feed becomes 0.35 mm². Why it works: magnetic pull depends on ampere-turns, not voltage, so engagement force (about 600 N) is unchanged. Voltage drop check: 12 m × 0.052 Ω/m × 1.1 A ≈ 0.7 V, 1.4% of 48 V, against about 1.0 V (8%) of 12 V on the old 1.0 mm² feed at inrush (12 m × 0.019 Ω/m × 4.5 A). Benchmark: Ineos Grenadier front and rear lockers are electronically actuated with mechanical engagement and automatically disengage at 75 km/h, which is the same solenoid-on-dog principle we keep.

title: Pneumatic locker piston fed from the air-suspension reservoir replaces solenoid actuator
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Every off-road pack car already has an air-suspension compressor and a 16-18 bar reservoir. A small single-acting piston engages the locker dog instead of a copper coil and steel can. One extra port on the existing valve block and a 4 mm air line replace the coil, its driver and its feed. Baseline: each e-locker (0.49 per fleet vehicle across MHEV and BEV pack cars) has an electromagnetic actuator: copper coil, steel can and armature, 0.65 kg and about €38, plus a coil driver. Proposal: a Ø30 mm single-acting piston cast into the diff cover pushes the dog ring through a fork. Supply comes from the air-suspension reservoir through a pressure-reducing 3/2 port added to the existing valve block, at 10 bar regulated. A return spring disengages the dog when air is vented. Why it works: force = 10 bar × 707 mm² ≈ 707 N, above the 600 N needed. Air use per engagement = 7 cm³ swept × 10 bar ≈ 70 cm³ free air, trivial against a 30 litre reservoir. Loss of air leaves the locker open, which is the safe state, and nothing in braking or steering depends on it. Wading: the line is sealed and vents at the valve block, above the 900 mm wading line. Benchmark: Ineos Grenadier lockers are electronically actuated with mechanical engagement; we keep the mechanical dog but actuate it with air already on the car.

title: Locker coil potted inside the axle oil; external can, boot and pushrod seal deleted
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Moves the locker coil inside the differential housing so the magnetic field acts directly on the armature. The steel coil can, the dynamic pushrod seal, the boot and their machining go; a single static hermetic feedthrough carries the two pins through the wall. Baseline: the e-locker coil sits outside the housing in a pressed steel can with an O-ring, and drives the dog through a sliding pushrod with a lip seal and a rubber boot. That dynamic seal is the main wading leak path. Proposal: the coil is potted in class H epoxy and mounted on the bearing-cap side inside the oil space, directly facing the armature. A glass-to-metal sealed 2-pin feedthrough in the housing wall replaces the pushrod, seal and boot. Why it works: the feedthrough is static, so it does not wear. Wading head at 900 mm: ρgh = 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.9 ≈ 8.8 kPa (0.09 bar), against a feedthrough rated to several bar; a hot axle quenched in cold water with a blocked breather can pull roughly 20-30 kPa of vacuum, still far inside a static hermetic seal's rating. Thermal check: axle oil peaks near 130 °C, raising coil resistance by about 1.4×, so hold current falls by the same factor; the coil keeps 30% force margin at that temperature. Benchmark: the Lexus GX 550 Overtrail has a driver-selectable electronic locking rear differential; we keep that function and move the coil into the oil.

title: BEV e-locker drivers moved onto EDU inverter control boards; standalone locker ECU deleted
description: [800V BEV] Deletes the standalone locker control module, its bracket, CAN node and harness on BEV pack cars. The coil driver becomes a €5.5 output stage on the inverter control board that already sits on each EDU with 12 V, CAN and a spare connector cavity. Baseline: BEV dual-motor pack cars (6% of fleet) have front and rear e-lockers; tri-motor cars (4%) have a front e-locker. Both use a standalone locker control module (€38) on a bracket, with its own CAN node and about 3 m of harness to each axle. Proposal: each EDU inverter control board gets a half-bridge coil driver with current sense and a two-pin output in its existing low-voltage connector. The locker task runs in its own partition of the inverter MCU with an ASIL B engagement guard (unintended front lock at speed is a steering hazard), separate from the ASIL-D torque path. Why it works: the coil needs 4 A for 50 ms then 1.5 A hold, about 18 W at 12 V; the driver dissipates roughly 0.3 W on a board that already handles kilowatt-class gate drives. The coil lead from the inverter to the locker is under 0.5 m because both sit on the same drive unit. Benchmark: Tesla Cybertruck lockers are selected from the off-road screen and were enabled by OTA, showing the locker is a function of the propulsion domain rather than a separate box.

title: Rear disc upgrade for brake-based traction deleted after measured thermal sizing
description: [MHEV] The MHEV off-road pack has its own larger rear disc and caliper, specified to soak up heat from brake-based traction. Thermal sizing shows the road rear brake, which is already rated for the heaviest platform GVW, carries the traction duty. Deleting the pack variant saves the larger parts and a part-number family. Baseline: MHEV pack cars (18% of fleet) use a 365 × 28 mm ventilated rear disc and a larger single-piston caliper instead of the road 345 × 20 mm set, a choice made only for brake-based traction heat. Proposal: carry the road rear brake over; it is already validated to UN R13-H at the 3,300 kg platform maximum, above every pack variant. Why it works: the sizing case is a long rock crawl, not a single event. Over 10 minutes at 25% traction duty the average heat is about 1.75 kW per rear disc. At crawl speed the disc sheds roughly 10 W/K, so it settles near 200 K above ambient, about 230-250 °C, well below the 550 °C fade onset of the pad compound and below the 400 °C limit set for the validation. Hill descent is carried mainly by the front brakes and engine braking in low range, and the road rear brake already passes the descent test at maximum GVW. Friction braking capacity does not fall, because road and pack cars share one GVW rating. Benchmark: the 2024 Land Rover Defender X lists braking-based torque vectoring, showing brake-based traction is routine duty in this segment.

title: BEV locker diff case in ADI EN-GJS-1050-6 replaces carburised 20MnCr5 forging
description: [800V BEV] The EDU locker diff case is a carburised 20MnCr5 forging because of the dog face. Austempered ductile iron gives 1,050 MPa tensile strength and good wear in a near-net casting, deleting the forging, carburising and most of the hard turning. Baseline: BEV e-lockers (dual-motor pack front and rear, tri-motor front, 0.16 lockers per fleet vehicle) use a diff case forged from 20MnCr5, rough machined, carburised to 58 HRC on the dog face and hard turned, about €46. Proposal: cast the case in EN-GJS-1050-6 ADI with the dog teeth cast near-net, austemper at 360 °C to about 32 HRC and 1,050 MPa, then induction-harden the dog face to about 50 HRC and finish-machine bearing seats only. Why it works: case torque check: rear motor 450 Nm × 11.5 ratio ≈ 5,175 Nm through the case. Twelve dog teeth on a 55 mm mean radius carry 5,175 / 0.055 ≈ 94 kN, about 7.8 kN per tooth; on a 6 × 12 mm tooth root that is about 110 MPa shear; even if pitch error leaves only four teeth carrying, about 330 MPa, still under the roughly 600 MPa shear strength of ADI. Flank contact pressure and engagement impact govern and are covered by the wear test. ADI also work-hardens at contact faces, which suits a dog clutch that engages at low slip. Benchmark: Tesla Cybertruck has mechanical lockers inside its drive units, enabled by software, showing lockers in a BEV drive unit carry full motor torque.

title: One wave spring replaces six coil return springs and retainer in the e-locker
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Six coil springs sit in six drilled pockets in the dog ring and are held by a stamped retainer. One multi-turn wave spring gives the same preload in less axial space, deleting the pocket drilling, the retainer and five parts. Baseline: each e-locker (0.49 per fleet vehicle) returns its dog ring with six Ø1.2 mm wire coil springs (EN 10270-1 SH) in six drilled pockets, held by a stamped DC04 retainer; the operator fits the springs by hand in about 45 s. Proposal: one crest-to-crest wave spring in 51CrV4 sits on a turned shoulder and gives 180-220 N over the 4 mm engagement stroke. Why it works: the release force has to overcome friction on the dog flanks when torque reverses. With a 3° back-taper on the dog flanks and µ 0.1, the residual friction after torque reversal is under 120 N, so 200 N releases cleanly. A wave spring gives a flat load over the stroke and uses about half the axial space of coil springs of the same load. Benchmark: the Jeep Wrangler Rubicon has Tru-Lok electric front and rear lockers, the reference for selectable mechanical dog lockers in the segment.

title: Locker armature in sintered Fe-0.45P replaces machined leaded free-cutting steel ring
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The armature ring is turned and ground from leaded 11SMnPb30 bar, which is costly and relies on an ELV lead exemption. A pressed-and-sintered Fe-0.45P ring comes off the press at net shape, with only a sizing step, and contains no lead. Baseline: each e-locker armature (0.49 per fleet vehicle) is turned and ground from 11SMnPb30 bar, 0.18 kg, about €4.8, with roughly 40% of the bar lost as chips. Proposal: a soft-magnetic Fe-0.45P powder-metal ring compacted to 7.1 g/cm³, sintered at 1,120 °C and sized to ±0.02 mm on the faces, about €2.3. Why it works: the armature only needs a good magnetic path and a flat face. Fe-0.45P at 7.1 g/cm³ saturates near 1.5 T against about 1.6 T for the steel. At 1,100 ampere-turns the working flux density in the ring is about 1.1 T, below saturation of both, so pull force changes by under 3%. Phosphorus also lowers coercivity, which helps the armature release quickly. Removing the leaded steel takes the part off the ELV Annex II exemption list. Benchmark: Ineos Grenadier lockers are electronically actuated with mechanical engagement, the same armature-on-dog principle we keep.

title: Locking side gear forged with net-form dog teeth; dog-face milling deleted
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The locking side gear already has net-forged bevel teeth, but its dog face is milled afterwards. Forging the dog teeth in the same die deletes a 4.5-minute milling operation and its cutters; the forging die costs slightly more per part. Baseline: in each e-locker (0.49 per fleet vehicle) the side gear that meshes with the dog ring is precision-forged in 16MnCr5 with net bevel teeth, then has its 12-tooth dog face milled in a second setup (about 4.5 minutes, €5.4 with cutter wear) before carburising. Proposal: add the dog teeth to the precision-forging die so that both tooth forms come out at net shape, with 0.1 mm stock on the dog flanks removed by the existing hard-turning pass. Why it works: dog teeth are short, axial and open, which forges well, unlike deep internal forms. Load check: at the rear-axle grip limit of about 5,650 Nm (ring-gear side, not the 1,515 Nm pinion torque) on a 50 mm mean radius, 12 teeth carry about 9.4 kN each; on a 5 × 10 mm root that is about 190 MPa shear, still well within carburised 16MnCr5, so forged-in teeth with the grain flow following the profile are stronger than milled ones. Carburising is unchanged. Benchmark: Jeep Wrangler Rubicon uses Tru-Lok electric front and rear lockers, a high-volume reference for selectable dog lockers in the side-gear position.

title: Insulation-displacement terminals in a PPS-GF40 coil bobbin replace soldered flying leads
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The locker coil ends are hand-soldered to flying leads with heat-shrink, about 1.2 minutes per coil and a known source of vibration failures. Two insulation-displacement terminals moulded into the bobbin take the wire ends during automatic winding and become the connector pins. Baseline: each e-locker coil (0.49 per fleet vehicle) is wound on a PA66 bobbin, then an operator solders the two wire ends to stranded flying leads, slides heat-shrink and dresses them into the can, about 1.2 minutes. Solder joints on 0.4-0.55 mm wire crack under axle vibration. Proposal: a PPS-GF40 bobbin with two moulded slots holding CuSn6 IDC terminals. The winding machine lays each wire end into its slot and presses the terminal, which cuts the enamel and makes a gas-tight joint; the terminal tails become the pins of the coil connector. Why it works: IDC joints are standard on motor and relay coils and remove heat input and flux. Vibration check: an axle-mounted coil sees about 30 g random vibration (ISO 16750-3 test IV); the IDC joint has no stiff solder fillet to crack, and the wire is strain-relieved by the slot. PPS keeps strength at 130 °C axle oil where PA66 absorbs oil and softens. Benchmark: Lexus GX 550 Overtrail has a driver-selectable electronic rear locker; we keep that function and change only the coil termination.

title: Single PTFE-lip combined seal on the e-locker pushrod replaces O-ring and shaft-seal pair
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Where the externally mounted coil and pushrod are kept, the pushrod is sealed by an O-ring and a separate radial lip seal, with two grooves to machine. One combined seal with a PTFE dynamic lip and an FKM static outer body seals both the bore and the rod in one part and one counterbore. Baseline: e-lockers with external coils (0.49 per fleet vehicle, where the wet-coil option is not adopted) seal the reciprocating pushrod with an NBR O-ring in an internal groove plus a separate radial lip seal pressed into a counterbore. Two grooves are machined and two parts fitted. Proposal: one combined seal: an FKM-coated steel case presses into a single counterbore and seals the static bore; a PTFE compound lip with an excluder seals the 6 mm rod. Why it works: the rod moves 4 mm at low frequency, which suits PTFE's low friction and dry-running ability. Wading check: at 900 mm wading the head is ρgh = 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.9 ≈ 8.8 kPa; the PTFE lip is rated to 0.5 bar (50 kPa), and the excluder lip keeps mud off the sealing edge. FKM tolerates 150 °C hypoid oil better than NBR. This idea is an alternative to the wet-coil concept and applies only if the coil stays outside. Benchmark: Jeep Wrangler Rubicon carries Tru-Lok electric front and rear lockers on axles that must survive water crossings, the reference for sealed selectable lockers.

title: Transfer case shares the gearbox ATF sump; own fluid, pump and seals deleted
description: [MHEV] Opens the transfer case to the gearbox rear extension so both run on the gearbox ATF. The transfer-case fluid, gerotor pump, two interface lip seals, its breather, fill and drain plugs and a separate end-of-line fill step are deleted; a cast gallery and return pipe are added. Baseline: every MHEV (60% of fleet) bolts a transfer box to the 8-speed automatic. The box has its own 1.3 litre fluid, a gerotor pump, two lip seals at the joint between gearbox output and box input, its own breather, fill and drain plugs, and its own fill station. Proposal: one common sump. The gearbox pump feeds a 4 mm cast gallery that sprays the chain, the planetary and the coupling; oil drains back by gravity through a screened port, and one breather vents both. Why it works: heat check: losses in the box are about 1.5% of 150 kW, about 2.25 kW at full load, which the gearbox cooler absorbs inside its 8 kW margin. Low-ratio lubrication check: in low the planets turn slowly under high load, a boundary-film case; grip-limited input is about 1,165 Nm (11,300 Nm at the wheels ÷ 3.73 ÷ 2.6), and low is used for under 1% of distance, so ATF with anti-wear additives reaches the planet-pin life with surface-hardened pins. Benchmark: the 2025 Mercedes G 550 uses a two-speed box at 1.00:1 and 2.93:1 with a 40:60 split; sharing the gearbox fluid is used in some integrated hybrid and AWD transmissions, though the benchmark G 550 case keeps its own fluid.

Validate gearbox shift quality with shared oil, clutch friction stability, low-range planet pin wear, thermal soak in a 45-minute low-range crawl, and wading at 900 mm (one breather above the line).

title: Low-range and transfer checks run on the gearbox hot-test dyno; separate rig deleted
description: [MHEV] Avoids a dedicated transfer-case end-of-line rig (NVH, range shift, clutch and leak test) by mating the transfer case to the gearbox before the gearbox hot test. One combined run adds about 45 s; the supplier keeps only a leak test. Baseline: every transfer case (60% of fleet) is tested on its own rig at the supplier: input motor, two output absorbers, NVH microphones, range shift and clutch map, about 2.5 minutes, on a rig costing about €2.5M. The gearbox is then hot-tested separately. Proposal: mate the transfer case to the gearbox first and run one extended hot test: the gearbox dyno gains a second output absorber for the front output and a 45 s sequence for range shift, centre-clutch torque map and transfer NVH. Why it works: the gearbox dyno already has an input motor, rear absorber, NVH sensing and gearbox control; only the front-output absorber is added. Torque check: testing low range at full input is not needed; a 300 Nm input check in low range (about 780 Nm at the transfer output) proves the gearset and the shift. Benchmark: Ford Bronco offers two transfer cases on one model, a part-time case with 2.72:1 low and a full-time Advanced 4x4 case with 3.06:1, showing how many driveline variants a test plant must cover; one combined test handles every variant on one machine.

title: Flat-tow neutral deleted from the two-speed transfer case; two-position range fork
description: [MHEV] The two-speed case carries a neutral position so the car can be flat-towed behind a motorhome, a mainly North American use. Deleting it shortens the fork travel, removes the neutral detent, the neutral state logic and interlocks, and a full flat-tow validation campaign. Baseline: the MHEV two-speed case (18% of fleet) has High, Neutral and Low, with a neutral detent, a longer range fork travel (about 18 mm), a neutral interlock that needs brake pressed and gearbox in N, a parking interlock (with range in neutral the gearbox park pawl no longer holds the wheels, so the EPB must be forced on), and a flat-tow validation (lubrication of an unpowered gearbox and case over 500 km at 100 km/h). Proposal: a two-position range fork, High and Low, with about 12 mm travel. Recovery towing over short distances stays possible with the gearbox in N and the case in High, as for every road AWD car; long-distance transport is on a flatbed. Why it works: neutral is a convenience function, not an off-road capability: it does not change crawl ratio (low range 2.6 × 1st 5.0 × final drive 3.73 ≈ 48.5:1), articulation or recovery. Removing it also removes a parking risk: in neutral, a car on a 30% slope (3,200 kg × 9.81 × sin 16.7° ≈ 9 kN) depends on the EPB alone. Benchmark: Ineos Grenadier keeps a manually operated two-speed Tremec case with a 2.5:1 low range, the kind of case where neutral is a lever position; ours is an electric shift that need not carry it.

title: Traction-limited duty cycle replaces continuous-rating spec; low-range planets narrowed
description: [MHEV] The low-range planetary was rated for 100 hours at full gearbox output torque, a figure the tyres can never transmit in low range. Rating it to the traction-limited torque plus a measured shock factor narrows the planets and ring gear, cutting steel and machining. Baseline: the low-range planetary (MHEV pack, 18% of fleet) is rated for 100 h at 2,500 Nm input, the gearbox first-gear output (500 Nm × 5.0), copied from a pickup specification. Proposal: rate it to what the tyres can transmit. Traction limit: 3,200 kg × 9.81 × µ 0.9 × 0.40 m ≈ 11,300 Nm at the wheels, ÷ 3.73 final drive ≈ 3,030 Nm at the transfer output, ÷ 2.6 low-range ratio ≈ 1,165 Nm at the input. The rating becomes 1,200 Nm for a measured customer spectrum (low range under 1% of distance), with a 2.2× static shock factor for rock drops and wheel-hop, which is above the shock peaks measured on comparable vehicles. Planet face width falls from 22 to 17 mm and the ring gear section thins by 2 mm. Why it works: in low range the engine torque is capped by traction control and the gearbox before it can exceed tyre grip; designing beyond the grip limit only adds steel. Benchmark: Jeep Wrangler Rubicon uses a 4.0:1 Rock-Trac low range, far deeper than ours, which illustrates low-range duty; the grip-limited rating rests on the traction calculation above, not on the benchmark.

title: Active-clutch full-time transfer case with low range replaces planetary centre differential
description: [MHEV] Deletes the planetary centre differential (sun, planets, carrier and pins) from every MHEV transfer box. An electronically controlled wet coupling, commanded by the driveline controller, sets the front share from zero to half and closes fully off road, as on-demand AWD systems do. Baseline: each MHEV (60% of fleet) has a full-time transfer box with a planetary centre differential splitting 40:60, plus a bias pack. Proposal: an on-demand architecture. The rear output becomes a straight-through shaft; the front output is fed through an electronically controlled wet coupling that sets the front share anywhere from zero to half, using wheel-slip, steering-angle and terrain-mode inputs, and closes completely for off-road. Low range stays as an input reduction on pack cars. Why it works: high-volume on-demand AWD already runs this way on road. Heat check: at 120 km/h with a 20% front share (about 7-8 kW of a 35-40 kW road load), 1% controlled slip wastes about 75 W, which the oil carries easily. Tight turns: on full steering lock the front wheels travel about 3% further than the rears, so the coupling is opened below a steering-angle threshold to avoid binding. If power is lost the coupling opens and the car is rear-driven, which is safe. This is an alternative to keeping the planetary and clamping its bias pack. Benchmark: the Ford Bronco sells a part-time two-speed case (2.72:1) and a full-time Advanced 4x4 case (3.06:1); one coupling-based box gives full-time drive and a fixed split from one design.

title: One three-position shift drum selects BEV rear drive-unit ratio and lock: high, low, locked
description: [800V BEV] Where the BEV dual-motor off-road pack carries a two-ratio rear drive unit, it also carries a separate e-locker solenoid. Cutting a second cam track into the ratio-shift drum lets the existing shift motor engage the locker too, deleting the solenoid, its driver and its harness. Baseline: BEV dual-motor pack cars (6% of fleet) with a two-ratio rear drive unit have a ratio-shift actuator (BLDC motor, worm and position sensor, €42) plus a separate rear e-locker solenoid (€38) with its own driver and lead. Proposal: one shift drum with two cam tracks, turned through 270° by the existing shift motor. Its three stops are High-open, Low-open and Low-locked. Locking in the high ratio is dropped: on sand and snow at speed, motor torque control and the ESC manage wheel slip, and lockers are normally released above about 40 km/h anyway. Why it works: the drum needs about 15 W for 0.4 s, and a lock change is one more 90° step. Force check: the dog needs about 600 N to engage; a 12° helix track on a 40 mm drum radius, driven by the 1.2 Nm motor through a 30:1 worm (about 36 Nm ideal, about 16 Nm at a typical 45% worm efficiency), gives about 400 N at the track, which the 12° track converts to well over the 600 N axial force needed. Benchmark: the Mercedes G 580 with EQ Technology selects its reduction ratio and its virtual diff locks with one set of dash buttons, treating ratio and locking as one off-road control set; we merge them in hardware too.

title: External transfer-case oil cooler deleted; finned housing sized to a 45-minute low-range crawl
description: [MHEV] The off-road pack transfer case has an oil-to-air cooler, two hoses and brackets for long low-range crawls and towing. A heat balance shows the finned housing, a higher permitted oil temperature and conduction into the gearbox remove the same heat, so the cooler loop is deleted. Baseline: the two-speed case on MHEV pack cars (18% of fleet) has an external plate-fin cooler, two EPDM hoses and brackets (€38). Proposal: delete the cooler; add 6 mm cast fins (+0.35 m² exposed area) and allow the sump to run to 120 °C in low range. Why it works: heat input: crawling in low range at 8 km/h with 8 kN tractive effort needs 8,000 × 2.2 m/s ≈ 17.8 kW; transfer losses at 3% are about 530 W. Heat out at 120 °C sump with 35 °C ambient (ΔT 85 K): fins 0.35 m² × 15 W/m²K × 85 ≈ 450 W, radiation about 90 W and conduction into the gearbox about 150 W, total about 690 W, above the 530 W input. Towing is done in high range where losses are about 1.5%. Hot-climate low-speed towing is the sizing case and is checked on the rig. Benchmark: Ineos Grenadier uses a 2.5:1 Tremec two-speed case designed for sustained low-range work; our case is checked against the same crawl duty.

title: Low-range planetary in profile-modified spur gears; helical thrust washers and bearing deleted
description: [MHEV] Planets turn only in low range, below about 40 km/h. Spur gears there remove the axial thrust, so four planet thrust washers and the carrier thrust bearing are deleted, and the internal ring gear can be broached instead of skived. Baseline: the low-range planetary in the MHEV two-speed case (18% of fleet) uses helical gears, four planet thrust washers and a carrier thrust bearing to take the axial load. The internal ring is skived. Proposal: spur gears with high contact ratio (εα about 2.0 from a longer addendum and a 17.5° pressure angle), tip relief and crowning. The ring gear is broached. Why it works: in high range the planetary is locked and turns as one block, so the planets do not spin relative to the carrier; they only mesh in low range, which is used below about 40 km/h for under 1% of distance. Noise check: at 30 km/h in low range the planet mesh frequency is about 600 Hz, at low road and tyre noise, so a contact ratio near 2 with tip relief keeps transmission error within about 1.5 µm, close to helical levels. Spur gears have no axial mesh component, so the four thrust washers and the carrier thrust bearing are replaced by hardened, ground carrier cheek faces that only see residual side float. Benchmark: Ineos Grenadier's 2.5:1 Tremec two-speed case shows that low range is a low-speed, high-torque mode, the case where spur planetary gears are normal practice.

ideaData.title: Low-range planetary in profile-modified spur gears; helical thrust washers and bearing deleted
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: the low-range planetary in the MHEV two-speed case (18% of fleet) uses helical gears, four planet thrust washers and a carrier thrust bearing to take the axial load. The internal ring is skived. Proposal: spur gears with high contact ratio (εα about 2.0 from a longer addendum and a 17.5° pressure angle), tip relief and crowning. The ring gear is broached. Why it works: in high range the planetary is locked and turns as one block, so the planets do not spin relative to the carrier; they only mesh in low range, which is used below about 40 km/h for under 1% of distance. Noise check: at 30 km/h in low range the planet mesh frequency is about 600 Hz, at low road and tyre noise, so a contact ratio near 2 with tip relief keeps transmission error within about 1.5 µm, close to helical levels. Spur gears have no axial mesh component, so the four thrust washers and the carrier thrust bearing are replaced by hardened, ground carrier cheek faces that only see residual side float. Benchmark: Ineos Grenadier's 2.5:1 Tremec two-speed case shows that low range is a low-speed, high-torque mode, the case where spur planetary gears are normal practice.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Planets turn only in low range, below about 40 km/h. Spur gears there remove the axial thrust, so four planet thrust washers and the carrier thrust bearing are deleted, and the internal ring gear can be broached instead of skived.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Ring gear moves from power skiving to a broaching machine (shorter cycle). Planet hobbing time falls. Assembly loses the thrust-washer and thrust-bearing fits. NVH end-of-line check runs in low range on the existing rig.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Planets become symmetric, so they cannot be fitted reversed. Fewer parts in the carrier stack shortens the case and removes a bearing preload setting. Spur planets can be loaded from either side, simplifying the carrier fixture.

MHEV pack 18% of fleet. Per case: thrust washers and carrier thrust bearing €6, spur hobbing saving €5, broached instead of skived ring €7 = €18. €18 × 18% = €3.2 fleet average. Low €2.8, high €3.6. Net €2.8-€3.6 per vehicle × 50,000 vehicles/yr = €140K-€180K per year (engineering estimate; tooling amortised over 7 years = 350,000 vehicles where stated).

title: Transfer-case actuator moved to 48 V BLDC with on-board driver; 12 V relay deleted
description: [MHEV] The transfer-case actuator draws up to 25 A at 12 V through a 2.5 mm² feed, with a separate position sensor and an H-bridge in the transfer-case control module. A 48 V BLDC with its own driver and encoder needs one quarter of the current, uses its rotor position for the actuator position and is controlled over LIN. Baseline: every MHEV transfer case (60% of fleet) has a 12 V brushed DC actuator for the clutch ball-ramp (and the range fork on two-speed cases), stalling at 25 A, with a separate Hall position sensor and a 30 A H-bridge in the transfer-case control module, fed by 2.5 mm² cable. Proposal: a 48 V BLDC actuator with integrated FET driver and magnetic encoder, fed from the MHEV 48 V rail with 0.75 mm² cable and commanded over LIN by the driveline controller. Why it works: power is the same (about 300 W peak), so current falls from 25 A to about 6.3 A. Position: the encoder counts rotor turns through the worm, giving better than 0.1° at the ball-ramp, so the separate sensor goes. Response: BLDC torque at stall is higher, cutting clutch apply time from about 150 to 100 ms. The fail state is unchanged: the ball-ramp spring opens the clutch on power loss, so the car becomes rear-drive. Benchmark: Ford Bronco offers both part-time and full-time Advanced 4x4 transfer cases, both electronically shifted, showing the actuator is common content across case types.

title: Twin-rear-motor BEV: one shift drum and cross-shaft drive both rear two-speed gearboxes
description: [800V BEV] On the tri-motor trim each rear motor has its own two-speed gearbox and its own range actuator. One actuator turning a cross-shaft shifts both gearboxes together, deleting an actuator, sensor and harness branch and making a left-right range mismatch physically impossible. Baseline: the tri-motor BEV (4% of fleet) has a twin-motor rear unit with a two-speed gearbox per motor, each with its own range actuator (BLDC, worm, sensor, €42). Proposal: one actuator mounted on the centre web of the twin-motor housing turns a 12 mm 42CrMo4 cross-shaft carrying both shift drums, so both gearboxes shift together. Why it works: shifting is done at standstill or below 5 km/h with motor speed matching, so the drums need only about 1 Nm each; one 2 Nm actuator drives both. Safety check: if one side were in low and the other in high, wheel torques would differ by the ratio step (about 2.5×), giving, for a 2,500 Nm wheel-torque difference, 2,500 / 0.40 ≈ 6.3 kN at the contact patch and a yaw moment of about 6.3 kN × 0.83 m half-track ≈ 5,200 Nm on a split command. A shared shaft removes that failure mode mechanically instead of relying on software plausibility. Benchmark: the Mercedes G 580 gives each of its four motors its own two-speed gearbox, which multiplies range actuators; we drive two gearboxes from one actuator.

title: Transfer-case gerotor pump replaced by chain-fed catch tray and cast oil gallery
description: [MHEV] The transfer-case gerotor pump and its machined pocket are replaced by a moulded tray above the chain that catches the oil the chain throws and feeds it by gravity through a cast gallery to the clutch and bearings. This is the alternative for programmes that keep a separate transfer-case sump. Baseline: every MHEV transfer case (60% of fleet) has a gerotor pump on the input shaft (€9), a machined pump pocket and a pick-up pipe to feed the clutch pack and bearings. Proposal: a PA66-GF30 catch tray above the front-output chain catches thrown oil; a cast gallery feeds the clutch hub and bearings by gravity. Why it works: flow check: at 50 km/h the chain runs at about 9 m/s and throws roughly 1-2 l/min, while the clutch and bearings need about 0.5 l/min in on-demand mode. At standstill crawl in low range the chain is slow, but the clutch is either locked (no slip heat) or open, and the planetary dips in the sump. Gradient check: the tray and sump are shaped to keep the clutch hub fed at 45% fore-aft and 35° side slope, the off-road attitude targets. This is the alternative to the shared-sump idea; only one would be adopted. Benchmark: the 2025 Mercedes G 550 two-speed transfer case (1.00:1 / 2.93:1, 40:60 split) shows the segment case architecture; splash-and-tray lubrication without a pump is general practice in on-demand transfer cases.

title: Transfer-case chain sprockets in sinter-hardened Fe-Cr-Mo powder metal replace machined forgings
description: [MHEV] Both chain sprockets are forged, turned, hobbed and carburised. Sinter-hardened chromium-molybdenum powder metal at 7.3 g/cm³, with surface rolling of the tooth flanks, comes off the press at net shape and hardens in the sinter cooling zone, deleting forging, hobbing and carburising. Baseline: the transfer-case drive and driven sprockets (every MHEV, 60% of fleet) are 16MnCr5 forgings, turned, hobbed and carburised, about €14 each. Proposal: press Fe-3Cr-0.5Mo-0.6C powder to 7.3 g/cm³, sinter-harden (fast cooling in the sinter furnace gives a martensitic structure, about 40 HRC core), then surface-roll the tooth flanks to full density 0.3 mm deep. Why it works: chain load check: the front output carries at most the front-axle traction torque, 5,300 Nm ÷ 3.73 ≈ 1,420 Nm; on a 60 mm pitch radius the chain tension is about 23.7 kN shared by about six engaged teeth, around 4 kN per tooth. The rolled flank raises contact fatigue strength close to wrought steel, and the bending root stress (about 450 MPa) is within the PM fatigue limit at 7.3 g/cm³ with rolling. Benchmark: Ford Bronco's Advanced 4x4 full-time case (3.06:1) shows chain-type front drives in this class; PM sprockets are general practice in transfer-case chains.

title: Low-range sun gear formed integral with the transfer-case input shaft
description: [MHEV] The low-range sun gear is a separate part splined to the input shaft and retained by a snap ring. Forging the sun teeth on the shaft removes two mating splines, the snap ring and its groove, and one assembly step. Baseline: in the MHEV two-speed case (18% of fleet) the sun gear is a separate 20MnCr5 part with an internal spline, pressed onto the externally splined input shaft and held with a snap ring. Both splines are broached or rolled and inspected. Proposal: an upset forging gives a shaft with an integral sun blank; the sun teeth are hobbed on the shaft and ground with it after carburising. Why it works: the sun runs at input speed and carries the input torque. Torque check: traction-limited input in low range about 1,165 Nm, 2.2× shock about 2,560 Nm; on a 35 mm sun pitch radius with four planets, each mesh carries about 18 kN at shock, which the existing tooth size already handles. Removing the spline joint removes a fretting site that sees reversing torque on rough ground. Benchmark: Jeep Wrangler Rubicon's 4.0:1 Rock-Trac two-speed case is the reference for high-ratio low range under rock-crawling shock loads, where spline fretting is a known wear mode.

title: One contactless 3D Hall sensor replaces three microswitches for range-fork position
description: [MHEV] Three sealed microswitches (high, mid-travel, low) each need a threaded port, seal and harness tail. One 3D Hall sensor reads a small magnet on the fork shaft and outputs the exact fork position over SENT, giving the three states plus fork wear and half-shift detection. Baseline: the MHEV two-speed case (18% of fleet) has three sealed microswitches in threaded ports, each with an O-ring and a harness tail, spliced into one connector (€14 total with machining). Proposal: one 3D Hall sensor in a single ported housing with one O-ring reads a Ø6 mm NdFeB magnet on the fork shaft and reports linear position over SENT. Why it works: fork travel is about 18 mm between high and low; a 3D Hall sensor resolves this to about 0.1 mm, so high, low and any half-engaged state are distinguished. Wading check: two of the three switch ports sit low on the housing and see 900 mm wading head ρgh ≈ 8.8 kPa; one higher-mounted port halves the low-mounted sealing points. The position signal is plausibility-checked against output-shaft speeds after every shift. Benchmark: Ineos Grenadier's 2.5:1 Tremec two-speed case is manually shifted, needing reliable range-position feedback to the controller, the job this sensor does.

title: Full-complement needle rollers replace caged needle bearings in the low-range planets
description: [MHEV] Planet bearings in a two-speed transfer case only turn in low range, at low speed and high load. Full-complement needles carry about 40% more load than a caged set in the same space and cost less, because the cage is deleted. Baseline: each of the four low-range planets in the MHEV two-speed case (18% of fleet) runs on a caged needle bearing (€3 each). Proposal: full-complement needles (about 22 × Ø3 mm per planet) with hardened spacer washers. Why it works: cages are needed at high speed to stop needles skewing and rubbing; here planets turn only in low range. Speed check: at 40 km/h in low range the planet spins at about 2,500 rpm relative to the carrier, a moderate speed for full complement with good lubrication, and most low-range running is below 15 km/h (under 1,000 rpm). Load check: at the 1,165 Nm traction-limited input, each planet pin carries about 17 kN (twice the 8.3 kN sun-mesh force); full complement raises the dynamic rating by about 40%, so L10 life at the spectrum rises too. In high range the planetary is locked and the needles do not turn. Benchmark: Jeep Wrangler Rubicon's 4.0:1 Rock-Trac low range is the reference for slow, high-load low-range duty, the case for full-complement planet bearings.

title: BEV rear EDU low-range dog sleeve in sinter-hardened powder metal replaces forged sleeve
description: [800V BEV] Where the BEV off-road variants carry a two-speed reduction, the dog sleeve that selects high or low is forged, turned, broached and carburised. A sinter-hardened powder-metal sleeve comes off the press with the internal spline and dog teeth at net shape. Baseline: the two-speed rear EDU (dual-motor pack, 6% of fleet, one sleeve) and the tri-motor twin-rear unit (4% of fleet, two sleeves) use 20MnCr5 dog sleeves: forged, turned, broached, carburised, about €15 each. Proposal: Fe-1.5Mo-2Cu-0.7C powder pressed to 7.2 g/cm³ and sinter-hardened, with the dog teeth and internal spline at net shape; only the fork groove is turned. About €8. Why it works: the sleeve shifts at standstill or with motor speed matching, so it sees low-slip engagement, not crash shifts. Load check: on the low-range intermediate shaft the torque is about 450 Nm × 3 ≈ 1,350 Nm; at a 40 mm mean radius with 18 teeth that is about 1.9 kN per tooth, and the root bending stress (about 300 MPa) is inside the PM fatigue limit at 7.2 g/cm³. Benchmark: the Mercedes G 580 gives each of its motors a two-speed gearbox, showing the dog-sleeve content a BEV low range adds; PM sleeves are general practice in manual and dual-clutch gearboxes.

title: Transfer-case output seals with integral V-ring excluder replaces seal plus dust shield
description: [MHEV] The transfer-case front and rear output seals each have a pressed steel dust shield on the companion flange to keep mud off the lip. A seal with an integral axial V-ring lip running on the flange face does the same job in one part and deletes the shield press-fit. Baseline: every MHEV transfer case (60% of fleet) has two output seals (front and rear), each a single radial lip seal plus a pressed steel dust shield on the companion flange, and an extra press-fit operation per flange. Proposal: an FKM dual-lip radial seal with a bonded axial V-ring lip that runs against a machined face on the flange; the dust shield is deleted. Why it works: the axial lip is the first barrier to mud and water spray, and the second radial lip excludes fines before the main lip. Wading check: at 900 mm wading the outputs are near 400 mm above ground, so the head is about 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.5 ≈ 4.9 kPa, well inside the seal rating; the risk case is a hot housing entering cold water, which pulls a vacuum, and the vent manifold limits that. FKM handles 150 °C oil where NBR hardens. Benchmark: the 2025 Mercedes G 550 two-speed transfer case (1.00:1 / 2.93:1) works in deep-water and mud duty, the duty these seals must cover.

title: Tank turn limited to loose surfaces and two rotations; road shafts carry over
description: [800V BEV] The quad-motor programme planned uprated half-shafts, extra inverter cooling and a large tyre validation for an unlimited tank turn on any surface. Limiting the feature to loose surfaces, low range and two rotations keeps every load within road hardware, as the benchmark does. Baseline: for the quad-motor trim (2% of fleet), the plan included CVJs uprated from size 33 to 36 on all four corners, a larger inverter coolant pump, and tyre-scrub validation for pivot turns on any surface, including high-grip rock. Proposal: enable the tank turn only when the friction estimate is below µ 0.5, in low-speed off-road mode, for at most two rotations, as G-Turn does. Why it works: in a pivot turn each tyre is dragged sideways, so the torque needed is set by grip. Loose surface: 0.5 × (3,200 kg × 9.81 / 4) × 0.40 m ≈ 1,570 Nm per wheel, well under the road CVJ rating (about 4,500 Nm). On rock at µ 0.9 it would be about 2,825 Nm with severe tyre scrub and shaft reversals, inside the static CVJ rating but with a full reversal at every pivot, the fatigue case that drove the upgrades. Heat: four wheels × 1,570 Nm × 0.5 rad/s ≈ 3.1 kW for 20 s per turn, trivial for the motors. Benchmark: the Mercedes G 580 G-Turn only works on a suitably loose surface and is deactivated after two full rotations.

title: Crab walk uses the road ±10° rear-steer actuator; no wide-angle unit for the pack
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The off-road pack planned a ±15° rear-steer actuator (longer stroke, bigger motor) plus larger rear arch liners for a wide crab angle. Running crab walk at the road actuator's ±10° keeps one actuator and one liner across the platform. Baseline: off-road pack cars (30% of fleet) were to get a ±15° rear-steer actuator (premium about €60 over the road ±10° unit) and enlarged rear wheel-arch liners and spats (about €8) for tyre clearance at full angle, so that crab walk could reach 15°. Proposal: crab walk uses the road ±10° actuator with front and rear wheels steered in phase. Why it works: at 10° in-phase steering the car moves sideways about 0.18 m per metre travelled (tan 10°), enough to step around a rock or a narrow-trail obstacle in a few metres. Clearance at 10° is already proven by the road car with off-road tyres. Load check: rear-steer rack force at crawl on loose ground is below the road parking-manoeuvre force the actuator is sized for. The rear actuator keeps its mechanical self-locking spindle, so if power is lost the rear wheels hold position and are centred at the next start; nothing depends on software to keep the car steerable. Benchmark: the GMC Hummer EV offers CrabWalk as a diagonal low-speed mode, and for 2026 added King Crab with a larger rear angle, showing the angle is an option, not a need.

title: Quad-motor trim uses four identical motor-inverter units at front and rear
description: [800V BEV] The quad-motor trim was planned with smaller front and larger rear corner units, so two motor designs, two inverter ratings and two calibrations at a volume of 1,000 cars a year. One 190 kW unit at every corner gives the same total power, doubles the per-part volume and deletes the second design's tooling and validation. Baseline: front corner units 160 kW and rear 220 kW, total 760 kW, each with its own stator stack, rotor, inverter power rating and calibration. Proposal: four identical 190 kW units (4 × 190 = 760 kW); the front-rear split is set by software. Why it works: rear traction check at launch with weight transfer: rear axle about 60% of 3,200 kg; per rear wheel 0.6 × 3,200 × 9.81 × µ 1.0 × 0.40 m / 2 ≈ 3,770 Nm. The 190 kW unit gives about 400 Nm × 10.9 ≈ 4,360 Nm at the wheel, a 16% margin. Front wheels can now deliver more torque than needed, useful for climbing where load moves rearward only partly. Crawl: four × 4,360 Nm ≈ 17,400 Nm at the wheels, 1.4 g of tractive force at GVW, beyond any grip. Benchmark: the Rivian Gen 2 Quad-Motor uses four separately controlled motors, one per wheel, showing four-corner drive is a production layout; we add the step of making all four corners identical.

title: Twin-motor drive units tested back to back, one motor loading the other
description: [800V BEV] A twin-motor unit has two independent outputs, so the planned end-of-line rig needed two 250 kW absorbing dynamometers. Coupling the two outputs with a rigid spool lets one motor drive and the other brake as a generator, so the test power circulates and the rig needs only a small supply for the losses. Baseline: tri-motor (4% of fleet, one twin-motor unit) and quad-motor cars (2%, two units) were planned with an end-of-line rig having two 250 kW absorbing dynamometers, a 500 kW regenerative grid supply and NVH sensing, about €1.6M. Proposal: a rigid spool couples the two output flanges of the twin-motor unit. Motor A runs in torque control and drives; motor B runs in speed control and regenerates, so power circulates through the shared DC bus and only losses are drawn from a 60 kW supply. A torque flange in the spool measures shaft torque; each motor is tested as driver and as load by swapping roles. Why it works: power check: at 2 × 380 Nm and 4,000 rpm the circulating power is about 160 kW, but losses at about 92% round-trip efficiency are only about 13 kW, inside a 60 kW supply. Tank turn and virtual lock need the two sides to hold equal and opposite torques, which this test proves directly. Benchmark: the Tesla Cybertruck Cyberbeast uses two rear motors to simulate a rear locker, the twin-motor-per-axle layout that makes back-to-back testing possible.

title: MHEV rear torque-vectoring clutches applied by two 48 V ball-ramp actuators, hydraulics deleted
description: [MHEV] The twin-clutch rear torque-vectoring unit on MHEV dynamic and off-road trims is applied by an electro-hydraulic power pack. Two 48 V ball-ramp actuators clamp the clutches directly, deleting the pump, accumulator, valve block, pressure sensor, filter and hydraulic fluid. Baseline: MHEV cars with the active rear drive module (15% of fleet) use a twin-coupling unit whose two wet packs are pressed by an electro-hydraulic power pack: a 12 V pump, accumulator, two proportional valves, pressure sensor and filter, about €120. Proposal: each pack is pressed by its own 48 V BLDC motor turning a ball-ramp, about €38 each. Why it works: force check: a pack needs about 20 kN for 1,000 Nm at the wheel; a 6° ramp on a 45 mm radius turns 1.5 Nm of motor torque through 60:1 gearing into about 21 kN. Response: the 48 V supply gives about 80 ms to full force, close to the hydraulic system. Off-road use: on loose ground the module sends drive to the outer or grounded rear wheel, helping turn-in and traction. Fail state: the ramps are spring-returned, so loss of power opens both packs and the module behaves as an open differential, which is safe. Benchmark: the 2024 Land Rover Defender X lists an electronic active rear differential with braking-based torque vectoring; electromechanical actuation of wet couplings is general practice in on-demand AWD.

title: Per-wheel torque control reads yaw from the ESC sensor cluster; chassis IMU deleted
description: [800V BEV] The tri-motor and quad-motor cars were given their own 6-axis inertial module for per-wheel torque control, although the ESC unit already contains a yaw-rate and acceleration sensor. Using the ESC signals over the private chassis CAN-FD deletes the module, its bracket, harness and calibration. Baseline: tri-motor (4% of fleet) and quad-motor (2%) cars carry a dedicated 6-axis IMU (€28) on a bracket near the centre of gravity, feeding the per-wheel torque controller for kick turn, tank turn and torque vectoring. Proposal: use the yaw rate, lateral and longitudinal acceleration from the ESC sensor cluster, sent on the private chassis CAN-FD at 5 ms. Why it works: latency check: the torque-vectoring yaw loop runs at 100 Hz (10 ms); adding 5 ms transport and a 2 ms filter keeps phase lag below 25° at 2 Hz, the highest yaw frequency the loop must control. In kick turn and tank turn the yaw rates are slow (below 60°/s, about 0.5 Hz), so resolution matters more than bandwidth, and the ESC sensor resolves 0.1°/s. The ESC already uses these signals for stability control, so the safety path is unchanged: brakes and stability stay with ESC and do not depend on the torque controller. Benchmark: the Rivian Gen 2 Quad-Motor states that Kick Turn works with stability control on, reduced or off, showing kick turn and stability control share vehicle-motion signals but are separate functions.

title: MHEV twin-coupling module closes both packs to lock the axle; separate dog lock deleted
description: [MHEV] A twin-coupling module that can close both packs fully behaves like a locked axle. On MHEV cars that take both the dynamic module and the off-road pack, the separate dog lock is deleted and two plates are added to each pack so that full closure holds the grip-limited wheel torque. Baseline: MHEV cars that take both the dynamic twin-coupling module and the off-road pack (5% of fleet) also carry a separate electromagnetic dog lock on the same axle, because each coupling pack holds only about 1,800 Nm at the wheel. Proposal: two more friction plates per pack (8 → 10) and a stronger ramp spring, and a Lock command that closes both packs fully; the dog lock, its coil, driver and lead are deleted. Why it works: a locked axle only needs each pack to carry the grip of its own wheel. Worst diagonal case: 1,100 kg × 9.81 × µ 0.9 × 0.40 m ≈ 3,880 Nm at one wheel. Ten plates lift capacity by 25% at the same force, and the stronger spring lifts it to about 4,000 Nm; with both packs closed nothing slips, so no heat is made and the lining only has to hold. Above that a pack slips briefly under a rock-drop shock, which protects the shafts. Loss of power opens both packs, as before. Benchmark: the 2024 Land Rover Defender X lists an electronic active differential with braking-based torque vectoring, showing one wet-pack device can serve both handling and off-road traction.

title: Per-wheel torque arbitration hosted in the rear inverter MCU; separate controller deleted
description: [800V BEV] The tri-motor and quad-motor cars carry a dedicated torque-vectoring controller that splits the driver torque request between wheels. Its function moves into a partition of the rear inverter MCU, which already runs at ASIL-D for torque safety, deleting a box, its bracket and harness. Baseline: tri-motor (4% of fleet) and quad-motor (2%) cars have a dedicated arbitration controller (€65) that takes the driver demand, vehicle motion and wheel speeds and sends a torque command to every drive inverter. Proposal: host the arbitration in a software partition of the rear inverter MCU, a dual-core lockstep device with spare capacity, moved up one memory size (+€6). Why it works: load check: arbitration at 100 Hz uses about 15% of one core, while the current loops run at 10-20 kHz in a separate timing partition. The inputs it needs already arrive at the rear inverter over the private chassis bus for traction control. The stability fail-safe is unchanged: brake intervention stays inside the ESC, so friction braking does not depend on the inverter software. Benchmark: Rivian says its Gen 2 Quad-Motor Kick Turn can be used with stability control fully on, reduced or off, showing that drive arbitration and stability control are separate functions that can live in different boxes.

title: Inboard tripod housing formed on the corner gearbox output shaft; flange and bolts deleted
description: [800V BEV] Each per-wheel drive output carries a bolted flange that joins the gearbox output to the inboard tripod housing. Forging the tripod tulip on the end of the output shaft deletes the two flanges, six bolts and their torque check per corner, with the half-shaft plunging straight into the gearbox. Baseline: each output of the twin-motor units (tri-motor 2 outputs on 4% of fleet, quad-motor 4 outputs on 2%) has a splined output flange, six M10 bolts and a flanged tripod housing on the half-shaft, about €8 per output plus a torque-and-mark step. Proposal: the gearbox output shaft is forged in C50 with an integral tripod tulip, induction-hardened on the roller tracks; the half-shaft spider plunges into it and the boot clamps onto the tulip. Why it works: torque check: peak per-wheel torque is about 4,360 Nm (400 Nm × 10.9); the tulip section of an AAR 3300-size tripod is rated near 5,000 Nm, and the bolted flange it replaces was the weaker joint in reversals during kick turn and tank turn. Articulation: plunge stays at ±25 mm, enough for the off-road wheel travel at the inboard joint; the outboard fixed joint takes the steering and suspension angle. Benchmark: the Yangwang U8 drives each wheel from its own motor, which gives four drive outputs instead of two and makes each output interface a cost multiplier.

title: Torque-vectoring clutch drums flow-formed from strip instead of machined forgings
description: [MHEV] Each clutch drum is a forging turned inside and out with an internal spline broached for the outer plates. Flow-forming a blanked steel disc over a splined mandrel forms the cup and the spline in one operation with no chips, then nitrocarburising hardens the spline flanks. Baseline: the twin-clutch rear unit on MHEV torque-vectoring cars (15% of fleet) has two drums: 16MnCr5 forgings, turned, internally broached for the outer-plate tabs, about €11 each, 1.4 kg. Proposal: blank a 4 mm S420MC disc, flow-form it over a splined mandrel so the wall thins to 2.5 mm and the internal spline forms at the same time, then nitrocarburise (about 500 HV surface). About €6 each, 0.9 kg. Why it works: the drum sees hoop and spline-flank loads, not heavy bending. Torque check: about 2,250 Nm per clutch at the wheel ÷ the final drive (about 3.2) gives about 700 Nm in the drum if the packs sit before the final drive; if they sit on the half-shaft side the drum carries the full 2,250 Nm, about 1,250 N per tab on a 75 mm spline radius with 24 tabs over a 2.5 × 15 mm flank, about 33 MPa bearing pressure, still trivial for a nitrocarburised surface. Flow forming also work-hardens the wall. Off-road relevance: the unit pushes torque to the grounded or outer rear wheel on loose ground. Benchmark: the 2024 Land Rover Defender X lists an electronic active rear differential, the class of clutch device these drums belong to; flow-formed drums are general practice in automatic transmissions.

ideaData.title: Torque-vectoring clutch drums flow-formed from strip instead of machined forgings
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: the twin-clutch rear unit on MHEV torque-vectoring cars (15% of fleet) has two drums: 16MnCr5 forgings, turned, internally broached for the outer-plate tabs, about €11 each, 1.4 kg. Proposal: blank a 4 mm S420MC disc, flow-form it over a splined mandrel so the wall thins to 2.5 mm and the internal spline forms at the same time, then nitrocarburise (about 500 HV surface). About €6 each, 0.9 kg. Why it works: the drum sees hoop and spline-flank loads, not heavy bending. Torque check: about 2,250 Nm per clutch at the wheel ÷ the final drive (about 3.2) gives about 700 Nm in the drum if the packs sit before the final drive; if they sit on the half-shaft side the drum carries the full 2,250 Nm, about 1,250 N per tab on a 75 mm spline radius with 24 tabs over a 2.5 × 15 mm flank, about 33 MPa bearing pressure, still trivial for a nitrocarburised surface. Flow forming also work-hardens the wall. Off-road relevance: the unit pushes torque to the grounded or outer rear wheel on loose ground. Benchmark: the 2024 Land Rover Defender X lists an electronic active rear differential, the class of clutch device these drums belong to; flow-formed drums are general practice in automatic transmissions.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Each clutch drum is a forging turned inside and out with an internal spline broached for the outer plates. Flow-forming a blanked steel disc over a splined mandrel forms the cup and the spline in one operation with no chips, then nitrocarburising hardens the spline flanks.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Flow-forming cell replaces forging, turning and broaching. Material yield rises from about 55% to over 90%. Nitrocarburising runs in a batch furnace shared with other driveline parts.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Same drum interface to the hub and the same plate tabs, so the clutch pack and assembly sequence are unchanged. The drum is 0.5 kg lighter each, cutting rotating inertia for faster torque response.

title: Twin-motor unit centred on the car; right-hand stub shaft and support bearing deleted
description: [800V BEV] The twin-motor units were packaged 60 mm off the car centreline to clear the HV junction, so the long side needs an intermediate shaft with a support bearing and bracket, and the two half-shafts differ. Centring the unit by moving the junction makes both half-shafts identical and deletes the intermediate shaft. Baseline: each twin-motor unit (tri-motor rear on 4% of fleet; quad-motor front and rear on 2%) sits 60 mm left of centre, so the right-hand side has an intermediate shaft (42CrMo4), a 6208 support bearing and a bracket bolted to the unit (about €28), and the left and right half-shafts are different parts. Proposal: move the HV junction box 70 mm forward on the subframe and centre the unit; both sides use one equal-length half-shaft. Why it works: articulation check: equal shafts give equal joint angles in bump and droop, so at full off-road droop (joint angle about 22° at the outer joint) both sides stay within the joint rating with the same margin. Equal torsional stiffness on both sides also helps kick turn and virtual lock, where the two motors hold different torques and unequal shafts would wind up differently. Benchmark: the Yangwang U8 drives each wheel from its own motor, a layout in which the drive units, not a differential, set the half-shaft geometry.

title: Symmetric end-cover casting serves both sides of the twin-motor drive unit
description: [800V BEV] The twin-motor drive units (one per axle) close each end with an end cover; the LH and RH covers are mirror images and need two dies. Designing the bolt pattern, bearing seat, breather boss and connector boss symmetric about the vertical plane lets one cover fit both ends. Baseline: each twin-motor unit (tri-motor rear 4% of fleet; quad-motor front and rear 2%) has a LH and a RH end cover, mirror images because the oil drain, breather boss and connector boss are offset. That is two HPDC dies (about €280K each), two part numbers and two machining programs at about 21,000 affected cars. Proposal: one symmetric cover: bolt pattern on a symmetric pitch, the bearing seat on the axis, and both a breather boss and a drain boss provided on the vertical centre line; the unused boss on each side is left blind. Fitting it rotated 180° gives the other side. Why it works: the cover carries the outer bearing and seals the motor; neither job cares about handing once the bosses are on the centre line. Wading: the breather stays at the top on both sides, above the 900 mm line. Benchmark: the Yangwang U8 drives each wheel with its own motor, the per-wheel layout that creates left and right handed drive-unit parts.

title: Torque-vectoring unit oil-temperature sensor replaced by a clutch slip-energy thermal model
description: [MHEV] The twin-clutch rear unit has an oil-temperature sensor in a threaded port to derate the clutches when they get hot. The controller already knows clutch slip speed and clamp torque, so it can calculate the heat put into the oil; a validated thermal model replaces the sensor, its port, O-ring and harness tail. Baseline: the MHEV torque-vectoring unit (15% of fleet) has an NTC oil sensor (€4.5) in a machined M12 port with an FKM O-ring and a harness tail, used to derate the clutches on long slip. Proposal: estimate oil and plate temperatures from a lumped thermal model: heat in = Σ(clamp torque × slip speed), heat out = housing convection at vehicle speed, with ambient from the vehicle sensor. Why it works: heat check for an off-road slip case: 1,000 Nm at 20 rad/s slip = 20 kW for 3 s = 60 kJ per event; with 1.2 litres of oil and 5 kg of plates and drum (about 4.3 kJ/K: oil 1.0 kg × 2.0 kJ/kgK plus steel 5 kg × 0.46 kJ/kgK), the rise is about 14 K per event, slow enough for a model to track within ±5 K once validated. The model errs high in uncertain cases (no airflow assumed below 10 km/h), so derating comes earlier, never later. Wading: one fewer threaded port low on the housing is one fewer leak path at a 900 mm crossing (head ρgh ≈ 8.8 kPa). Benchmark: the 2024 Land Rover Defender X lists an electronic active rear differential, the class of clutch device whose thermal derate this replaces; model-based clutch temperature is general practice in dual-clutch gearboxes.

title: Terrain Response calibrated on hardware-in-the-loop terrain models, halving proving-ground trips
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Moves terrain-mode calibration iterations from seasonal proving-ground trips onto a hardware-in-the-loop rig with fitted soft-soil tyre models, keeping two confirmation trips and using three fewer prototypes. The added cost is the rig, its model upkeep and one correlation week. Baseline: the terrain modes (Grass-Gravel-Snow, Mud-Ruts, Sand, Rock Crawl, Wade, Auto) are calibrated on both MHEV and 800V BEV, on three tyre fitments, over four seasonal trips (Arctic, desert, UK mud, rock) with six prototypes, about €5.6M per programme. Proposal: a hardware-in-the-loop rig carries the real ESC, terrain manager, transfer-case and locker actuators and the air-suspension valve block, driven by a vehicle model with Magic Formula tyres and a Bekker-Wong soft-soil model fitted from one instrumented sand and mud week. Calibrators converge the slip targets, torque ramps and ride-height choices on the rig, and only two confirmation trips with three prototypes stay. Why it works: most calibration iterations are slip-target and torque-ramp sweeps that the rig repeats in minutes, while a trip needs fresh terrain for every run. Back-of-envelope: sand rolling resistance 0.15-0.30, so a 2,850 kg BEV at 0.25 needs F = 0.25 × 2,850 × 9.81 = 7.0 kN, or 2.8 kNm at a 0.40 m wheel radius. That sits inside both powertrains' low-speed torque, so the job is slip management, which a model reproduces well once fitted to measured sinkage. Benchmark: the Defender's Terrain Response reconfigures transmission, suspension and traction per mode, which shows how many actuator calibrations each

title: Seven terrain presets cut to four plus Auto, halving the calibration matrix
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes three calibration presets and their high/low-range, powertrain and tyre combinations, plus their validation runs and HMI strings. The only added cost is developing the sinkage-scaled Soft slip table that replaces the separate Mud and Sand sets. Baseline: seven presets (Comfort, Eco, Grass-Gravel-Snow, Mud-Ruts, Sand, Rock Crawl, Dynamic) plus Auto, each in high and low range on the MHEV and as separate sets on the 800V BEV, across three tyre fitments: more than 40 calibration cells, each with its own validation and HMI strings. Proposal: Auto plus four driver presets: Road, Slippery (grass, gravel, snow and ice), Soft (mud and sand) and Rock. Wade stays as an overlay programme for ride height, HVAC recirculation and speed advice, not as a separate traction set. Soft uses one slip-target table scaled by estimated rolling resistance (a sinkage proxy), from wheel torque against vehicle acceleration. Why it works: mud and sand both want controlled wheel slip of about 10-25% and early upshift avoidance, so they differ mainly in slip target and pedal gain, which one scaled table covers. Back-of-envelope: on sand the optimum slip is about 20% and on mud about 12%. At 10 km/h, 12% to 20% slip is 1.2-2.0 km/h of wheel-speed excess, a range a single scaling parameter spans without changing the controller structure. Benchmark: the Lexus GX 550 Overtrail already offers different mode sets in high and low range (Auto, Dirt, Sand, Mud, Deep Snow; Auto, Sand, Mud, Rock), which shows that presets can be trimmed by range.

title: End-of-line actuator self-test replaces the rolling-road sweep of off-road actuators
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Moves actuator function checks from the 4WD rolling road to an on-board self-test at the static electrical station, cutting 55 s of roller time per off-road car. It also avoids a second roller station; the added costs are self-test software and 30 s more at the static station. Baseline: every off-road-pack car (35% take) spends 95 s on the 4WD rolling road: transfer-case range shift (MHEV), centre and rear locker engagement, air-suspension height sweep and terrain-mode change. Road cars spend 40 s for the AWD check. At peak off-road mix the plant needs a second 4WD roller station (€1.8M). Proposal: the EOL tester triggers an on-board self-test over DoIP while the car stands on the static electrical station. Each actuator is driven through its travel, and current signature, position-sensor transitions and timing are compared with limits: range-shift actuator peak 6 A for 0.3-0.5 s, locker engagement confirmed by the sensor within 250 ms, ride height ±3 mm. The rolling road keeps only the 40 s torque-transfer check that every car needs. Why it works: the rolling road was only proving that the actuators move, which the actuators' own feedback already shows at standstill. Back-of-envelope: a range-shift fork needs about 900 N over 12 mm, 10.8 J per shift, which the actuator delivers stationary just as it does on rollers. Benchmark: the Defender's Terrain Response reconfigures transmission, suspension and traction per mode, so every mode change exercises several actuators that need an EOL check.

title: Off-road actuators join the chassis CAN-FD backbone, deleting the private off-road bus
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the private off-road CAN (twisted pair, splices, terminations, cavities and the terrain manager's second transceiver) by putting off-road actuators on the existing chassis CAN-FD backbone. The added cost is a CAN-FD transceiver upgrade on three actuator ECUs whose MCUs already carry FD-capable CAN controllers. Baseline: the off-road pack (35% take) adds a private 500 kbit/s CAN linking the terrain manager with the transfer-case controller (MHEV), the rear locker controller and the active anti-roll-bar controller. That is about 7.5 m of twisted pair, two splice packs, two termination resistors, eight extra connector cavities and a second transceiver with choke on the terrain manager. Proposal: the off-road actuators connect to the chassis CAN-FD backbone (500 kbit/s arbitration, 2 Mbit/s data) that already passes them. The private bus, its splices, terminations and the second transceiver are deleted, and actuator ECUs move from classical CAN to CAN-FD (this assumes their MCUs already have FD-capable CAN controllers; a classical-CAN controller on the FD backbone would raise error frames, so only the transceiver changes). Why it works: the off-road messages are low-rate set-points and status, not fast control loops, which stay inside each actuator. Back-of-envelope: four actuators × 100 frames/s × about 340 µs per 64-byte CAN-FD frame (60 µs arbitration + 280 µs data) adds 13.6% bus load. The backbone's measured 38% rises to about 52%, below the 60% design limit, and the worst-case latency of a 10 ms set-point stays under 2 ms. Benchmark: the Lexus GX

title: Terrain manager rated QM, with ASIL-B guard limits inside each actuator

title: Published terrain-mode interface specification lets the ESC be dual-sourced
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Makes the terrain-function interface OEM-owned and supplier-neutral, so the ESC and air-suspension controller can be dual-sourced at a typical 4% piece-price reduction. The added cost is writing and maintaining the interface specification and its conformance test suite. Baseline: terrain functions are built on the incumbent ESC supplier's proprietary function interface, so the ESC (about €145 with off-road functions) and the air-suspension controller (€38, fitted to 60%) are effectively single-sourced. Proposal: the OEM publishes a terrain-mode request interface as an AUTOSAR software-component specification (terrain ID, slip-target scaling, hold and release requests, descent set-speed, status and degradation flags) with a conformance test suite on the HIL rig. The next ESC and air-suspension RFQs then go to two qualified suppliers. Why it works: once the interface is the OEM's, switching supplier no longer means rewriting terrain logic, and competitive quotes typically move piece price by 4-6%. Back-of-envelope: why the interface carries targets, not commands: a 1.6 kgm² wheel with 1,000 Nm excess torque accelerates at 625 rad/s², so it passes the slip limit within milliseconds. The fast loop must stay inside the ESC, and the interface only sets targets every 10 ms, which any supplier can meet. Benchmark: the Bronco's G.O.A.T. modes coordinate throttle, transmission, traction and differential behaviour across up to eight trim-dependent modes, which shows how much vehicle logic sits on that interface.
