title: Off-road ESC functions written in-house on the ESC open platform, ending per-unit licences
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces per-unit supplier licence fees for HDC, gradient release, crawl/progress control and off-road ABS with OEM-written applications on the ESC open platform. The added costs are in-house development and a small per-unit platform-access fee. Baseline: Hill Descent Control and gradient release (on every car) are bought as supplier ESC function packages at about €3.0 per unit. The off-road pack's crawl and off-road progress control and off-road ABS calibration (35% take) cost about €7.0 per unit more. Proposal: the OEM writes these functions as applications on the open software platform that major ESC suppliers now offer. They run on the ESC's application partition and call the supplier's brake-pressure request interface. The supplier's base braking, ABS and pressure limits stay in the supplier's safety layer and are unchanged. Why it works: the functions are speed and pressure request logic above the supplier's safety layer; once written they carry no per-unit fee and carry over to the next platform. Back-of-envelope: HDC on a 35% grade (19.3°) for a 2,850 kg BEV needs F = 2,850 × 9.81 × sin 19.3° = 9.2 kN of retarding force, or about 0.93 kNm per wheel at 0.40 m. That is roughly 25 bar at the calipers, well inside the hydraulic unit's range, so no hardware changes. Benchmark: Land Rover's HDC brakes each wheel separately, is selectable below 80 km/h, takes its set speed from the cruise switches, and pairs with Gradient Release Control, the same function set this idea brings in-house.

title: One vehicle-wide wade state service replaces separate wade triggers in five controllers

title: HDC long-descent thermal sign-off on brake dynamometer replaces alpine test trips
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces two alpine HDC thermal trips and two prototypes with dynamometer descent cycles plus one correlation descent per powertrain. The added cost is the dynamometer programme and the correlation runs. Baseline: the HDC thermal strategy (brake temperature model, fade-out warning, speed reduction) is signed off on two alpine trips with three prototypes per powertrain, about €1.9M. Proposal: an inertia brake dynamometer runs descent duty cycles built from m·g·h, with cooling airflow set to crawl speeds of 1-3 m/s. One instrumented descent per powertrain correlates the dynamometer and the in-ESC thermal model, and the trips are deleted. Why it works: HDC thermal behaviour is set by energy, power and cooling at low airspeed, all of which a dynamometer reproduces exactly and repeatably. Back-of-envelope: a 2,850 kg 800V BEV descending 600 m with regeneration unavailable (full pack) must dissipate 2,850 × 9.81 × 600 = 16.8 MJ. With 60% on the front axle that is 5.0 MJ per front disc. Over a 24-minute descent at 6 km/h that is about 3.5 kW per disc. A 13 kg disc (cp 460 J/kgK) would rise 830 K if it could not shed heat, so convection at low airspeed governs the result, and that is what the dynamometer tests. Benchmark: Land Rover documentation states that HDC fades out when brake temperatures exceed pre-set limits, which is exactly the boundary this test signs off.

title: Shadow-mode fleet validation of crawl and descent updates cuts dedicated test-fleet mileage
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces most of the dedicated validation fleet mileage for each crawl and HDC software release with shadow-mode comparison on customer cars, keeping three cars for actuation sign-off. The added cost is the shadow-mode framework, telemetry and cloud analysis. Baseline: each software release of crawl control, off-road progress control and HDC is validated on an eight-car fleet driving about 40,000 km, about €0.9M per release over four releases in the life cycle. Proposal: a new release first runs in shadow mode on consenting customer cars. The new controller computes its brake-pressure and torque requests in parallel with the live version but never actuates. Disagreement statistics are uploaded: set-speed error, pressure-request differences, mode-transition timing. The physical fleet shrinks to three cars for actuation sign-off. Why it works: most release risk is in logic and calibration edge cases, which shadow mode sees over millions of customer kilometres, while actuation itself changes little between releases. Back-of-envelope: on a 25% descent a 2,850 kg BEV needs 2,850 × 9.81 × 0.243 = 6.8 kN of retarding force. Shadow mode compares the new controller's demanded force with the force implied by the driver's or live HDC's actual deceleration, flagging gaps above 0.5 kN. Benchmark: Rivian added Soft Sand as a new drive mode by over-the-air update after launch, which shows that off-road functions now change post-SOP and need a release validation route.

title: Off-road event recorder in the existing telematics unit cuts no-fault-found warranty
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Halves no-fault-found warranty part swaps on terrain-system components and trims diagnosis labour on genuine claims, using a DTC-triggered snapshot from the existing telematics unit. The added costs are recorder software and upload data. Baseline: OEM-paid warranty claims on terrain-system components (transfer-case and locker actuators, wade transducers, ride-height sensors, terrain selector) run at about 4% of cars in warranty at €520 each. About 35% are no-fault-found parts swapped because the dealer cannot reproduce an intermittent off-road fault. Proposal: a ring buffer in the existing telematics unit records 40 terrain-system signals at 50 Hz and freezes 30 s before and after any related DTC. The snapshot is uploaded and attached to the dealer's guided diagnosis, so the dealer sees what actually happened. Why it works: intermittent off-road faults (mud on sensors, articulation-dependent connector faults) show up in the snapshot even after the car is clean. Back-of-envelope: memory 40 signals × 2 bytes × 50 Hz × 60 s = 240 kB, inside the telematics unit's free RAM. Upload is about 60 kB after compression, a few cents of data per event. Benchmark: the Defender's Wade Sensing monitors water depth with sensors, the kind of off-road component whose intermittent faults are hard to reproduce in a dealer bay. Customer repair costs outside warranty are not counted.

Proposal: a ring buffer in the existing telematics unit records 40 terrain-system signals at 50 Hz and freezes 30 s before and after any related DTC. The snapshot is uploaded and attached to the dealer's guided diagnosis, so the dealer sees what actually happened. Why it works: intermittent off-road faults (mud on sensors, articulation-dependent connector faults) show up in the snapshot even after the car is clean. Back-of-envelope: memory 40 signals × 2 bytes × 50 Hz × 60 s = 240 kB, inside the telematics unit's free RAM. Upload is about 60 kB after compression, a few cents of data per event. Benchmark: the Defender's Wade Sensing monitors water depth with sensors, the kind of off-road component whose intermittent faults are hard to reproduce in a dealer bay. Customer repair costs outside warranty are not counted.

title: Breadcrumb trail recorder on open offline maps replaces a licensed off-road map layer
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces the per-unit licensed off-road map layer and its paid updates with an in-house breadcrumb recorder and OEM-hosted open topographic tiles. The added costs are tile hosting with licence compliance and app development. Baseline: the off-road pack (35% take) carries a licensed topographic trail-map layer at €9 per unit plus three annual updates at €2 each. Proposal: an on-device trail recorder logs GNSS fixes at 1 Hz, fused with the existing dead-reckoning, simplifies them with a Douglas-Peucker filter at 2 m tolerance, and shows them on the existing navigation base map. Routes can be followed back, saved and shared through the vehicle app. The off-road pages add OEM-hosted topographic tiles built from OpenStreetMap and public elevation data under ODbL, downloadable for offline use. Why it works: off-road drivers mostly need to know where they have been and the terrain relief, not a curated trail database. Back-of-envelope: an 8-hour trail at 1 Hz is 28,800 fixes × 12 bytes = 346 kB raw, about 40 kB simplified, trivial for the head unit's storage. A 50 × 50 km tile set at zoom 15 is about 150 MB. Benchmark: Ineos Pathfinder lets Grenadier drivers plan, follow and save routes as waypoints off paved roads, and reviewers note it records a breadcrumb trail without built-in mapping.

title: Consented fleet telemetry replaces most of the instrumented off-road duty-cycle fleet
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces 18 of 24 instrumented duty-cycle cars with consented fleet histograms, keeping six cars for wheel-force and strain correlation. The added cost is the analytics pipeline that turns uploaded histograms into durability load spectra. Baseline: off-road duty cycles for durability targets (time in low range, locker cycles, HDC energy per descent, ride-height dwell, pitch and roll occupancy, wading events) come from 24 customer-loaned cars with data loggers for 12 months, about €2.6M per programme. Proposal: opt-in telemetry from about 5,000 cars of the predecessor and sister connected fleet (available before design sign-off) uploads on-board histograms and rainflow counts, and this programme's early cars confirm the targets after SOP. Six instrumented cars are kept for wheel-force and strain correlation, which telemetry cannot measure. Why it works: the questions durability engineers ask (how often, how long, how much energy) are counts and histograms, which the cars already compute from existing signals, with sample sizes 200 times larger. Back-of-envelope: HDC energy per descent is m·g·h: 2,850 kg × 9.81 × 150 m = 4.2 MJ for a typical 150 m descent. A 16-bin histogram of descent energy over 5,000 cars gives the 99th-percentile customer far more reliably than 24 loggers. Benchmark: Rivian release 2023.38.0 let R1 owners use Snow, Sand, All-Terrain and Rock Crawl modes while towing, delivered over the air, which shows the connected fleet already carries off-road software that could report usage.

title: Ethernet DoIP flashing of off-road ECUs cuts end-of-line software load time
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Cuts end-of-line flash time for off-road-relevant ECUs from about 98 s to 20 s by loading only calibration deltas over Ethernet DoIP in parallel, and avoids a second flash station. The added cost is the suppliers' pre-flash step. Baseline: at end of line the ESC (4 MB) and terrain manager with air-suspension controller (3 MB) are flashed on every car, and the off-road pack's transfer-case and locker controllers (2 × 0.5 MB) on 35%, all over CAN-FD through the OBD port at an effective 0.8 Mbit/s. That takes about 98 s with session overheads, and peak mix needs a second flash station (€0.6M). Proposal: suppliers deliver the ECUs pre-flashed with the released base image. At EOL only the calibration delta (at most 400 kB per ECU) and VIN coding are loaded, over 100BASE-T1 DoIP to the central gateway, which fans out to the ECUs in parallel. Why it works: most of the bytes are fixed code, which belongs at the supplier's flash step, while the plant only needs the vehicle-specific data. Back-of-envelope: 7.35 MB fleet average × 8 = 58.8 Mbit ÷ 0.8 Mbit/s = 74 s plus overheads. The new delta is 400 kB × 8 = 3.2 Mbit ÷ 0.8 Mbit/s = 4 s per ECU, run in parallel behind the gateway, so about 20 s in total. Benchmark: Jeep delivered Off-Road Pages to early 2018 Wrangler JLs by over-the-air update, which shows off-road ECU software keeps changing after build and suits a base-plus-delta release model.

title: Configurable Terrain Response tuned within a validated parameter envelope, not combinations
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Cuts Configurable Terrain Response validation from sampled combinations of 81 to 20 points, made safe by monotonic interpolation and cross-constraints. The added cost is a one-off envelope tool that proves monotonicity from the parameter tables. Baseline: Configurable Terrain Response lets the driver set four subsystems (powertrain response, steering weight, differential behaviour, traction slip) to three levels each, 3⁴ = 81 combinations. The validation plan samples worst cases across these at about €1.4M. Proposal: each slider maps monotonically to parameter sets that are interpolated between validated end points. A small set of cross-constraints is enforced (lowest traction slip blocks the most aggressive powertrain map above 50 km/h; the most relaxed steering is blocked above 80 km/h). Validation covers the 2⁴ = 16 corner combinations plus 4 centre points, and monotonicity is proven by analysis. Why it works: when every output depends monotonically on each slider, the extreme behaviours occur at the corners. Validating corners bounds every combination in between. Back-of-envelope: pedal-to-torque gain varies ±30% across the powertrain slider, and the worst split-µ yaw case is gain 1.3 with minimum traction slip, which is a corner and is tested. Benchmark: the Defender's Configurable Terrain Response lets drivers tune powertrain, steering, differentials and traction individually, the same four-axis space.

title: One terrain selector module for left- and right-hand drive, symmetric icons
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the second set of light-guide and bezel tools, the second EOL fixture and the second part number's logistics by making the selector symmetric. The only added cost is a slightly more diffuse light-guide surface. Baseline: the left- and right-hand-drive terrain selector modules differ. Icons on the light-guide ring are tilted 8° towards the driver, and the connector exits on the driver side, giving two part numbers, two light-guide and bezel tool sets and two EOL test fixtures. Proposal: one module with icons arranged symmetrically around the ring, legible from either front seat, a centre-exit connector, and a wider-angle diffuser on the light guide. Why it works: the tilt and connector exit were packaging conventions, not functional needs. A diffuser with a wider emission angle keeps icon luminance from both seating positions. Back-of-envelope: the driver's eye sits about 380 mm laterally and 650 mm from the knob, about 30° off-axis. A diffuser with a 60° half-angle keeps about cos 30° = 87% of on-axis luminance, above the 70% legibility target, so no tilt is needed. Benchmark: the Ford Bronco's G.O.A.T. dial is a symmetric centre-console rotary with a centre button, a layout that suits either hand of drive.

title: Terrain pedal and shift maps generated from three parameters, not stored per mode
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces stored per-mode pedal and shift maps with three-parameter families on a base map. This cuts calibration hours and the transmission supplier's mode-calibration billing, with no hardware change. Baseline: every terrain mode stores its own 16 × 16 pedal-to-torque map, in the MHEV engine controller and in the 800V BEV's vehicle controller, and on the MHEV its own shift schedule in the 8-speed transmission controller. Calibration takes about 2,400 engineer-hours, and the transmission supplier bills about €0.35M for mode shift-map calibration. Proposal: one base road map per powertrain. Each mode is three parameters: pedal gain, a progression exponent, and a low-speed creep offset. On the MHEV, shift behaviour per mode is an upshift-speed offset and a kick-down threshold applied to the base schedule. Why it works: the terrain modes differ in progression and creep, not in map shape. A parameter family captures them with a fraction of the calibration points, and the transmission supplier only calibrates offsets. Back-of-envelope: in Rock Crawl an exponent of 1.8 gives 20% pedal = 0.2¹·⁸ = 5.5% of maximum wheel torque. With about 19 kNm available in MHEV low range that is 1.0 kNm, enough for fine control on a rock step without lurching. Benchmark: the Jeep Wrangler's Off-Road+ button adjusts throttle, transmission and traction responses in 4H and 4L, showing that mode differences are response tweaks on a common base.

title: One LIN smart actuator drives both low-range shift and centre lock on MHEV
description: [MHEV] Commonises the range-shift and centre-lock actuators into one LIN smart-actuator design, lowering piece price through volume and deleting the controller's H-bridge stage, a harness branch and one actuator validation programme. Baseline: the MHEV off-road pack's transfer case uses two actuators from two suppliers. The range shift is a BLDC with worm gear and CAN interface (€38), and the centre lock is a DC motor with ball ramp driven by a PWM H-bridge in the transfer-case controller (€34 plus €3.5 driver stage), with separate harness branches. Proposal: one LIN smart actuator family: the same BLDC, gear train and integrated driver with position sensing, with two output adaptors (a cam for the range fork, a pinion for the ball ramp), both on one LIN branch from the transfer-case controller. Why it works: both jobs are slow, low-torque rotary positioning tasks, so one motor and gear design covers both, and the actuator's own driver deletes the controller's H-bridge. Back-of-envelope: the range fork needs about 900 N through an 8 mm cam lever, 7.2 Nm. The ball ramp needs about 3 Nm at 30° of rotation. Both are inside an 8 Nm actuator rating, with shift times near 300 ms. The rear e-locker stays as a separate solenoid. Benchmark: the Lexus GX 550 Overtrail combines full-time 4WD with E-KDSS and an electronically locking rear differential, showing how many separate driveline actuators an off-road grade carries.

title: Off-road pack switched on by end-of-line coding on one software part number
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Removes four software part numbers (release, PPAP, supplier pre-flash variant handling) and wrong-variant rework by enabling off-road functions through signed EOL coding. The added cost is securing that coding against tampering. Baseline: the ESC and the terrain manager each have a road and an off-road-pack software part number per powertrain, eight software part numbers in all. Each is released, PPAP'd and logistically tracked at the supplier's pre-flash, and about 0.3% of cars get the wrong variant and need re-flashing at a rework station. Proposal: one software image per ECU per powertrain, with the off-road functions (crawl, progress control, off-road ABS, low-range HDC tables) enabled by signed VIN-based variant coding at EOL. Why it works: the off-road functions are a small part of the image, so carrying them on every car costs flash space, not money, while every software variant carries a release cost. Back-of-envelope: the off-road functions take about 180 kB of the ESC's 4 MB flash, which has 1.1 MB free. Even after the calibration-partition split there is ample margin. Benchmark: Rivian delivered a new Snow drive mode to existing R1 vehicles over the air, which shows that drive-mode functions can be enabled on fielded hardware by software.

title: Wade-alert plausibility logic cuts false wade warnings and transducer warranty swaps
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Adds plausibility gates to the wade-alert logic so false alerts stop driving no-fault-found transducer swaps under warranty. The only added cost is the logic development, with no hardware change. Baseline: Wade Sensing (fitted to 60% of cars) raises false depth alerts from rain on the mirror, spray, snow and tall grass. Customers report faults and dealers swap mirror wade transducers: about 3.5% of wade cars in warranty at €310 per claim (transducer plus mirror-glass removal), 45% of them no-fault-found. Proposal: alert logic with plausibility gates. The echo must be stable within ±30 mm for 1.5 s. Left and right depths must agree within 80 mm after correcting for roll angle. Vehicle speed must be at or below 15 km/h. Depth must be consistent with ride height and pitch (water surface stays level as the body pitches). Failed gates show 'wade reading uncertain' rather than a depth. Why it works: a real water surface is flat and stable while spray and grass are not, so plausibility gates separate them without new hardware. Back-of-envelope: at 3° roll across a 1.7 m track the two sides differ by 1,700 × sin 3° = 89 mm, so the 80 mm gate is applied after roll correction. Warning thresholds keep their physical meaning: at 0.9 m depth the head on the lowest seals is ρgh = 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.9 = 8.8 kPa. Benchmark: Defender's Wade Sensing uses sensors to monitor water depth and alert the driver, with wading quoted up to 900 mm.

title: Wade Sensing logic runs in the park-assist controller, deleting the standalone wade module
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the standalone wade-sensing module and its bracket on 60% of cars by running wade logic on the park-assist controller's spare ASIC channels. The added costs are the 16-channel ASIC variant and a slightly longer harness branch. Baseline: the two mirror-mounted wade transducers on 60% of cars are wired to a standalone wade-sensing module (€22 with housing, MCU, CAN transceiver and connector) under the passenger seat, plus a €1.2 bracket. Proposal: the park-assist controller, which already drives 12 ultrasonic channels, moves to its 16-channel ASIC variant (+€1.8). Two channels drive the mirror transducers, and the wade logic runs as a software component on the park-assist MCU. The mirror harness branch is rerouted to the park-assist controller (+€0.6). Why it works: wade transducers are ultrasonic transceivers like parking sensors, so the park-assist driver ASIC and echo processing already do the hard part. Back-of-envelope: the transducers ping at about 48 kHz. The echo from water 1.05 m below the mirror returns in 2 × 1.05 / 343 = 6.1 ms, well inside the park-assist ASIC's 20-30 ms cycle, so the extra channels need no faster hardware. Benchmark: the Yangwang U8 uses multiple sensors to monitor water depth and shows depth and attitude on its central screen, showing wade sensing as an integrated software function rather than a separate box.

Why it works: wade transducers are ultrasonic transceivers like parking sensors, so the park-assist driver ASIC and echo processing already do the hard part. Back-of-envelope: the transducers ping at about 48 kHz. The echo from water 1.05 m below the mirror returns in 2 × 1.05 / 343 = 6.1 ms, well inside the park-assist ASIC's 20-30 ms cycle, so the extra channels need no faster hardware. Benchmark: the Yangwang U8 uses multiple sensors to monitor water depth and shows depth and attitude on its central screen, showing wade sensing as an integrated software function rather than a separate box.

title: Crawl and descent calibrations scaled across tyre options from measured slip curves
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces two full tyre-option re-calibrations of crawl, progress control and HDC with slip-curve measurement plus scaled parameters and a short verification drive. The added cost is the slip-curve test campaign. Baseline: crawl control, off-road progress control and HDC are fully re-calibrated for each of three tyre options (22-inch road, 20-inch all-season, 20-inch all-terrain), at about €0.3M each. Proposal: the base calibration is done once on the all-terrain tyre. For the other options the longitudinal slip curve µ(s) is measured on four reference surfaces (gravel, wet grass, sand, packed snow) on a mobile tyre test rig. The controllers' slip targets and pressure-ramp gains are then scaled by the ratios of peak slip and peak µ, and a two-day verification drive replaces the full calibration. Why it works: these controllers act on slip and deceleration targets, so tyre differences enter mainly through where µ peaks and how high, which scaling captures. Back-of-envelope: holding HDC on a 30% gravel slope needs µ = tan 16.7° = 0.30. If the all-terrain tyre peaks at µ 0.55 and slip 12% while the road tyre peaks at µ 0.50 and slip 9%, the road tyre's slip target scales to 9/12 of the base, still with 40% µ margin. Benchmark: the Bronco limits Trail Control to 20 mph in 4H and 9 mph in 4L, showing that speed-control envelopes are calibrated per driveline state, the kind of table scaled here.

title: Software-defined auxiliary outputs replace the pre-wired accessory switch panel and relays
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the auxiliary switch panel, its relays and fuses and part of the pre-wired harness by switching accessories through eFuse channels in the zone controllers. The added costs are the populated eFuse channels and configuration software. Baseline: the expedition sub-pack (12% of fleet) adds an overhead auxiliary panel with four switches (€26), four relays and fuses in an auxiliary fuse box (€14) and pre-wired circuits to the front bumper and roof (€18) for a light bar, winch control and spare loads. Proposal: four populated eFuse channels in the front and roof zone controllers (two at 15 A, two at 5 A; +€6 on the zone controller variant) feed two sealed accessory connectors. Loads are named, assigned and switched from the touchscreen, voice or a programmable steering-wheel button. The winch's 400 A motor current stays on its own battery cable and contactor; the eFuse channel only drives the contactor coil at about 2 A. Why it works: the switches and relays only route power to loads that software can now switch and protect, and an eFuse also diagnoses open and short loads. Back-of-envelope: a 180 W light bar draws 180 / 13.5 = 13.3 A, inside a 15 A channel. The front connector sits below the 0.9 m wade line, so it is IP6K7-rated: 1 m immersion is 9.8 kPa versus ρgh = 8.8 kPa at 0.9 m. Benchmark: the Ineos Grenadier's overhead panel holds the off-road switchgear, including the diff-lock buttons and pre-wired auxiliary switches for winches or light bars.

title: Symbol-led off-road pages cut translated strings and localisation testing
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Cuts the off-road pages' translated strings from about 420 to 120, saving translation, linguistic review and truncation testing in 38 languages each release. The added cost is a one-off symbol design and ISO 2575 compliance check. Baseline: the off-road pages (terrain mode, pitch and roll, wheel angle, locker and ride-height status, wade depth, hints and warnings) carry about 420 text strings in 38 languages. Translation, linguistic review and on-screen truncation testing cost about €9 per string-language, €144k per release over five releases. Proposal: a symbol-led design using ISO 2575 symbols and numeric readouts, cutting strings to about 120. Legal warnings and safety advice stay as full text. Why it works: most off-road page text labels things that a symbol and a number express unambiguously in every market. Back-of-envelope: the pitch readout resolves 1°, which equals about 1.7% grade, so a numeric angle and a slope graphic carry the information without words. The roll warning threshold comes from the static stability factor: SSF = T / 2h = 1.70 / (2 × 0.80) = 1.06, tip-over near 47°, and the warning sits at 35°. Benchmark: the Tesla Cybertruck's Off-Road app displays pitch and roll angles to show how well the truck can climb an obstacle, a numeric, language-neutral presentation.

title: Inclinometer zeroed at the wheel-alignment stand, deleting the separate levelling step
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Moves inclinometer zeroing onto the wheel-alignment stand, deleting the separate levelled-plate station's operator time and fixture. The only added cost is a small routine in the alignment tester and the inertial host. Baseline: on off-road-pack cars (35%) the pitch and roll offsets for the off-road pages and progress control are zeroed at a dedicated levelled-plate station, with a 35 s operator step and a €0.25M fixture. Proposal: the wheel-alignment stand already levels the car to ±0.05°. While the car sits there, the alignment tester sends a DoIP routine that averages the inertial sensor over 2 s and stores the offsets. Why it works: the alignment stand is the most accurately levelled place in the plant, and the car is already stationary on it. Back-of-envelope: a 0.05° level error gives an acceleration offset of g × sin 0.05° = 0.0086 m/s². Against a ±0.5° display accuracy target that is a tenfold margin, and 2 s of averaging at 100 Hz cuts sensor noise (0.01 m/s²) to about 0.001 m/s². Benchmark: the Jeep Wrangler's Off-Road Pages display pitch and roll, which need a correct zero to be credible.

title: Off-road pages built in the existing HMI framework, deleting a second 3D runtime licence
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Removes a second 3D HMI engine's per-unit runtime royalty by rebuilding the off-road pages in the already-licensed infotainment framework. The added cost is a one-off rebuild of the pages and their assets. Baseline: the off-road pages (3D vehicle with articulating wheels, pitch and roll, locker and ride-height states) run on a separate 3D HMI engine whose runtime licence costs about €2.8 per head unit. It is installed on every head unit because the pages are part of the common image. Proposal: rebuild the pages in the infotainment's existing HMI framework, already licensed per unit, using a pre-baked 8,000-triangle vehicle mesh with skinned wheel and suspension joints driven by live ride-height and steering signals. Why it works: the off-road pages need modest 3D, well inside the existing framework's renderer, so the second engine only adds royalty. Back-of-envelope: 8,000 triangles at 30 frames/s is 0.24 M triangles/s against an SoC GPU capacity above 100 M triangles/s, under 1% load. Benchmark: the Land Cruiser 250's Multi-Terrain Monitor runs camera views of the trail on the 12.3-inch touchscreen inside the main infotainment system.

title: Terrain calibration kept in a signed data partition so updates ship as data
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Separates terrain and off-road calibration into a signed, bounded data partition, so calibration-only releases need focused regression and a short install instead of a full image. The added cost is the one-off partition and bounds architecture. Baseline: any change to terrain or off-road assist calibration in the ESC or terrain manager after SOP ships as a full software image (about 8 MB). That triggers full regression (about €0.35M per release) and an 18-minute over-the-air install with the car immobilised. Proposal: an AUTOSAR calibration-data partition in a separate flash sector, versioned, signed and CRC-protected. Code enforces hard bounds on every parameter (for example HDC set speed 2-30 km/h, crawl wheel-torque ramp at most 2 kNm/s), so a data update cannot leave the validated envelope. A calibration-only release then needs focused regression (about €0.12M) and a 40-second install. Why it works: most post-SOP off-road changes are calibration, and the bounds-in-code rule makes their risk testable without re-proving the code. Back-of-envelope: data is 8 MB versus 0.2 MB per update. Over six calibration releases and 350,000 cars the full-image route would move 16.8 TB, and the data route 0.42 TB. Install time scales the same way. Benchmark: Rivian added a Soft Sand drive mode to R1T and R1S by over-the-air update after launch, showing that off-road behaviour keeps changing post-SOP.

title: Edge-summarised off-road telemetry uploads histograms instead of raw signal logs
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Cuts OEM-paid cellular data and cloud storage for off-road telemetry by more than 99% by summarising sessions on board into histograms and event lists. The added cost is the summarisation agent. Baseline: the connected-car platform's default logging uploads raw snapshots of 30 off-road signals at 20 Hz (4 bytes each), 2.4 kB/s, whenever an off-road mode is active. For a pack car (35%) with about 60 hours a year of off-road use that is 0.52 GB a year, at OEM-paid cellular cost of €0.9/GB and cloud storage of €0.03/GB-month retained for 7 years, over the 5-year included connectivity period. Proposal: the telematics unit computes on-board summaries per off-road session: 32-bin histograms and rainflow counts per signal and event lists (locker engagements, HDC descents with energy, wade events with depth), about 4 kB per session. Raw logs are captured only on demand for a specific engineering query. Why it works: engineering and warranty use the distributions and events, not the raw time history. Back-of-envelope: 2.4 kB/s × 3,600 s = 8.6 MB per off-road hour versus 4 kB per session, a reduction of more than 99%. Benchmark: Rivian's release 2023.38.0 brought Snow, Sand, All-Terrain and Rock Crawl modes to towing over the air, showing that the connected fleet already runs off-road software that can report usage.

title: Road drive modes and terrain modes merged into one mode manager
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the arbitration layer between separate road drive-mode and terrain managers, and the validation of their 28 combinations, by merging them into one ordered mode manager. The added cost is the one-off merge and re-validation of the merged states. Baseline: two state machines choose vehicle behaviour. A road drive-mode manager in the powertrain domain (Comfort, Eco, Dynamic, Individual) and a terrain manager in the chassis domain (terrain modes, low range, Wade) each send requests to dampers, ride height, steering and powertrain, and an arbitration layer resolves conflicts: 4 road modes × 7 terrain states = 28 combinations, many invalid. Proposal: one mode manager with a single ordered state list (road modes, then terrain modes, then overlays such as Wade and towing), each defining all actuator targets. Invalid combinations cannot exist, so the arbitration layer and its validation are deleted. Why it works: the driver only ever experiences one vehicle behaviour, so modelling two independent managers creates conflicts that then need arbitration. Back-of-envelope: a typical conflict is Dynamic (lower 15 mm, firm dampers) with Wade (raise 75 mm). Arbitration had to pick a 90 mm swing on the move. In one manager Wade simply supersedes Dynamic, and the ride-height move is ramped at 10 mm/s. Benchmark: Defender OCTA mode is reached by a long press of the steering-wheel logo button and works alongside Terrain Response calibrations, an example of road-performance and off-road behaviour handled as one mode family.

title: MHEV low-range shift interlock uses networked gear state, deleting hardwired neutral circuit
description: [MHEV] Deletes the hardwired neutral-confirmation circuit, its connector cavities and interface components on the MHEV off-road pack by using E2E-protected networked gear-state and speed signals. The added cost is a small software change. Baseline: on the MHEV off-road pack the transfer-case controller allows a high/low range shift only when the transmission is in N (or P) and speed is below 3 km/h. Neutral is confirmed by a hardwired circuit from the transmission controller (4.2 m, two cavities each end, an interface circuit), plus a hardwired brake-switch input. Proposal: the interlock uses the transmission controller's gear-state signal and the ESC's vehicle-speed and brake-pressure signals on the chassis CAN-FD, protected end to end (AUTOSAR E2E Profile 5 counter and CRC). A missing or invalid signal inhibits the shift. Why it works: the safe state of the interlock is 'no shift', which is exactly what a lost message produces, so the hardwired path adds no safety. Back-of-envelope: why the interlock matters: at 3 km/h the propshaft turns at 3 / 3.6 / 0.40 × 3.73 = 7.8 rad/s, and across the 2.6:1 low range the dog-clutch speed difference is about 12.4 rad/s. With 0.05 kgm² inertia that is ½Iω² = 3.8 J, acceptable. At 30 km/h it would be about 380 J, which the interlock prevents. Benchmark: the Land Cruiser 250's Multi-Terrain Select works in both 4WD High and Low, so its range state gates which mode set is available, the same networked range state used here.

title: Magnetic TMR angle sensor replaces the optical encoder in the terrain dial
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces the optical code wheel, emitter, phototransistors and index switch with one magnet and one absolute TMR angle sensor. This saves piece cost and assembly steps, and removes the optical path that fails with contamination. Baseline: the terrain selector reads knob position with a 24-position optical incremental encoder (slotted code wheel, IR emitter and dual phototransistor pair, €3.4) plus a separate index switch for absolute position at start-up (€0.6). Proposal: a diametrically magnetised NdFeB disc (6 mm) pressed into the knob shaft over a single-die TMR angle sensor (for example a 12-bit absolute angle IC) on the module PCB: €1.9 for magnet and sensor together. Why it works: an absolute magnetic angle sensor knows the knob position at power-up and has no optical path for dust, cleaning fluid or coffee to block. The detent feel comes from the mechanical cam, not from the sensor. Back-of-envelope: 24 detents means 15° per position. A 12-bit sensor resolves 0.09°, and even ±1.5° of air-gap and tilt error is a tenth of the detent pitch, so the position decoding has a wide margin. With 1.5 mm air gap a 6 mm N35 disc gives about 40 mT at the die, inside the 20-80 mT working range of TMR sensors. Benchmark: the Bronco's G.O.A.T. Modes dial is a console rotary mode selector, the same kind of part whose position sensing is changed here.

A 12-bit sensor resolves 0.09°, and even ±1.5° of air-gap and tilt error is a tenth of the detent pitch, so the position decoding has a wide margin. With 1.5 mm air gap a 6 mm N35 disc gives about 40 mT at the die, inside the 20-80 mT working range of TMR sensors. Benchmark: the Bronco's G.O.A.T. Modes dial is a console rotary mode selector, the same kind of part whose position sensing is changed here.

ideaData.dfmDfa: Magnet centring tolerance ±0.3 mm is held by a moulded pocket in the shaft. The sensor die sits under the shaft axis on the existing PCB with no light shield. No light shield needed.

title: One laser-etched PMMA light guide replaces individual terrain icon windows and LEDs
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces seven icon windows, seven light pipes and 14 LEDs with one etched PMMA ring guide and six LEDs. This cuts part count, PCB placements and assembly time; there is no added part. Baseline: the terrain selector ring shows seven mode icons, each a separate two-shot PC icon window with its own light pipe and white LED, plus a separate amber 'selected' LED per icon: 14 LEDs, 7 light pipes and 7 windows (€4.6 parts, €0.7 assembly). Proposal: one injection-moulded PMMA ring light guide with laser-etched icons, side-lit by 4 RGB LEDs, plus a selected-mode highlight from a narrow lit segment under the active icon driven by two further LEDs and an internal mask: €2.1 parts, €0.2 assembly. Why it works: the icons do not need individual light sources; a single guide with etched extraction features lights all of them evenly, and colour change marks the active mode. Back-of-envelope: a ring of 45 mm diameter is about 141 mm of guide. With 4 entry points the longest path is about 18 mm, and PMMA attenuation (about 0.2 dB/m in the visible) is negligible, so uniformity is set by the etch density, graded to ±15% luminance. Benchmark: the Lexus GX 550 Overtrail's Multi-Terrain Select offers distinct mode sets in high and low range, which shows how many icons a terrain selector has to show.

title: Zinc die-cast terrain knob grip ring with PVD finish replaces machined aluminium
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces a CNC-turned, knurled and anodised aluminium grip ring with a die-cast Zamak 5 ring with cast-in knurl and PVD finish. This removes the machining time and the anodising step; the only added item is the die-cast tool. Baseline: the terrain knob's grip ring is CNC-turned from 6061-T6 bar, diamond-knurled, bead-blasted and anodised: €5.8 at about 4 minutes machining per part. Proposal: a Zamak 5 (ZnAl4Cu1, EN 12844) high-pressure die-cast ring with the knurl cast in, vibratory-finished, base-coated (Cu-Ni plate or UV-cured basecoat lacquer, included in the €3.4) and PVD-coated (chrome-nitride, dark titanium or satin nickel colours to match trims): €3.4. Why it works: the knurl is a decorative and grip feature with no structural duty, and zinc die-casting reproduces a 0.6 mm pitch knurl sharply while PVD gives a hard metallic finish that resists rings and watches. Back-of-envelope: ring mass rises from 9 g (aluminium, ρ 2.7) to 22 g (zinc, ρ 6.6). The knob's rotational inertia at 22 mm radius is still only 22 g × 0.022² = 1.1 × 10⁻⁵ kgm², so the detent feel against the 0.12 Nm cam is unchanged to the hand. The surface is genuinely metal, so it still feels cold and heavy. Benchmark: the Bronco's G.O.A.T. Modes dial is the rotary mode selector that the driver grips, which is the part whose grip ring is re-specified here.

title: Low range selected by press-and-hold on the terrain dial, deleting the range switch
description: [MHEV] Deletes the separate range rocker switch, its illumination, connector cavity and harness branch on the MHEV off-road pack by using a press-and-hold on the terrain dial's existing push switch. Baseline: the MHEV off-road pack has a separate two-position High/Low range rocker switch in the console switch bank (€4.2 including switch, illumination, cavity and harness branch; €0.6 extra on the switch-bank PCB). Proposal: low range is requested by pressing and holding the terrain dial for 1.5 s, confirmed by the dial's illumination and a cluster message. The shift then runs only when the interlock conditions are met (transmission in N, speed below 3 km/h). The switch-bank cavity becomes a blank on MHEV pack cars, matching the road car and BEV. Why it works: range selection is infrequent and must be deliberate, which a press-and-hold gives better than a rocker, and the dial already has a push switch. Back-of-envelope: the press uses the existing 15 N tact switch under the knob. A 1.5 s hold with a release-before-shift rule cannot be triggered by a knock: a 1 kg hand bumping at 0.3 m/s delivers about 30 ms of contact, about fifty times shorter than the hold. Benchmark: the Bronco's Trail Control is switched on from a button in the centre of the G.O.A.T. Modes dial, showing that the dial's centre press can carry an off-road function.

title: Moulded POM cantilever detent replaces steel ball-plunger in the terrain dial
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces the steel ball, coil spring, brass sleeve and greasing step with a POM spring arm moulded into the knob carrier running on a glass-filled cam. This deletes three parts and an assembly step at no added piece cost. Baseline: the terrain dial's detent is a hardened steel ball and a coil spring in a brass sleeve, running on a 24-lobe zinc cam ring and greased at assembly: €1.15 parts and €0.35 assembly. Proposal: a POM (polyoxymethylene copolymer, low-friction grade) cantilever spring arm with a moulded nose, integral with the knob carrier moulding, running on a PA66-GF30 cam ring moulded into the housing, with no grease. Why it works: a dial detent needs about 0.1-0.15 Nm of torque and 200,000 cycles, within what a POM spring arm on a glass-filled cam gives, and integrating the spring into a moulding deletes three parts and a greasing step. Back-of-envelope: a 12 mm × 2.0 mm × 3 mm POM arm (E = 2.8 GPa) deflected 0.4 mm gives F = 3EIδ / L³ with I = 3 × 2³ / 12 = 2 mm⁴: 3 × 2,800 × 2 × 0.4 / 1,728 = 3.9 N. On a 15 mm cam radius with a 45° lobe flank that is about 3.9 × 0.015 = 0.06 Nm per arm, so two arms give 0.12 Nm. Peak strain is 3δt / 2L² = 0.8%, close to POM's room-temperature fatigue strain of about 1%, so the arm length is confirmed by fatigue test at 85 °C. Benchmark: the Land Cruiser 250's Multi-Terrain Select is a driver-selectable terrain control in 4H and 4L, and its selector feel is the reference attribute for this part.

title: Board-mounted connector on the terrain selector replaces the flying pigtail lead
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the flying pigtail, its strain relief, inline connector pair and console clip by using a board-mounted header on the module, extending the console harness branch slightly. This saves parts and a mating step and removes a rattle source. Baseline: the terrain selector module leaves the factory with a 180 mm flying pigtail (eight 0.35 mm² wires, PVC sleeve, overmoulded strain relief and inline connector: €1.6), which is clipped to the console frame and mated to the console harness during console assembly. Proposal: a sealed eight-way board-mounted header moulded into the module housing, with the console harness branch extended by 170 mm to reach it (+€0.4) and the clip deleted. Why it works: the pigtail exists only to bridge a gap the harness can bridge itself. Removing it also removes a connector pair, one of the commonest sources of console rattles and intermittent faults. title: Snap-in terrain selector with clip towers replaces three-screw fixing
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces three self-tapping screws and their torque-monitored driving cycle with four moulded snap hooks and a locating pin, saving fasteners and operator time with no added part. Baseline: the terrain selector module is fixed into the console frame with three M4 × 12 self-tapping screws into PP-T20 bosses, driven by a DC tool with torque monitoring: €0.12 screws plus about 24 s of operator time (€0.40). Proposal: four integral snap hooks on the module housing engage clip towers on the console frame, plus one locating pin for position, with a 40 N push-in and an audible click. A release slot lets service tools unclip it. Why it works: the module only needs to stay put against knob torque and push force, which snaps handle, and a push-in is faster than three screw cycles. Back-of-envelope: the worst operating load is the 15 N push plus a rough 40 N grab-and-pull on the knob. Four PC/ABS hooks with 1.2 mm undercut and a 90° retention face hold about 4 × 60 N = 240 N, six times the pull case. Detent torque of 0.12 Nm reacts on the locating pin at 20 mm radius, only 6 N. Benchmark: Defender's Terrain Response is controlled from a console switch module reconfiguring transmission, suspension and traction, the kind of interior control module whose fixing is simplified here.

title: Single-sided CEM-3 laminate replaces two-layer plated FR-4 in the terrain selector
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces two-layer plated FR-4 laminate with single-sided CEM-3 once the TMR sensor and single light guide reduce parts. This saves bare-board cost and keeps the same assembly process. Baseline: the terrain selector module's circuit carrier (about 48 × 48 mm) is two-layer FR-4 laminate with plated through-holes carrying a small MCU, LIN transceiver, angle sensor, push switch, six to fourteen LEDs and connector: €1.35 bare board. Proposal: with the TMR sensor and single light guide the parts count falls enough to route on one copper layer. Single-sided CEM-3 laminate with two zero-ohm jumpers and a printed carbon ground shield over the sensor area costs €0.55. Why it works: the circuit is low-speed (LIN at 19.2 kbit/s, LED PWM at 400 Hz) and low-current, which needs neither a second copper layer nor plated holes once the part count drops. Back-of-envelope: LED current at most 6 × 15 mA = 90 mA, plus MCU 20 mA, so 1 oz copper tracks of 0.3 mm carry this with under 5 K rise. LIN's slow edges radiate well below the UN R10 limits even without a ground plane, and CEM-3's Tg of about 125 °C exceeds the 85 °C console peak with margin. Benchmark: the Land Cruiser 250's Multi-Terrain Select is a driver terrain control module, the kind of small interior electronics whose board specification is set here.

title: Crawl and descent speeds set from the steering-wheel cruise switches, deleting console buttons
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the dedicated HDC button on every car and the crawl button and speed dial on the off-road pack, using the existing steering-wheel cruise switches and a touchscreen tile instead. No hardware is added. Baseline: the switch bank carries a dedicated HDC button on every car and, on the off-road pack (35%), a crawl and progress control button plus a five-position crawl speed dial: €2.6 for HDC (switch, illumination, cavity) and €6.4 for the crawl button and dial on pack cars. Proposal: the cruise-control switches on the steering wheel set off-road speeds. Below 30 km/h in an off-road mode, the cruise 'set' engages progress control, '+/−' steps the set speed in 0.5 km/h steps, and a long press on 'set' arms HDC. HDC also arms automatically in low range and Rock modes. A touchscreen tile gives the same functions. Why it works: the driver already holds the wheel, and speed setting is the same task as cruise control, so separate console controls duplicate it. Back-of-envelope: the five fixed crawl speeds of about 1-5 km/h become ten 0.5 km/h steps. At 2 km/h a 0.5 km/h step changes distance covered by only 0.14 m per second, fine enough for rock work. Benchmark: Range Rover Sport's Adaptive Off-Road Cruise Control is set with the steering-wheel switches that also run adaptive cruise, choosing one of four comfort settings, so dedicated console buttons are not needed.

title: 800V BEV crawl speed read from motor resolvers, keeping standard 48-pole wheel encoders
description: [800V BEV] Deletes the 800V BEV off-road pack's high-resolution 96-pole wheel-speed encoders and sensors by fusing the standard wheel-speed signals with traction-motor resolver speeds at crawl. The added cost is the speed-fusion software in the ESC. Baseline: to hold 1-2 km/h smoothly, the off-road pack fits high-resolution 96-pole wheel-speed encoder rings and matching sensors (€3.6 per car over the standard 48-pole set) on both powertrains. Proposal: on the 800V BEV the standard 48-pole encoders stay, and at crawl speed the ESC fuses them with the front and rear traction-motor resolver speeds, which are already on the chassis bus. The MHEV keeps the 96-pole set for now, because its gearbox output sensor is coarser and its driveline lash larger. Why it works: a resolver gives a continuous rotor angle, and the motor turns nine times faster than the wheel, so at walking pace it gives a smooth speed while the wheel encoders still give per-wheel slip. Back-of-envelope: at 1 km/h (0.278 m/s) a 2.55 m tyre turns 0.109 rev/s, so a 48-pole ring gives 5.2 edges/s, one every 190 ms, too coarse for a speed loop. A motor at 9:1 turns 0.98 rev/s, and a 12-bit resolver resolves 0.09° of rotor angle continuously, a speed update every millisecond. Benchmark: the G 580 with EQ Technology runs a crawl function as off-road cruise on four individually controlled motors, which shows that motor signals already carry the speed information.

title: Wade transducer thermistor deleted; ambient temperature corrects the speed of sound
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the NTC thermistor, its filter and a connector pin in each mirror wade transducer by correcting the speed of sound from the existing ambient-temperature signal. The added cost is a small logic change. Baseline: each of the two mirror wade transducers (60% fitment) carries an NTC thermistor, a filter and an extra connector pin to correct the ultrasonic time of flight for air temperature (€0.55 per transducer, two per car). Proposal: the wade logic uses the vehicle's ambient-air temperature (already measured behind the front grille and filtered for solar load) and the transducer's own resonant-frequency drift as a cross-check. The thermistor, its filter and the pin are deleted. Why it works: the air column between mirror and water is outdoor air close to ambient, so ambient temperature is the relevant figure and is already on the network. Back-of-envelope: c = 331.3 + 0.606 T. From −10 to +40 °C, c runs from 325.2 to 355.5 m/s, a 9% spread. Using ambient instead of a local thermistor leaves about ±3 K error after solar filtering, ±1.8 m/s, or ±0.5%. On a 1.05 m mirror-to-water path that is about ±5 mm of depth, small against the 50 mm display resolution. Benchmark: the Defender's Wade Sensing uses sensors to monitor water depth and alert the driver, with wading quoted up to 900 mm.

On a 1.05 m mirror-to-water path that is about ±5 mm of depth, small against the 50 mm display resolution. Benchmark: the Defender's Wade Sensing uses sensors to monitor water depth and alert the driver, with wading quoted up to 900 mm.

title: 800V BEV one-box brake estimates wheel pressures, deleting four wheel-circuit sensors
description: [800V BEV] Lets the 800V BEV off-road pack use the standard one-box brake unit by estimating wheel pressures from plunger position and a pressure-volume model, deleting four wheel-circuit pressure sensors. The added cost is the estimator development. Baseline: on the 800V BEV, whose integrated one-box brake unit (electric plunger, needed for regenerative blending) builds pressure for HDC, crawl and off-road progress control, the off-road pack specifies the variant with four wheel-circuit pressure sensors in addition to the plunger-circuit sensor (€9.5 premium). Proposal: the standard one-box unit. Wheel-circuit pressures are estimated from plunger position and speed, valve states and a per-circuit pressure-volume model, and off-road speed control closes its loop on wheel and vehicle deceleration. Why it works: with a plunger, the fluid volume pushed into each circuit is known from the plunger position, which makes the pressure estimate far tighter than on a pump-based unit, and the controller's real target is deceleration anyway. Back-of-envelope: holding 2 km/h on a 40% grade (21.8°) with a 2,850 kg BEV needs 2,850 × 9.81 × 0.371 = 10.4 kN, about 30 bar at the calipers. A ±3 bar estimate error is ±1 kN, a ±0.35 m/s² deceleration error, which the deceleration loop removes within 200 ms. Benchmark: Land Rover's HDC brakes each wheel separately to hold a steady descent speed, the per-wheel control this idea runs on estimated pressures.

title: Vector-drawn off-road graphics let the cluster use the next smaller flash device
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces pre-rendered bitmap sprite sheets for off-road views with run-time vector rendering, freeing about 176 MB so the cluster can use the 256 MB flash device instead of 512 MB. The added cost is the one-off asset conversion. Baseline: the cluster's off-road views (pitch and roll vehicle sprites at 1° steps, wheel-angle overlays, locker and ride-height states) are stored as pre-rendered bitmap sprite sheets, about 180 MB in all. That pushes the cluster's serial NOR flash from 256 MB to 512 MB (€2.3 premium on every car). Proposal: off-road graphics become vector paths and parametric 2D shapes rendered by the cluster's GPU at run time: vehicle outline transformed by pitch and roll, wheel graphics rotated by steering angle, states as tinted vector icons. About 4 MB of assets replace the 180 MB of sprites. Why it works: the sprites store the same few shapes at hundreds of angles, while a GPU can rotate and tint one shape per frame at negligible cost. Back-of-envelope: 2 views × 91 pitch × 91 roll angles would need about 16,500 frames; even at 1° in one axis at a time, 360 sprites of 480 × 480 × 4 bytes is 330 MB uncompressed, about 180 MB compressed. A vector outline of about 400 path points transformed per frame at 60 fps is trivial GPU work. Benchmark: the Cybertruck's off-road digital gauges show heading, pitch and roll in degrees, numeric and graphic views that suit vector rendering.

title: Off-road camera views called from a configurable steering-wheel button and auto-triggers
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the dedicated console camera button, its illumination, cavity and harness branch on the off-road pack by defaulting the existing configurable steering-wheel button to camera view and adding automatic open and close triggers. Baseline: the off-road pack (35%) adds a dedicated console 'camera view' button with illumination to open the terrain camera views (€3.1 including switch, cavity and harness branch, plus €0.4 on the switch-bank PCB). Proposal: the existing configurable steering-wheel button (already fitted for a driver-chosen shortcut) defaults to the camera view on off-road-pack cars. The views also open automatically when an off-road mode is active and speed is below 15 km/h, or when the pitch exceeds 10° at crest approach, and close above 20 km/h. Why it works: the driver wants the cameras at specific moments that the car can detect, and the configurable button already exists. Back-of-envelope: at a crest, the bonnet hides the ground ahead. With a 0.9 m bonnet height at 2 m from the eye, the driver loses sight of the ground within about 4.5 m. At 5 km/h (1.4 m/s) that is about 3 s of approach, so an automatic trigger on pitch gives the view early enough. Benchmark: the HUMMER EV's underbody cameras let drivers monitor wheelspin and tyre placement from the driver's seat, which shows the value of quick camera access off-road.

title: Off-road inclinometer computed from airbag and ESC inertial sensors, deleting the IMU satellite
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the off-road pack's separate six-axis IMU satellite, bracket and harness branch by computing pitch and roll from the ESC and airbag controller's existing inertial sensors. The added cost is the fusion software and bus signals. Baseline: the off-road pack (35%) fits a separate six-axis IMU satellite on the tunnel (€11.5 with bracket, connector and harness branch) to feed the off-road pages' pitch and roll and progress control's side-slope logic. Proposal: pitch and roll are computed from inertial sensors already on every car: the ESC's yaw-rate and lateral and longitudinal accelerometers, and the airbag controller's roll-rate and vertical accelerometers, broadcast on the chassis bus. A complementary filter fuses them, with longitudinal acceleration corrected by wheel-speed derivative to separate grade from acceleration. Why it works: static pitch and roll are just the gravity vector in body axes, which the existing accelerometers see once vehicle acceleration is subtracted, and the rate sensors smooth the transients. Back-of-envelope: on a 30% grade (16.7°) gravity gives a_x = 9.81 × sin 16.7° = 2.82 m/s². A wheel-speed-derived acceleration error of 0.05 m/s² is 0.3° of pitch, inside the ±0.5° display target. The rollover warning at 35° sits well below the static tip angle of about 47° (SSF 1.06). Benchmark: the Jeep Wrangler's Off-Road Pages display pitch and roll for the driver.

title: Head-unit dead-reckoning gyro and mirror compass deleted; ESC signals and GNSS replace them
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the head-unit dead-reckoning gyro on every car and the off-road pack's mirror magnetometer by using ESC yaw-rate and wheel speeds plus GNSS course for navigation and compass heading. The added cost is fusion software in the head unit. Baseline: the head unit carries its own dead-reckoning sensor (gyro plus accelerometer, €2.4) for navigation in tunnels and under tree cover, and the off-road pack's compass display uses a magnetometer module in the interior mirror (€3.2 on 35%). Proposal: dead reckoning uses the ESC's yaw-rate sensor and wheel speeds over the bus (both already published at 10-20 ms). Heading comes from dual-frequency GNSS course-over-ground when moving, held through stops and slow crawling by integrating ESC yaw rate. The head-unit gyro and the mirror magnetometer are deleted. Why it works: the ESC sensors are better than a consumer-grade head-unit gyro and are calibrated by the ESC, and a GNSS heading avoids the magnetometer's need for compensation for the steel body and the large currents of a 48 V or 800 V system. Back-of-envelope: a yaw-rate offset of 0.1°/s, after the ESC's standstill offset learning, drifts 6° per minute, but GNSS course corrects it whenever speed exceeds about 2 m/s. On a 10-minute rock crawl at under 1 m/s, offset learning at each stop keeps drift to a few degrees. A magnetometer near 300 A of 48 V current sees field changes around 60 µT at 1 m, larger than Earth's 50 µT. Benchmark: the Cybertruck's off-road gauges show heading, pitch and roll in degrees, a heading display this idea sources from ESC and GNSS.

Proposal: dead reckoning uses the ESC's yaw-rate sensor and wheel speeds over the bus (both already published at 10-20 ms). Heading comes from dual-frequency GNSS course-over-ground when moving, held through stops and slow crawling by integrating ESC yaw rate. The head-unit gyro and the mirror magnetometer are deleted. Why it works: the ESC sensors are better than a consumer-grade head-unit gyro and are calibrated by the ESC, and a GNSS heading avoids the magnetometer's need for compensation for the steel body and the large currents of a 48 V or 800 V system. Back-of-envelope: a yaw-rate offset of 0.1°/s, after the ESC's standstill offset learning, drifts 6° per minute, but GNSS course corrects it whenever speed exceeds about 2 m/s. On a 10-minute rock crawl at under 1 m/s, offset learning at each stop keeps drift to a few degrees. A magnetometer near 300 A of 48 V current sees field changes around 60 µT at 1 m, larger than Earth's 50 µT. Benchmark: the Cybertruck's off-road gauges show heading, pitch and roll in degrees, a heading display this idea sources from ESC and GNSS.

title: In-car off-road guide replaces the printed off-road owner supplement
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces the 96-page printed off-road supplement in 38 language versions with an in-car, app and online guide, keeping a one-page printed quick card for safety limits. This saves printing and language-sequenced logistics; the added cost is content production. Baseline: every off-road-pack car (35%) ships with a printed off-road supplement of about 96 pages in the market language, covering terrain modes, wading, recovery and crawl control, printed in 38 language versions with small print runs, plus language-sequenced delivery to the line: €3.8 per car. Proposal: the off-road guide lives in the head unit as context-linked pages with short animations, opened from each off-road page's info icon. It is also in the owner app and online. A one-page quick card with the regulatory and safety content (wading depth limit, recovery-point use, HDC limits) stays in the glovebox pack. Why it works: off-road guidance is most useful at the moment of use, which an in-car page delivers, and printing many small-language runs is costly. Back-of-envelope: 96 pages on 60 g/m² paper weigh about 180 g, so 17,500 pack cars a year carry about 3.2 t of print. The quick card keeps the vital limits physical: for example the 0.9 m wading limit, where the head on door seals is ρgh = 8.8 kPa. Benchmark: the G 580's G-Turn only works under specific conditions and reviewers call it finicky to engage, which shows that off-road functions need instructions at the point of use.

title: Coolant-jacketed compressor head on BEV LT loop allows a smaller off-road air compressor
description: [800V BEV] Downsizes the air-suspension compressor from a 360 W to a 280 W motor by removing its thermal duty-cycle limit, so the BEV no longer buys flow it can only use half the time. Fin shroud and the head thermal cut-out relay are deleted (the motor-winding bimetal fuse is kept as the hardware backstop, so a stopped LT pump or a hot LT loop during DC fast charge cannot overheat the head); added cost is a cast-in coolant jacket and two quick connectors on the existing LT loop. Baseline: every air-suspended car uses an air-cooled 12 V dry-running single-stage compressor of 360 W (about 35 l/min free air at 10 bar). It was sized up from 280 W because off-road cycling (extended height, cross-link re-levelling on rock steps) reaches the 160 °C head cut-out after about 6 minutes, so the unit runs at roughly 50% duty. Proposal: on the 800V BEV, the low-temperature coolant loop that already serves the pack and EDU (25-40 °C) is routed through a jacket cast into the AlSi9Cu3 cylinder head, with two 10 mm spigots and a 1 l/min branch. A 280 W unit then runs at 100% duty. Why it works: the lift is served from the reservoir; the compressor only refills, so delivered air per 20 minutes is what matters. Check: 280 W × 0.6 heat fraction = 170 W; at 1 l/min coolant, ΔT = 170 / (0.0167 kg/s × 3,600 J/kg·K) ≈ 2.8 K, so the coolant barely warms; the head temperature (target below 110 °C) is set by the jacket film coefficient and must be confirmed on an instrumented dyno. Air over 20 min: 27 l/min × 20 = 540 l(n) versus 35 l/min × 10 min = 350 l(n) for the baseline. One 75 mm off-road lift

Applies to BEV air-suspended cars = 40% × 70% = 28%. Per affected vehicle: compressor −€22, shroud and relay −€3, jacket +€6, hoses and connectors +€7, net about €12. Compressor motor 360 W → 280 W: (€22 − €0) × 28% = €6.16. Fin shroud and thermal cut-out relay: (€3 − €0) × 28% = €0.84. Cast-in coolant jacket: (€0 − €6) × 28% = €-1.68. LT-loop branch hoses and quick connectors: (€0 − €7) × 28% = €-1.96. Net mid €3.36 per vehicle; range ±15% engineering uncertainty → €2.9-€3.9 per vehicle (fleet average) × 50,000 vehicles/yr = €145K-€195K per year (engineering estimate; tooling and one-off costs amortised over 7 years = 350,000 vehicles where stated).

ideaData.riskNotes: Coolant leak into the compressor head must be impossible: jacket is a separate gallery with no shared seal to the air path, validated by 3 bar helium leak test and 1,000 h thermal cycling. Validate the off-road duty cycle in 45 °C desert rock-crawl, ISO 20653 IP6K9K, and the wading depth case (900 mm) with the head hot. Coolant branch must not starve pack cooling during DC fast charge (FMVSS 305 / UN R100 thermal checks unchanged). title: BEV air-supply unit moved into frunk above wading line, dropping submersion sealing
description: [800V BEV] Moves the whole BEV supply unit (compressor, dryer, valve block) from the underfloor to a frunk side pocket above the 900 mm wading line. This deletes the IPX7 submersion-grade motor seals and connector, the long breather line and the unit's own underfloor splash shield. Added cost is longer air lines and a decoupled bracket. title: Single 6-litre reservoir sized from lift-cycle air mass replaces twin 5-litre tanks
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Sizes reservoir volume from the air mass one off-road lift actually needs, so one 6 l tank replaces two 5 l tanks. This deletes one tank, its bracket, a tee and a line. The only added cost is the slightly larger single tank. Baseline: two 5 l steel reservoirs at 16 bar gauge, each with its own bracket, joined by a tee and an extra PA12 line. The volume was carried over from a heavier earlier programme. Proposal: one 6 l reservoir. The spec becomes 'one full standard-to-off-road lift from the reservoir with the compressor running alongside', instead of 'two lifts from the reservoir'. Check: lifting 75 mm with effective areas of 0.0110 m² (front) and 0.0095 m² (rear) changes spring volume by ΔV = 2 × (0.0110 + 0.0095) × 0.075 = 3.1 l at about 10 bar abs. That is about 31 l(n) of free air. Discharging 6 l from 17 bar abs down to 11 bar abs (1 bar margin above spring pressure) gives 6 × (17 − 11) = 36 l(n) if the tank stays at ambient temperature. A 20 s lift is nearly adiabatic, though: the tank air cools to about 260 K and only about 27 l(n) is delivered, so the compressor runs during the lift to cover the last 10-15% (validate at −30 °C). The second lift that 10 l allowed is rare, because the driver stays at off-road height on a trail. The compressor refills the 6 l tank in about 1.5 minutes. Lift time stays within 20 s because valve-block flow, not reservoir size, sets the rate. title: One air-suspension calibration for MHEV and BEV using on-line axle-load estimation
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces the separate MHEV and BEV air-suspension calibrations (and their off-road-pack sub-variants) with one data set that adapts to the axle loads it estimates from spring pressure and height. This removes three of four calibration variants, their winter and desert test campaigns and their variant management. Baseline: four air-suspension calibrations: MHEV, BEV, and an off-road-pack sub-variant of each. Each has its own levelling gains, lift-rate limits, cross-link thresholds and wheel-lift detection set for a fixed axle-load range. Each is signed off in winter, desert and trail campaigns (about €0.45M per variant). Proposal: one calibration whose gains are scheduled on axle load estimated on line. Load is spring pressure × effective area at the measured height: F = p·Aeff(h), using the rolling-piston area curve from the supplier. Check: front spring at 9 bar gauge with Aeff 0.0110 m² carries 0.9 MPa × 0.0110 m² = 9.9 kN of spring force (the spring sits inboard on the arm, so this is more than the wheel load). A ±3% error in Aeff gives ±30 kg per corner, well inside the 2,450 kg (MHEV) to 2,950 kg (BEV) kerb spread the schedule covers. Wheel-lift detection on articulation (spring pressure drop with height at full droop) is a ratio test, so it works at any mass. Off-road-pack functions (cross-link, extended height) are switched by coding, not by a separate calibration. Benchmark: the Rivian R1S offers several heights up to about 380 mm maximum ground clearance on one air system, the kind of multi-mode range one adaptive calibration must cover.

title: Damper-integrated stroke sensors replace four arm-linkage ride-height sensors on BEV

title: Aramid-fibre outer cover on rolling bellows deletes the off-road stone-guard sleeve
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the off-road pack's split PA6 stone-guard sleeves and the front TPE gaiters, with their bands and clips, at every corner. All air springs get a 0.8 mm chloroprene outer cover loaded with aramid pulp that resists abrasion on its own. The added cost is the cover compound on every air spring. Baseline: at off-road height more bellows is exposed, so the off-road pack fits a split PA6 stone-guard sleeve and a TPE gaiter at each corner. Both are fixed with clamping bands. Sand trapped between gaiter and bellows is a known wear mechanism. Proposal: every air spring is built with a 0.8 mm CR outer cover compounded with 3 phr para-aramid pulp. DIN ISO 4649 abrasion loss is below 90 mm³, against about 140 mm³ for the standard CR cover. The sleeve and gaiter are deleted, so there is no cavity to trap grit. Check: a 10 g stone thrown from the tyre at 20 m/s carries ½ × 0.01 × 20² = 2 J. Drop-weight testing of 2 J at 23 °C and −30 °C on the aramid cover must show no cord exposure, which a standard cover only passes with the sleeve. The sleeve also takes branch and rock contact at full droop, so the bare cover must match the sleeve-protected spring on the same sharp-edge puncture and impact energy the sleeve is released to (measured on the current sleeve), not just 2 J. The bellows reinforcement and burst margin (4× working pressure) are unchanged because the cover is outside the cord plies. Benchmark: listed Defender 110 air-suspension ground clearance spans 218-290 mm, so at top height much more rolling bellows is exposed to spray and stones than at road heigh

title: Front cross-link valve moved into a seventh valve-block cartridge, deleting its remote housing
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Moves the off-road pack's left-right cross-link valve from its own housing on the front crossmember into a spare seventh cartridge bore in the main valve block. This deletes the remote housing, its bracket, connector, harness branch and two of its four line joints. Baseline: the off-road pack has a separate 2/2 cross-link valve in its own aluminium housing on the front crossmember. It is teed into the FL and FR spring lines, with its own bracket, connector, harness branch and four line joints. Proposal: the valve block is moulded with a seventh cartridge bore on all cars. On off-road-pack cars it holds a normally-closed cross-link cartridge using the common coil, connecting the FL and FR galleries inside the block; on other cars the bore is plugged. Check: the left and right springs only need to equalise slowly, at about 1 l(n)/s, so the extra 4.2 m of 6 mm line between block and springs (about 0.13 l each) adds less than 0.2 s to a settling time of about 2 s on a twisted ramp. Normally closed means that when power or software is lost the axle is not cross-linked, so road roll stiffness from the springs is kept by hardware. Cross-link is commanded only below 30 km/h. Benchmark: the Defender OCTA's hydraulically interlinked 6D suspension lets the wheels articulate more off-road; our pneumatic cross-link does the same job at lower cost inside the existing valve block.

title: Compressor thermal model in valve-block ECU replaces head NTC sensor and its pigtail
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the compressor head NTC thermistor, its two-wire pigtail and connector pins. A calibrated lumped thermal model in the valve-block ECU estimates head temperature from motor current, supply voltage, run time and ambient temperature. The motor's bimetal thermal fuse stays as the hardware backstop. Baseline: an NTC thermistor pressed into the compressor head, with a pigtail and two extra pins, reports head temperature so the ECU can stop the compressor at 160 °C during repeated off-road levelling. Proposal: a two-node thermal model, head and motor, runs at 10 Hz in the valve-block ECU. Inputs are motor current (already measured for stall detection), supply voltage, run time and the ambient sensor, plus a local-air offset for the MHEV underfloor position near the downpipe (local air reaches about 110 °C on a low-range climb). Time constants are identified on the dyno: head about 240 s, motor about 600 s. The model trips at 150 °C estimated, 10 K below the old limit, to cover model error. Check: at 300 W input and 60% heat fraction, the head rise rate from cold is about 180 W / (0.9 kg × 900 J/kg·K) ≈ 0.22 K/s. The model error band seen in correlation (±8 K over 30-minute cycles) is inside the 10 K margin. The bimetal fuse in the motor winding (opens at 180 °C) stays as the independent hardware protection, so overheating never depends on software alone. Benchmark: GMC states that frequent Hummer EV air-suspension use may require a cooling period, which shows OEMs already manage compressor heat in software visible to the driver.

title: Reservoir pressure read through the valve-block gallery sensor, deleting the separate reservoir sensor
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the dedicated reservoir pressure sensor, its harness branch and connector. The ECU briefly opens the reservoir valve to the valve-block gallery, with all corner valves closed, and reads the existing gallery sensor. Only software is added. Baseline: the valve block has one gallery pressure sensor used to read each corner in turn, plus a separate pressure sensor screwed into the reservoir port with its own harness branch. The ECU uses reservoir pressure to choose between lifting from the reservoir and running the compressor. Proposal: before every height change, and every 60 s when stationary, the ECU closes all corner valves and opens the reservoir valve to the gallery for 150 ms. It reads the gallery sensor and closes the valve. Check: the gallery volume is about 8 cm³. Equalising with a 6 l reservoir at 16 bar changes reservoir pressure by less than 0.03 bar, so the reading is true to ±0.05 bar. A 150 ms opening of a 12 W coil once a minute uses about 0.03 Wh per hour (polling every second would use about 1.8 Wh per hour, add 3,600 valve cycles and click audibly, so it is not done). Off-road the decision to lift from the reservoir or the compressor is taken once per command, so a reading before each command, refreshed every 60 s, is ample. Benchmark: the Cybertruck manual describes Extract as a deliberate, speed-limited maximum lift, so a reading of stored air taken before the lift is enough to decide whether the reservoir can serve that one lift.

title: Injection-moulded PA66-GF35 valve-block body replaces machined 6082-T6 aluminium block
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces a machined and anodised 6082-T6 valve-block body with a heat-stabilised PA66-GF35 moulding. Galleries are moulded by core pulls and the solenoid seats are brass inserts. Machining time, aluminium and anodising are removed; inserts and a laser-welded cover are added. Baseline: the valve-block body is a 6082-T6 extrusion slug machined with 22 drillings and five valve seats, then anodised. It weighs 0.42 kg and costs about €19. Proposal: a heat-stabilised PA66-GF35 moulding. Straight galleries come from core pulls, cross-drillings are replaced by a moulded channel plate laser-welded to the body, and the five valve seats are moulded-in CuZn39Pb3 brass inserts. Check: hoop stress in a 6 mm gallery with a 3 mm wall at 20 bar (relief setting) is σ = p·r/t = 2.0 × 3 / 3 = 2 MPa. The 10,000 h creep limit for PA66-GF35 at 85 °C is about 25 MPa, so the margin is more than 10×. Burst test is 4× working pressure (64 bar). The off-road wading case is a hot block (85 °C) plunged into 5 °C water. That thermal shock suits glass-filled PA well, because it has no anodising to craze and no galvanic pair with the steel fixings. The block sits inside the supply unit housing and is not a strike-exposed part. Benchmark: listed 2024 Defender 110 trims carry electronic air suspension with 900 mm wading, which shows the valve block must survive repeated hot-to-cold immersion.

title: Hard-anodised 6082 cylinder bore deletes the pressed steel liner in the air compressor
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the pressed-in stainless cylinder liner and its honing operation. The cylinder becomes a 6082-T6 extruded tube with a 40 µm type III hard-anodised bore running against a PTFE piston ring upgraded to 25% bronze filler. Baseline: the compressor cylinder is an AlSi9Cu3 casting with a pressed-in 1.0 mm stainless liner, honed to Ra 0.2 µm, running against a PTFE piston ring. The liner exists because high-silicon cast alloy anodises poorly. Proposal: the cylinder is a 6082-T6 extruded tube (low silicon), hard-anodised type III to 40 µm (about 400 HV) and diamond-honed in the same fixture as the head face. The PTFE ring gets 25% bronze filler. Check: piston speed at 3,000 rpm with a 12 mm stroke is 2 × 0.012 × 50 = 1.2 m/s, mean. Ring contact pressure at 16 bar is about 0.5 MPa. So PV is about 0.6 MPa·m/s, well inside the roughly 1.5 MPa·m/s limit for bronze-filled PTFE on hard anodise. Off-road dust: intake air is filtered, but the filter lets through particles below 10 µm; the fine dust that passes the filter is mostly quartz (about 1,100 HV), harder than the 400 HV anodise, so wear life rests on the filter rating and the dust-injection test, not on hardness. Wear test target: < 15 µm bore wear in 1,000 h duty. Benchmark: the Rivian R1 tyre guide describes an onboard compressor used for tyre sealing, which shows compressors in this segment are expected to cope with dusty roadside duty.
