title: Push-in fitting with moulded cross-link orifice replaces brass in-line restrictor and two joints
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Combines the brass in-line orifice that limits left-right cross-flow when the off-road cross-link is open with the push-in fitting at the valve block, as a laser-drilled orifice in the PA66 fitting body. This deletes two brass restrictors and four line joints per car. Baseline: when the off-road cross-link valve connects left and right air springs on an axle, a 0.8 mm brass orifice fitting in each cross-link line limits the flow rate. This prevents sudden body lurch when a wheel drops off a rock step. Each restrictor is a separate brass part with two push-in ends, adding two joints per line. Proposal: the orifice is laser-drilled (0.80 ± 0.02 mm) into the PA66-GF30 body of the push-in fitting at the valve block, ahead of the collet. Check: choked flow through 0.8 mm at 10 bar abs upstream is about ṁ = 0.0404 × A × p0 / √T0 = 0.0404 × 5.0e-7 × 1.0e6 / √293 = 1.2 g/s, about 1.0 l(n)/s. Moving 10% of a 3 l front spring's air (0.3 l at 10 bar abs = 3 l(n), a 50 mm wheel-travel shift) takes about 3 s at that upper-bound rate, and longer in practice because the left-right pressure difference is far below the ratio needed for choked flow; this keeps body motion slow as intended. The orifice is protected from dirt by the existing dryer and the fitting's 100 µm inlet screen. Benchmark: the Defender OCTA's hydraulically interlinked suspension lets the wheels articulate more off-road; our cross-link does the same pneumatically and needs the flow limit.

title: Snap-off PA66 ball-cup height-sensor links replace crimped steel rods on MHEV
description: [MHEV] Replaces four crimped steel ride-height sensor links with moulded PA66-GF30 links whose ball cups snap off at 250 N and can be clipped back on. Part cost is lower and off-road warranty for bent links and recalibration is avoided, because a branch strike releases the link instead of bending it. Baseline: the MHEV keeps rotary height sensors (the BEV moves to damper stroke sensors). Each has an M6 steel rod with crimped steel ball joints. A branch or rock pushing the rod bends it permanently. The sensor then reads wrong, the car levels to a wrong height and a dealer has to replace the link and recalibrate (about €160). Proposal: a one-piece PA66-GF30 link with moulded ball cups that hold 120 N in normal use and release at 250 ± 30 N. Afterwards the link can be pushed back by hand without tools, and the calibration is kept because the link length is fixed. Check: normal link force from sensor spring and inertia at 15 g suspension acceleration is below 20 N, so 120 N retention gives 6× margin. A 250 N release is well below the 600 N that bends the M6 rod or the 900 N that damages the sensor shaft. When a cup is off, the ECU sees an implausible height (rate above 1 m/s or mismatch with spring pressure), holds height, lowers to normal height on the other three sensors and spring pressure before road speed is reached, and shows a message. Headlamp levelling (UN R48) falls back to a safe low aim. Benchmark: the mild-hybrid Defender 110 D350 is sold with electronic air suspension, so height sensing on an MHEV must survive off-road use.

title: Dryer regeneration silencer moulded into dryer end cap with check-valve exhaust port
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Moves the exhaust silencer into the dryer end cap as a moulded chamber packed with PET fibre, with an EPDM duckbill check at the port. This deletes the bolt-on silencer, its bracket and its hose. Baseline: when springs are lowered or the dryer regenerates, air vents through a separate bolt-on silencer (PA6 body with sintered bronze element) on a bracket, connected by a short hose. The silencer port has its own check flap so wading water cannot enter. Proposal: the PA66-GF30 dryer end cap gets a moulded 45 cm³ expansion chamber packed with needle-punched PET fibre, and the exhaust port is closed by an EPDM duckbill valve. Check: the duckbill opens outward at about 1 kPa, so venting is not restricted. Inward it holds more than 30 kPa. Static head at a submerged port at 900 mm wading (port at 350 mm) is ρgh = 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.55 = 5.4 kPa, so the margin is more than 5×. A 1.5 l spring venting from 10 bar through a 2 mm port takes about 1.5 s, and the 45 cm³ chamber plus fibre cut peak noise by about 12 dB(A), matching the old silencer in the acoustic test. Benchmark: listed 2024 Defender 110 trims carry air suspension with 900 mm wading, so exhaust ports on the air supply must hold out water under head pressure.

title: One solenoid coil and armature serve every valve in the air-suspension valve block
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Cuts the valve block's three coil variants and two armature types to one 9 W coil with PWM hold and one armature. The high-flow exhaust valve becomes pilot-operated so it can use the same coil. The added cost is the pilot stage. Baseline: the valve block has four corner valves with 6 W coils, a reservoir valve with an 8 W coil and a high-flow exhaust valve with a 12 W coil, plus two armature sizes. That is three coil part numbers, two armatures and three winding set-ups. Proposal: all six valves use one 9 W coil (pull-in at 9 W, then 3 W PWM hold) and one armature. The exhaust valve becomes a pilot-operated valve: the common solenoid opens a 1.2 mm pilot and system pressure opens the 4 mm main seat. Check: force to open a 1.2 mm seat at 20 bar is F = p·A = 2.0 MPa × 1.13e-6 m² = 2.3 N, well within the common armature's about 6 N pull-in. The main seat area is 12.6 mm², so at 10 bar the pressure on it is about 12.6 N; the main stage opens because the pilot vents the chamber behind a larger main piston or diaphragm, so the opening force is set by that area, not the seat. Exhaust flow is unchanged, so off-road lowering from extended height still takes less than 8 s. PWM hold reduces coil heat during long cross-link holds on a trail. Benchmark: the Rivian R1S uses multiple air-suspension heights up to about 380 mm, each needing reliable valve hold, which PWM hold improves.

title: Pneumatic disconnect actuator fed by the air-suspension supply replaces motor-gear disconnect drive
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces the disconnect's 12 V DC motor, three-stage gear, ball screw and magnetic holding brake with a single-acting pneumatic piston. The piston is fed from a spare valve-block port of the air suspension every off-road-pack car already has. The driver stage in the chassis ECU is deleted. A 3/2 solenoid valve and a short air line are added. Baseline: the front anti-roll bar has a centre dog-clutch disconnect driven by a 12 V DC motor through a gear set and ball screw. A magnetic brake holds it open, a spring re-engages it and a Hall sensor reports its state. Proposal: keep the dog clutch, spring and Hall sensor. Replace the drive with a Ø 40 mm PA66-GF30 piston, single-acting against the 450 N engagement spring. Air comes from a spare valve-block port through a 3/2 solenoid valve. Check: at 10 bar the piston gives F = p·A = 1.0 MPa × 1.26e-3 m² = 1,260 N, which overcomes the 450 N spring plus 300 N of dog friction with 1.7× margin. Air per actuation is 40 mm bore × 12 mm stroke = 15 cm³ at 11 bar abs, about 0.17 l(n), which is negligible next to a 31 l(n) lift. Fail-safe: loss of air, power or software vents the piston and the spring engages the bar. So the road-going connected state never depends on software or pressure. Re-engagement is also forced above 30 km/h by venting. Benchmark: owners describe the factory Jeep disconnect as a DC motor and piston with a magnetic holding brake and spring re-engagement. We keep the spring fail-safe and delete the motor and brake.

title: Warp-compliant front axle makes a second, rear-axle disconnect redundant off-road
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the rear disconnect actuator, the rear split-bar premium and its harness on the off-road pack. Once the front bar is disconnected and the front air springs are cross-linked, the warp stiffness of the whole car is already low (about 2.9 kN/m against 1.5 kN/m with both axles open), because the two axles act in series in warp. Baseline: the off-road pack fits a disconnect on each axle plus left-right air cross-link on both axles. Proposal: keep disconnect and cross-link on the leading axle only; the trailing axle gets the road car's one-piece hollow stabiliser. Why it works: in warp (diagonal articulation, one wheel up at each end) the two axles' roll stiffnesses act in series, so the car's warp stiffness is kw = k1·k2 / (k1 + k2). With the leading stabiliser open and its springs cross-linked, k1 falls to about 3 kN/m at the wheel (bushes and dampers only), while k2 stays at about 60 kN/m. Then kw = 3 × 60 / 63 ≈ 2.9 kN/m, against 1.5 kN/m with both axles open. At 300 mm of diagonal articulation the wheel-load change is 2.9 × 0.3 = 0.87 kN, against 0.45 kN, and both are small next to an 8 kN static wheel load. So traction and wheel lift are essentially unchanged on a cross-axle ramp. What changes is that the body follows the locked axle instead of floating, so side-slope body angle on twisted ground must be checked. Benchmark: the Lexus GX E-KDSS unlocks its two stabilisers independently; series warp stiffness shows that unlocking one, with cross-linked springs, is enough.

title: Anti-roll bar, disconnect and drop links arrive as one supplier-tested subframe module

title: Multibody articulation sign-off replaces two prototype ramp-and-twist build series
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces two physical prototype series (12 vehicles) used for twist-ditch, RTI ramp and component-clearance checks across connected, disconnected and cross-linked states. A correlated flexible multibody model is used instead, and one two-vehicle confirmation build is kept. Prototype and test-track cost falls; model building and correlation are added. Baseline: articulation clearances are signed off on two prototype series of six vehicles each. These cover brake hoses, ABS leads, air lines, half-shaft angles, tyre-to-liner contact and bar-half sweep, at every ride height with bars connected and disconnected and cross-link open and shut. The cost is about €3.2M. Proposal: build a flexible multibody model (Adams Car with flexible subframe and hoses as beam elements). Correlate it to one instrumented mule on a 600 mm axle-twist ramp to within ±5 mm on clearances and ±0.5° on joint angles. Run the full state matrix virtually, about 3 ride heights × 2 bar states × 2 cross-link states × both powertrains = 24 configurations. Keep one two-vehicle confirmation build on the twist ditch for durability. Check: target diagonal articulation is 560 mm. A brake hose must keep 20 mm of slack at full droop, and on a 0.47 m half-length bar each half sweeps about 0.13 rad at 60 mm of bar-end travel. All of these are geometric states a model resolves exactly once correlated. Benchmark: the Lexus GX E-KDSS is marketed on increased articulation, which shows articulation figures are a headline specification that must be signed off across every state.

title: Hydraulic compression stop in front damper replaces PU jounce bumper for off-road landings
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Fits a hydraulic compression stop in the off-road-pack front dampers, so the off-road reinforced top mounts and the second-stage PU bumpers can be deleted. The stop's flat force curve cuts peak top-mount load. The hydraulic stop premium is added. Baseline: front dampers have a 90 mm microcellular PU jounce bumper. The off-road pack adds a second-stage bumper and reinforced top mounts because a landing after a wheel drops off a step loads the tower to about 45 kN peak. Proposal: an extra piston near the end of compression stroke enters a restricted cup and builds hydraulic force over the last 60 mm. Check: front quarter sprung mass is about 800 kg. A 250 mm drop gives E = m·g·h = 800 × 9.81 × 0.25 = 1.96 kJ. The air spring and main valving take about 0.8 kJ, leaving about 1.2 kJ for the stop. A PU bumper's rising force curve peaks at about 45 kN for that energy. A hydraulic stop at a near-flat 20 kN over 60 mm absorbs 20 × 0.06 = 1.2 kJ, cutting peak load by 55%. So the road car's standard top mount and tower reinforcement cover the off-road pack, and the second-stage bumper is not needed. The PU bumper stays as a shorter 40 mm progressive element for road feel. Benchmark: the Defender OCTA fits active dampers with separate accumulators and tougher wishbones, which shows that controlling landing loads is part of off-road suspension design.

title: Off-centre bar split moves MHEV disconnect actuator clear of downpipe, deleting heat shield
description: [MHEV] Moves the MHEV front bar's split point 240 mm left of centre, so the disconnect actuator sits under the left rail instead of 70 mm from the I6 downpipe. This deletes the stainless heat shield and lets the actuator use standard 120 °C materials instead of high-temperature grades. Baseline: on the MHEV the front bar passes behind the sump with the split and actuator at the centre, about 70 mm from the downpipe and catalyst (550-650 °C). The actuator needs a stainless heat shield, a PA46 housing, fluorocarbon seals and 150 °C grease. The BEV has no exhaust and uses the standard actuator. Proposal: split the MHEV bar at 240 mm left of centre, so the halves are 0.43 m and 0.57 m. When connected, the bar's stiffness is unchanged because the dog joint is rigid. Disconnected, each half is free anyway, so asymmetry has no effect. Check: radiant flux from a pipe falls roughly with distance. Moving from 70 mm to 310 mm cuts it by about 75%, so the actuator surroundings drop from about 140 °C to about 95 °C on a sustained low-range climb at 20% grade. That lets the actuator use the BEV's PA66 housing, HNBR seals and standard grease. Benchmark: the Land Cruiser 250's SDM is described as an actuator mounted directly on the front stabiliser bar, which shows the actuator sits in the hot zone next to the engine and exhaust.

title: BEV front subframe casting node doubles as the anti-roll-bar disconnect housing
description: [800V BEV] Deletes the disconnect's separate die-cast housing and its two bar-clamp brackets on the BEV. The split joint sits in a cylindrical pocket cast into the BEV's aluminium front subframe centre node, and an actuator cartridge slides in. Added cost is pocket machining on off-road-pack subframes and a seal plate. Baseline: the disconnect housing is a 0.9 kg AlSi9Cu3 die casting (€16 plus €6 machining) clamped onto the bar halves, with the bar carried in two bushes on the subframe. The BEV front subframe is an AlSi10MnMg HPDC structure with a centre node above the front EDU mounts. Proposal: the node is cast with a Ø 72 mm cylindrical pocket on the bar axis on all BEV subframes. On off-road-pack subframes it is bored and faced (+€5). The dog-clutch actuator is a cartridge pushed in and closed by a seal plate (+€3), and the bar halves run in PTFE-lined bushes in the node. Check: peak bar torque is about 1.3 kN·m (6 kN link force × 0.22 m lever). That load passes through the dog teeth, not the housing, and the reaction into the node is the two bush radial loads of about 6 kN each, already designed into the subframe's bar-mount load case. The pocket wall of 6 mm sees a bearing stress of 6 kN / (72 mm × 25 mm) = 3.3 MPa, which is trivial for AlSi10MnMg-T7. The node sits 330 mm above ground behind the EDU, so it is shielded by the existing front skid plate. Benchmark: Toyota's Land Cruiser 250 uses a separate actuator mounted on the bar, the conventional arrangement we integrate.

title: Slim torsion core across split joint deletes disconnect centring spring and rotation stops
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the disconnect's centring torsion spring and the two bar-half rotation-stop brackets with buffers. A Ø 12 mm 51CrV4 torsion core links the two halves through the joint and keeps about 8% of bar rate when the dog is open. The core holds the halves near alignment and stops them flailing. Baseline: when disconnected, each bar half rotates freely. To stop the halves flailing into the subframe and to bring them back into line for re-engagement, the pack has a coaxial centring spring and two cast rotation-stop brackets with rubber buffers. Proposal: a Ø 12 mm 51CrV4 torsion core, 380 mm long, runs through the hollow halves and is splined into each half about 190 mm either side of the joint. When the dog is engaged it carries almost nothing. When the dog is open it provides the only coupling. Check: torsional stiffness of the core is k = G·J / L = 79 GPa × (π × 0.012⁴ / 32) / 0.38 = 79e9 × 2.04e-9 / 0.38 ≈ 424 N·m/rad. The main bar is about 5.3 kN·m/rad, so the core keeps about 8%. Shear stress at 0.4 rad of twist (full disconnected articulation) is τ = T·r / J = 170 × 0.006 / 2.04e-9 ≈ 500 MPa, within the about 700 MPa torsion fatigue limit of shot-peened 51CrV4. The 8% residual warp stiffness adds about 0.25 kN of wheel-load change at 300 mm of articulation, against an 8 kN static load. Benchmark: owners describe the factory Jeep disconnect as re-engaging by a spring when power is removed, which shows that re-centring is a standard function we can do with the core instead.

title: One 30 mm bar diameter, tuned by wall thickness, shares disconnect across powertrains
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Sets both powertrains' front bars to one 30 mm outside diameter, tuning stiffness by wall thickness. This removes a second disconnect dog-clutch and spline size, a second bush set and the duplicate tooling and PPAP for them. Baseline: the MHEV front bar is Ø 28 mm with a 5 mm wall and the heavier BEV bar is Ø 32 mm with a 4.5 mm wall. So there are two spline sizes, two dog-clutch sleeve sets, two actuator bores and two bush sizes for the off-road disconnect. Proposal: both bars are Ø 30 mm. The MHEV gets a 4.0 mm wall and the BEV a 6.0 mm wall. Check: torsional stiffness scales with J = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/32. Ø 28 × 5 gives J = π(28⁴ − 18⁴)/32 = 5.0e4 mm⁴. Ø 30 × 4.0 gives π(30⁴ − 22⁴)/32 = 5.6e4 mm⁴ (+12%, trimmed back by a 2% longer lever arm and bush rate). Ø 32 × 4.5 gives π(32⁴ − 23⁴)/32 = 7.5e4 mm⁴. Ø 30 × 6.0 gives π(30⁴ − 18⁴)/32 = 6.9e4 mm⁴ (−8%), which is within what the BEV needs with the lower centre of gravity. Stress at the 1.3 kN·m peak torque on the BEV bar is τ = T·r / J = 1,300 × 0.015 / 6.9e-8 = 283 MPa, inside the 34MnB5 Q&T fatigue limit. The MHEV bar must also be checked: 1,300 × 0.015 / 5.6e-8 ≈ 350 MPa in the tube, with only about 2.8 mm of wall left under a 1.2 mm spline, so its spline ends need local upsetting. Benchmark: Toyota reports SDM fitted to the Land Cruiser 250 range, with owner reports that it became optional on some trims, which shows the disconnect has to be cheap across variants.

title: 48 V smart disconnect actuator with on-board LIN driver deletes 12 V ECU
description: [MHEV] Moves the MHEV disconnect motor to the 48 V bus, with its driver and logic on a small board in the actuator connected by LIN. This deletes the separate 12 V disconnect ECU, its bracket and connector. Motor current falls by 4×, so the harness drops from 2.5 mm² to 0.5 mm² wire. Baseline: the MHEV disconnect uses a 12 V brushed motor (peak about 15 A) controlled by a small dedicated ECU on the front-end carrier. A 2.5 mm² feed runs to the actuator, plus Hall-sensor and CAN wiring. Proposal: a 48 V brushless motor (peak about 3.8 A for the same 180 W). A board in the actuator carries the half-bridge, Hall interface and LIN transceiver, reporting state to the chassis domain controller, which commands it over LIN. Check: same power at 4× voltage means 4× less current. I²R loss in a 1.8 m 0.5 mm² wire at 3.8 A is 3.8² × (1.8 × 2 × 0.036 Ω/m) ≈ 1.9 W, against 15² × (1.8 × 2 × 0.0072) ≈ 5.8 W at 12 V. The speed gate (relock above about 30 km/h) is done in the domain controller, and the actuator's own logic re-engages if LIN is lost. The engagement spring stays, so the connected state is mechanical and never depends on the 48 V bus or software. Benchmark: Toyota's Land Cruiser 250 SDM relocks automatically above about 30 km/h; we keep that rule, with a mechanical spring as the fail-safe.

title: Sinter-hardened powder-metal dog rings replace machined case-hardened 20MnCr5 rings in disconnect
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces the machined, carburised 20MnCr5 dog-clutch rings in the bar disconnect with net-shape sinter-hardened powder-metal rings. Hobbing, shaping, carburising and grinding are deleted. Baseline: the disconnect's two dog rings (12 teeth each) are turned from 20MnCr5 bar, the teeth are shaped, the rings carburised to 58-62 HRC and the faces ground. A pair costs about €11. Proposal: compact the rings net-shape in FLN2-4405 (Fe-Ni-Mo) to 7.2 g/cm³ and sinter-harden by fast cooling in the sinter furnace to about 600 HV. Only the bore is sized. Check: peak bar torque is about 1.3 kN·m. With 12 teeth at a 22 mm mean radius and 6 teeth sharing load (allowing for pitch error), the force per tooth is 1,300 / (0.022 × 6) = 9.8 kN. On an 8 × 6 mm face that is 205 MPa of contact pressure. That is within the about 400 MPa allowable for sinter-hardened FLN2-4405 at 7.2 g/cm³, and tooth-root bending at 9.8 kN is below its about 450 MPa bending fatigue limit. Engagement happens only below 30 km/h with near-zero relative speed, so impact wear is low. Benchmark: the Land Cruiser 250 adds a front stabiliser disconnect to a mass-market Land Cruiser, which shows dog-clutch disconnects are now built in high-volume vehicles.

title: ePTFE membrane vent replaces the disconnect actuator's breather hose to a high point
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the 1.8 m breather hose, its clips and the high-point bracket that vent the disconnect actuator above the wading line. A screw-in ePTFE membrane vent on the actuator lets air through but holds out water at the wading head pressure. Baseline: the actuator sits about 300 mm above ground. A 1.8 m breather hose runs up to a bracket in the engine bay (MHEV) or frunk (BEV) so that, when a hot actuator is plunged into cold water, the vacuum it draws pulls in air rather than water. Proposal: a screw-in ePTFE membrane vent (IP68 / IP69K rated, water entry pressure above 70 kPa) directly on the actuator. Check: static head at the actuator at 900 mm wading plus a 200 mm bow wave is ρgh = 1,000 × 9.81 × (1.1 − 0.3) = 7.8 kPa, so the membrane margin is about 9×. Thermal pumping: 0.25 l of internal air cooling from 80 °C to 10 °C wants to contract by 20%, i.e. about 50 cm³. Under water the vent cannot draw air, so the contraction is not breathed in: internal pressure falls by up to about 20 kPa and the shaft and cover seals see about 28 kPa including the 7.8 kPa head. The membrane (70 kPa) holds, so the seals must be validated to at least 30 kPa inward; above water the membrane breathes the 50 cm³ in about 10 s at its 0.3 l/min. Benchmark: listed 2024 Defender 110 trims quote 900 mm wading with air suspension, which is the head our vent must resist.

title: PTFE-lined steel-backed bushes replace needle bearings at the anti-roll-bar split joint
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces the two drawn-cup needle bearings that support the bar halves inside the disconnect housing with PTFE-lined steel-backed plain bushes. Relative rotation at the joint is small and slow, so a plain bearing is enough and costs less. Baseline: two drawn-cup needle bearings (about €1.9 each) carry the bar halves in the disconnect housing so the halves can rotate relative to each other when disconnected. Proposal: two PTFE-lined steel-backed bushes (DU type, about €0.6 each) pressed into the housing. Check: relative rotation at the joint is at most ±0.4 rad at about 0.5 rad/s when crawling. On a 30 mm journal that is a sliding speed of 0.015 × 0.5 = 0.0075 m/s. Radial load is at most 6 kN on a 30 × 20 mm projected area, so p = 10 MPa. PV = 0.075 MPa·m/s, far below the about 1.8 MPa·m/s limit for PTFE-lined bushes. When connected there is no relative rotation, so wear only accumulates off-road. Life target: < 0.05 mm wear in 200 h of disconnected crawling. Benchmark: owners describe the factory Jeep disconnect as a mechanism used at crawling speeds only, which is exactly the low-PV duty in which a plain bush suits.

title: Hall switch with magnet moulded into the shift fork replaces contactless angle sensor
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces the contactless linear position sensor on the disconnect's shift sleeve with a two-state Hall switch and a ferrite magnet moulded into the PA shift fork. The sensor only has to report engaged or open; it does not need to measure position. Baseline: a contactless linear position sensor (PCB, ASIC and target, about €7) reads the dog sleeve position over 12 mm, so the ECU knows the disconnect state and can light the dash indicator. Proposal: a unipolar Hall switch (about €0.9) in the actuator end cap and a ferrite magnet moulded into the PA66-GF30 shift fork (about €0.4). The switch trips at 9.5 ± 0.5 mm of sleeve travel (fully engaged = 10 mm) and the ECU confirms 'connected' only with the switch made and spring-side travel complete. Check: Hall switch hysteresis is about 0.5 mm, so a partly engaged dog (below 9 mm) reads 'not connected'. The ECU then shows a warning and limits speed to 80 km/h until confirmed. The spring keeps pushing the dog into engagement, so the indicator never controls the mechanical state. Benchmark: Toyota's manual notes that on uneven ground the stabiliser state may not switch and can differ from the indicator, which shows that the sensor only needs to tell engaged from not.

title: Nested wave spring replaces coil engagement spring, shortening disconnect housing by 18 mm
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces the coil spring that engages the dog sleeve with a nested multi-turn wave spring of the same load. Taking about half the coil's axial space, it shortens the actuator housing by 18 mm, saving aluminium and machining. The wave spring costs a little more. Baseline: a 51CrV4 coil spring, 45 mm free length, preloaded to 450 N and rising to 600 N at 12 mm of disengaged travel, pushes the dog sleeve into engagement. The housing is long enough to hold its solid height plus travel. Proposal: a nested multi-turn wave spring in 17-7PH stainless, with the same 450-600 N over 12 mm and an 18 mm shorter working height. Check: wave springs typically reach a given load in about 50% of a coil spring's axial space. The rate needed is (600 − 450) / 12 = 12.5 N/mm, which a 3-turn nested wave of 0.5 mm × 4 mm flat wire on a 42 mm diameter meets. The housing gets 18 mm shorter, which removes about 90 g of AlSi9Cu3 and 18 mm of turning. Stainless 17-7PH also avoids the coil's corrosion risk in the actuator when water gets past a seal after wading. Engagement force stays above 450 N, so the spring fail-safe (connected) is unchanged. Benchmark: owners describe the factory Jeep disconnect as relying on a spring to re-engage the gears, which is the fail-safe function we keep.

title: Air-suspension supply gains a tyre-inflation port, deleting the 12 V accessory inflator
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Gives the air-suspension valve block an auxiliary port with a check valve, piped to a capped coupling in the rear bumper. A coiled hose with a gauge chuck lets the owner re-inflate aired-down tyres from the car's own compressor and reservoir. This deletes the 12 V portable inflator and its storage tray in the off-road pack. Baseline: the off-road pack ships a 12 V portable inflator (about 35 l/min free flow, 25 minutes for four tyres) in a foam tray, because owners air down to about 1.2 bar for sand and rock. Proposal: a fourth auxiliary port on the valve block, behind its own 2/2 valve and a check valve, feeds a 6 mm PA12 line to a capped quick coupling behind the rear bumper. The kit is a 7 m coiled PU hose with a clip-on chuck and gauge. Check: a 275/70R18 tyre holds about 85 l of air. Going from 1.2 to 2.4 bar gauge needs 85 × 1.2 ≈ 100 l(n) per tyre, about 410 l(n) for four. The reservoir supplies about 36 l(n) first, then the compressor delivers about 40 l/min against 2 bar back-pressure. That makes roughly 10 minutes of running for four tyres. It is split into runs with cool-downs inside the compressor's duty limit, so about 20 minutes in total, still quicker than the 25-minute portable inflator. The valve block isolates the springs: the corner valves stay shut and the check valve stops tyre air flowing back, so ride height is held. Benchmark: Rivian's R1 tyre guide describes an onboard air compressor used with the sealant kit, which shows owners in this segment expect built-in tyre air.

title: Supplier sends TPMS IDs with sequenced tyre-wheel sets, deleting plant learn station
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the end-of-line TPMS trigger-and-learn station. The tyre-wheel supplier already reads each sensor's ID during its function test; it now sends ID and wheel position with the sequenced delivery. The plant writes the IDs to the car during end-of-line configuration and confirms by first drive-off. Baseline: at end of line an operator triggers each sensor with a 125 kHz LF tool and writes the IDs. That covers four sensors, or five on the off-road pack with a full-size spare. It takes about 1.6 minutes, with a 0.8% rework rate for missed or swapped IDs. Proposal: the wheel-and-tyre line reads each sensor ID and pressure during its own 100% sensor test. It then sends ID, position (FL, FR, RL, RR, spare) and VIN through the sequencing advance notice. The end-of-line diagnostic flash writes the IDs with the rest of the configuration, and the first drive at the plant's roll-test confirms reception from each sensor. Check: labour saved is about 1.4 minutes × €0.85 = €1.19. Rework falls by 0.8% × €15 = €0.12. LF tool upkeep saves €0.2. The off-road pack's aired-down use makes position accuracy matter, because a swapped ID shows a wrong corner pressure on the trail. A supplier mis-sequence is caught at roll-test. Benchmark: Ford sells Bronco and Bronco Raptor TPMS as 5-piece sets, i.e. a sensor in the spare too, so position and spare IDs are part of the data set.

title: Satin single-colour powder finish replaces diamond-cut bi-colour on off-road-pack wheels
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the diamond-cut lathe operation, the second clear coat and the bi-colour mask on off-road-pack wheels. They get a satin single-colour powder coat plus one clear, which is also less prone to chip and filiform corrosion when stones and mud hit the cut face. Baseline: off-road-pack 20-inch wheels are dark base powder, wet paint, CNC diamond-cut face and acrylic clear (about €38 per wheel for finishing, five wheels with a matching spare). Diamond-cut bare aluminium under thin clear is prone to filiform corrosion once stone chips break the clear, which off-road use guarantees. Proposal: a satin single-colour polyester powder (60-70 µm) over a chrome-free pretreatment, plus one satin clear, at about €21 per wheel. Check: stone-chip resistance (ISO 20567-1, multi-impact at −20 °C) improves from about rating 3 to about 1.5, because there is no thin clear over a machined edge. Filiform corrosion (EN 3665, 1,000 h) on a cut-face wheel typically shows creepage from scribes above 2 mm, while a fully powdered face shows less than 1 mm. The cut lathe op (about 2.5 minutes per wheel) and its cycle and scrap (about 3% of cut wheels) are removed. Benchmark: Ford's Bronco Sasquatch package uses black-painted aluminium wheels, which shows a plain painted finish is accepted on off-road-pack wheels.

title: Three pressed wheel studs on spare carrier replace adaptor plate, cone and lock nut
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Presses three M14 × 1.5 studs into the tailgate spare carrier at the wheel's own pitch circle. The full-size spare is held by three of its own lug nuts, which deletes the steel adaptor plate, the centring cone and the special central lock nut with its key. Baseline: the full-size tailgate spare is clamped by a central threaded spigot through a stamped steel adaptor plate, a rubber-faced centring cone and a special locking hand nut (about €14 in total, plus fitting). Proposal: three M14 × 1.5 10.9 knurled studs pressed into bosses on the carrier at the wheel's 5 × 120 pitch circle. The spare is held by three standard lug nuts from the road kit, one being the locking nut. Check: the spare and tyre weigh about 36 kg. A 4 g vertical rough-road load gives 36 × 9.81 × 4 = 1.4 kN, plus the overhang moment. Three M14 10.9 studs torqued to 140 N·m give about 60 kN of clamp each, far above the separating load, and the wheel's own conical seats centre it. Tailgate hinge loads are unchanged because the mass is unchanged. Rattle on corrugations is removed because the wheel is clamped on its seats rather than on a cone and rubber face. Benchmark: the Ineos Grenadier carries its spare on the rear 30/70 split doors, a carrier layout that must stay tight on corrugated tracks.

title: Knitted TPU-coated spare-wheel cover replaces two-piece painted PP-T20 hard cover
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces the off-road pack's two-piece injection-moulded, painted PP-T20 hard spare cover and its lock with a 3D-knitted polyester cover coated in TPU. It has an elastic drawcord, a moulded-in logo patch and retention under the spare's own nuts. Two moulds, painting and the cover lock are deleted. Baseline: a two-piece PP-T20 hard cover (face and band) is painted body colour and held by a key lock. It costs about €62 per car with two moulds (about €0.9M) and a paint process. Stone strikes chip the paint and the face can crack on impact with a tree. Proposal: a seamless 3D-knitted PET cover with a 0.3 mm TPU coating, a knitted-in logo and colour, and an elastic band. The cover's inner flange is trapped under the three spare-wheel nuts, so no separate lock is needed. Cost is about €22. Check: knitting has no mould, so a colour or logo change is a yarn change. The TPU coat holds water out at a 1,000 mm hydrostatic head (ISO 811) and resists UV (ISO 105-B02, grade 4 after 300 h). Spray from the wheels and branches cannot crack it. Wind load at 180 km/h is q = ½ × 1.2 × 50² = 1.5 kPa on 0.5 m², about 750 N, carried by the trapped flange and band. Benchmark: aftermarket suppliers sell hard ABS covers shaped for the Ineos Grenadier's door-mounted spare, showing the cover is a styled, owner-visible part.

title: Flat-face spokes replace clip-in aero inserts on BEV off-road-pack all-terrain wheels
description: [800V BEV] Deletes the four clip-in PA6 aero inserts on BEV off-road-pack wheels, which pack with mud, crack on rocks and come off in deep ruts. Flat-faced spokes recover about 40% of the insert's drag benefit. The inserts and their warranty go; there is a small range penalty. Baseline: every BEV wheel carries a clip-in PA6-GF15 aero insert (about €15 per wheel, four per car; the spare has none). It closes the spoke windows and is worth about 0.006 m² of CdA. Off-road the inserts trap mud (wheel imbalance), crack on rocks and get lost in ruts, with an off-road-pack warranty claim rate of about 3%. Proposal: off-road-pack BEV wheels drop the inserts and use flat-faced spokes, with the spoke face flush to the rim flange within 8 mm. That recovers about 40% of the drag benefit (0.0024 m²). Check: a net CdA rise of 0.0036 m² at 120 km/h adds F = ½ × 1.2 × 33.3² × 0.0036 = 2.4 N, about 0.08 kW, roughly 0.7 Wh/km at 120 km/h, and about 0.2-0.3% over the slower WLTP cycle (0.5% is used below as a conservative figure). All-terrain tyres already cost 5-7% of range through rolling resistance and tread drag, so the insert's share is small. Mud packing: an open face lets water jets clean the spokes, avoiding a 30-50 g imbalance from mud trapped behind the insert. Benchmark: the Defender OCTA rides on 33-inch all-terrain tyres developed for the model, which shows off-road-pack tyres are specified for capability rather than range.

title: MHEV off-road pack moves to 18-inch wheels with 275/70R18 all-terrain tyres of equal diameter
description: [MHEV] Replaces the MHEV off-road pack's 20-inch wheels and 275/60R20 tyres with 18-inch wheels and 275/70R18 tyres of the same rolling diameter. The smaller wheel is cheaper, the tyre is cheaper, and the 27 mm taller sidewall suits airing down. MHEV front brakes still fit inside the 18-inch wheel, so they are not downsized. Baseline: MHEV and BEV off-road packs share 20-inch wheels with 275/60R20 AT tyres (diameter 508 + 2 × 165 = 838 mm). Proposal: on the MHEV only, an 18-inch 8.5J flow-formed wheel with 275/70R18 AT tyres (457 + 2 × 192.5 = 842 mm, +0.5%). Speedometer and gearing are unchanged within tolerance. Check: the MHEV's 363 mm front disc with its four-piston caliper needs a 395 mm radial envelope. An 18-inch wheel's inner barrel gives about 418 mm, a 23 mm clearance after the 3 mm minimum dust allowance. The BEV's 400 mm front disc (sized for a heavier car and descent-with-full-battery thermal duty) does not fit, so the BEV stays on 20-inch. Brakes are not reduced on either powertrain. The taller sidewall gives 27 mm more tyre deflection at 1.2 bar, which lowers rim-strike risk on rocks. Wheel cost falls about €38, and tyre cost about €8 per corner. Benchmark: Ford's Bronco Sasquatch pairs 35-inch tyres with 17-inch wheels, showing that big rolling diameter on a small wheel is the off-road norm.

title: BEV all-terrain tyres delivered without PU cavity-foam absorbers on the off-road pack
description: [800V BEV] Deletes the bonded polyurethane cavity-noise foam from BEV off-road-pack all-terrain tyres. AT tread noise and the taller sidewall already mask the cavity tone, and the foam gets in the way of plug repairs and bead-breaking on the trail. Baseline: every BEV tyre has a 20 mm PU foam ring bonded to the inner liner (about €9 per tyre, five on the off-road pack). It damps the tyre-cavity resonance that is otherwise audible in a quiet BEV. Proposal: delete the foam on the off-road pack's AT tyres only; road BEVs keep it. Check: the cavity mode is about f = c / (π × D_mean) = 343 / (π × 0.63) ≈ 173 Hz. Foam typically cuts that peak by 6-8 dB in the cabin. On an AT tyre with a 70-series sidewall, tread-block noise in the 500-1,000 Hz band sits about 3 dB(A) above the road tyre's overall level, and the softer sidewall passes less of the 173 Hz mode into the hub. Measured overall cabin noise with and without foam on AT tyres is expected to differ by about 1 dB(A), against about 3 dB(A) on summer tyres. Off-road: a plug repair through foam often fails because the foam tears and blocks the plug, and foam soaked with water after bead-breaking unbalances the wheel. Benchmark: the Defender OCTA's 33-inch Goodyear AT tyres were developed specifically for the model, which shows off-road-pack tyres get their own specification.

title: Full-size spare without fifth TPMS sensor, declared not for five-tyre rotation
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the fifth TPMS sensor and its valve from the off-road pack's full-size spare. The regulations require monitoring of the road wheels fitted, not the spare, so the spare reports a malfunction indicator only while it is fitted. The cost is a customer feature: five-tyre rotation is no longer supported. Baseline: the full-size tailgate spare carries a fifth TPMS sensor (about €24 with clamp-in valve) so it can be rotated into use like a road wheel. Proposal: the spare has a plain clamp-in metal valve (about €3). When it is fitted, the system shows the TPMS malfunction indicator, which UN R141 and FMVSS 138 allow when a wheel without a sensor is fitted. The handbook states the spare is for emergencies and short trail recovery and should not be rotated in. Check: spare pressure is checked at each service and owners are reminded by the car every 90 days. A full-size AT spare loses about 0.1 bar per month, so a 2.4 bar spare is still at about 2.1 bar after 3 months, enough to drive on. This is honest decontenting: the saving is real OEM cost, and the feature loss is stated, not hidden. Benchmark: Ford sells Bronco and Bronco Raptor TPMS as 5-piece sets, which shows a spare sensor is the norm we choose to depart from.

title: 3-ply sidewall XL or HL passenger-construction all-terrain tyre replaces LT-construction tyre
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Specifies the off-road-pack AT tyre in passenger construction with a 3-ply sidewall, as an extra-load (XL) tyre for MHEV and a high-load (HL) tyre for the heavier BEV, instead of an LT 10-ply tyre. The tyre is cheaper and about 4-5 kg lighter per corner, with about 80% of the LT tyre's sidewall puncture energy, a capability reduction that is stated to customers. Baseline: the off-road pack fits LT275/70R18 125/122S (load range E) AT tyres, about 25 kg each, five per car. That is more carcass than a 3.2-3.5 t passenger SUV needs. Proposal: a passenger-construction AT tyre with a 3-ply sidewall and 3PMSF marking. MHEV: 275/70R18 XL 116T (1,250 kg per tyre). BEV: HL 120T (1,400 kg) because GVW is about 3,450 kg. Check: the BEV's heavier axle (1,850 kg) puts about 925 kg on each tyre, × 1.1 margin = 1,018 kg, well below 1,400 kg. The MHEV's 1,700 kg axle puts about 850 kg on each tyre, × 1.1 = 935 kg, below 1,250 kg. A 3-ply sidewall gives about 80% of the LT tyre's sidewall puncture energy in plunger tests, much better than a 2-ply passenger tyre. Mass is about 20.5 kg versus 25 kg, saving about 18 kg of unsprung and rotating mass per car (four fitted). That gives BEV rolling-resistance and range benefits we do not count in the saving. Benchmark: Ford's Bronco Sasquatch uses LT315/70R17 tyres, the LT construction we step back from for a passenger luxury SUV.

title: BEV off-road pack drops the tyre-sealant bottle that duplicates its full-size spare
description: [800V BEV] Deletes the sealant bottle and its holder from BEV off-road-pack cars, which also carry a full-size spare. Road BEVs keep the sealant kit because they have no spare. Tyre air for the plug kit comes from the pack's inflator, or from the onboard inflation port where that idea is adopted. Baseline: every BEV ships a tyre-mobility kit (sealant bottle about €14, holder and foam tray about €4) because road BEVs have no spare. The off-road pack adds a full-size spare on the tailgate but keeps the sealant kit, so it carries two puncture solutions. Proposal: BEV off-road-pack cars delete the sealant bottle and holder, and the boot tray is the MHEV off-road-pack tray. Check: sealant cannot seal sidewall cuts or holes over 6 mm, which are the typical off-road punctures from rocks and branches, while a full-size spare covers all of them. A second puncture on a trail is the case where sealant helps; we keep the plug-repair kit (€3), which also works on AT tyres without cavity foam. Sealant also has a 4-year shelf life, so deleting it removes one service replacement (about €14 to the customer at year 4, a customer cost we do not count in the saving). Benchmark: Rivian's R1 tyre guide limits its sealant kit to roadside use and says sidewall holes or holes larger than 6 mm call for repair or replacement, which shows sealant does not cover typical off-road damage.

title: Clip-in TPV spare-carrier buffers replace screwed and bonded rubber buffers on steel cups
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces three NR buffers on screwed steel cups, bonded with adhesive, on the tailgate spare carrier with three fir-tree clip-in TPV buffers. Parts, adhesive, screws and 1 minute of fitting are saved. Baseline: the spare bears on the carrier through three NR rubber buffers vulcanised to steel cups, each screwed and bonded to the carrier (about €5.6 plus €0.8 of labour). They stop the tyre rattling on corrugations. Proposal: three TPV (70 Shore A) buffers with fir-tree stems clipped into 8 mm holes cast in the carrier, at about €1.6 for three. Check: the spare is about 36 kg. On a 3 g corrugation event the three buffers share about 36 × 9.81 × 3 = 1.06 kN, about 350 N each. A Ø 30 mm TPV pad at 70 Shore A deflects about 1.5 mm at 350 N, enough to preload the tyre against the carrier without rattle. Fir-tree pull-out is above 400 N, and the buffer is in compression so it cannot be pulled out in use. Compression set (ISO 815, 70 h at 100 °C) for TPV is about 35%, similar to NR. Benchmark: the Ineos Grenadier carries its spare on the rear door, a rear-carried spare that has to stay quiet on corrugations.

title: One wheel-bolt length across road and off-road wheels by matching hub-face pad thickness
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Sets the bolt-seat pad of every road and off-road wheel, spare included, to one 22 mm thickness. One M14 × 1.5 wheel-bolt length then serves all cars. This deletes a bolt variant, its kanban and the camera check that guards against fitting short bolts to thick off-road wheels. Baseline: off-road wheels have a 28 mm bolt-seat pad (thicker for kerb and rock strike), against 22 mm on road wheels. So there are two bolt lengths (M14 × 1.5 × 36 for road and × 42 for off-road, each giving 14 mm of engagement in the hub), and a vision check stops a × 36 bolt going onto an off-road wheel, where it would engage only 8 mm (about 5 threads). Proposal: off-road wheels get the 22 mm pad at the seat and keep the thicker section between seats, and every car uses the × 36 bolt. Check: required thread engagement is at least 1.0 × D = 14 mm, about 9.3 threads at 1.5 mm pitch; 36 − 22 = 14 mm meets it on every wheel. Rock-strike resistance comes from the spoke root and rim, not the seat pad; the UN R124 13° impact test passes with a local fillet and +1.5 mm at the spoke root. Mis-build of the wrong bolt, a safety-critical error, is designed out rather than inspected out. Benchmark: Ford's Bronco Sasquatch package fits its own off-road wheel to a mass-market platform, the variant problem this commonisation removes.

title: Two-section spine skid from front beam to transfer case replaces three overlapping plates
description: [MHEV] Merges the separate sump, transmission and transfer-case plates of the MHEV off-road pack into two press-formed sections with one shingled lap. Deletes 11 fasteners, 4 brackets, one press die and two fitting operations while every zone keeps at least its baseline gauge. Baseline: the MHEV off-road pack (35% take on a 60% MHEV mix, so 21% of the fleet) carries three bolt-on plates in 5083-H111 aluminium (EN 485/573): a 5 mm sump plate (6.8 kg), a 4 mm transmission plate (4.9 kg) and a 4 mm transfer-case plate (4.1 kg). Each joint overlaps by 30 mm, and the set needs 26 M10 fasteners and 9 brackets. Proposal: a two-section spine. The front section is one 5 mm 5083-H111 blank (about 1,250 × 780 mm) press-formed over sump and gearbox. The rear section is 4 mm over the transfer case. One shingled lap puts the rear section's leading edge above (inboard of) the front section's trailing edge, so a rock sliding rearward steps off a trailing edge and never meets an open forward-facing one. 15 fasteners and 5 brackets remain. Why it works: the transmission zone goes from 4 to 5 mm, so no zone gets thinner; mass rises only about 0.2 kg because two 30 mm overlaps disappear. Back-of-envelope strike check: OEM rock-drop case (assumed) of half the 1,760 kg front-axle GVW share falling 300 mm = 0.5 × 1,760 × 9.81 × 0.30 ≈ 2.6 kJ at the sump zone, which is unchanged in gauge and support span (bracket pitch held at ≤ 420 mm). The removed joint was itself a weak point: an open forward-facing edge that can catch and peel. Benchmark: Ford quotes continuous driveline coverage on the Bronco

title: Skid plates and driveline guards pre-hung on subframes at the module supplier
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Moves fitting of the front skid and driveline guards from an overhead station on the final line to the subframe module supplier, where they are bolted at bench height before the module is sequenced. Removes an overhead station, a lifting aid and rework from cross-threaded bolts. Baseline: on both powertrains the off-road pack front skid plate (MHEV sump plate or BEV front-EDU plate, 5 mm 5083-H111, 6.8 kg) and the two driveline guards (3 mm S355MC steel, CV/prop) are fitted overhead on the final line after marriage. That needs a dedicated station, a lifting aid and an operator working above head height, and gives about 1.8% rework from cross-threaded M10 bolts. Proposal: the subframe module supplier bolts the plate and guards to the front subframe at bench height, using the same hard points, before the module is sequenced to the line. Only two rear bolts into the body crossmember remain at the final line, fitted from the pit. Why it works: the plate already loads mainly into the subframe (6 of 8 bolts). The strike path is unchanged: the OEM rock-drop case (assumed) of 0.5 × 1,760 kg × 9.81 × 0.30 m ≈ 2.6 kJ is reacted by the same bolts in the same subframe. Bench fitting gives better torque-angle control than overhead fitting. Weight per module rises 9 kg, inside the 25 kg margin of the module lift-assist. Benchmark: Lexus lists GX 550 dealer skid plates that install with no drilling on the vehicle existing attachment mounts, which shows the value of designing the mount interface first. We use it to move the job off the line.

title: One front skid die serves MHEV sump and BEV front-EDU plates via trim inserts
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces two separate front skid-plate press dies and part families (MHEV sump plate, BEV front-EDU plate) with one common draw die and a trim die with interchangeable inserts. The outer shape, fixing grid and gauge are common; only the cut-outs differ. Baseline: the MHEV and 800V BEV off-road packs each have their own front skid plate in 5 mm 5083-H111: the MHEV plate has an oil-drain cut-out and a deep sump pocket; the BEV plate is flatter with a front-EDU coolant-drain cut-out. Two draw dies, two trim dies, two sets of CAE and two strike test series. Proposal: one common outer shape and fixing grid, with the deeper MHEV sump pocket drawn for both (BEV gets 18 mm extra clearance under the EDU, which costs nothing). One trim die carries interchangeable inserts for the drain and coolant cut-outs. One full test series at the BEV mass, plus a single MHEV confirmation drop for the sump-to-plate deflection gap, covers both. title: Rear subframe cross-tube carries the fuel-tank rear guard, deleting four tank-guard brackets
description: [MHEV] Moves the MHEV off-road fuel-tank rear guard from four body-mounted brackets onto the rear subframe front cross-tube, which already sits 40 mm behind the tank. Deletes four pressed brackets and eight fasteners and shortens the guard while keeping its strike load path. Baseline: the MHEV 80 l HDPE fuel tank is protected on the off-road pack by a 3 mm S355MC guard (5.6 kg) under its rear half. The guard hangs on four pressed 2.5 mm brackets bolted to the floor rails, with eight M10 fasteners. The rear subframe front cross-tube (60 × 3 mm S420MC tube) sits 40 mm behind the tank. Proposal: the guard rear edge bolts directly to two welded-on tabs on the subframe cross-tube, and the front edge to two existing tank-strap bolts. The guard is 120 mm shorter because the cross-tube itself covers the rearmost band. Why it works: the strike path becomes shorter and stiffer. Check: OEM tank-strike case (assumed) of a 200 mm rock pushing 1.0 × rear-axle GVW share upward, 1,750 × 9.81 ≈ 17 kN, at mid-span. The guard span drops from 520 to 400 mm, so bending moment F·L/4 falls from 2.2 to 1.7 kN·m, and the 3 mm plate gauge is kept, so stress margin rises about 30%. The FMVSS 301 / UN R34 rear-impact case must be re-checked in CAE: the subframe moves forward in a rear crash and must not drive the guard edge into the tank, so the tab joint is designed to shear or slide first. Benchmark: Ford sells a 4-door Bronco full bash-plate kit whose difference from the 2-door kit is the added fuel-tank guard, which shows that tank protection is a standard part of an off-road skid set.

title: Structural transfer-case skid doubles as the gearbox-mount crossmember on MHEV
description: [MHEV] Combines the separate pressed-steel gearbox-mount crossmember and the off-road transfer-case skid into one hot-formed steel skid-crossmember that carries the rear transmission mount. Deletes a crossmember, eight fasteners and a bracket on off-road cars; road cars keep the standard crossmember. Baseline: on the MHEV, an 8-speed automatic with a two-speed transfer case hangs on a 2.5 mm S420MC pressed crossmember (4.2 kg) bolted to the floor rails with four M12 bolts. The off-road pack adds a 4 mm 5083-H111 aluminium transfer-case skid (4.1 kg) on four more bolts and a bracket. Proposal: on the off-road pack, one 2.0 mm 22MnB5 press-hardened skid-crossmember (Usibor 1500, 6.4 kg, Al-Si coated) carries the rear mount on a welded pad and protects the transfer case. Road cars keep the standard crossmember. Why it works: the structure already sits under the transfer case, so making it wider removes one layer. Strength check: mount load 3 × gearbox mass 120 kg × 9.81 ≈ 3.5 kN vertical is small. The governing case is the transfer-case strike of 0.5 × 1,600 kg × 9.81 × 0.30 ≈ 2.35 kJ (assumed OEM rock-drop). Plastic bending capacity per mm width σy t²/4: 22MnB5 (≥ 1,000 MPa yield) at 2.0 mm = 1,000 N·mm/mm, versus 5083 (125 MPa) at 4 mm = 500 N·mm/mm, so the new skid is about twice as strong locally with swaged ribs keeping the 350 mm span stiff. Benchmark: Ford sells a Bronco steel bash-plate kit covering front, engine and transfer case, a precedent for steel transfer-case protection.

title: One extruded underbody conduit carries brake and fuel lines past the strike zone
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces three clip-on steel line guards and about 40 plastic P-clips along the underbody with one extruded 6063-T6 aluminium conduit, bolted to the floor rail, that carries the brake lines (and the fuel feed on MHEV) inside a closed section. Protection improves, so the cost cut is in clips and guards. Baseline: the two rear brake lines (Ø4.75 mm steel), and on MHEV the Ø8 mm fuel feed, run exposed along the inner floor rail and are clipped by about 40 PA66 P-clips. Off-road cars add three 1.5 mm galvanised steel guards (0.9 kg total) at the zones a rock can reach behind the front wheel and ahead of the rear axle. Proposal: one 6063-T6 extrusion (40 × 30 mm, 2.0 mm wall, open slot to the rail side) runs 1.6 m along the rail, bolted on six M6 weld-studs. Lines snap into moulded TPE inserts inside the slot. All cars get the conduit; the three off-road guards are deleted. Why it works: a closed aluminium section shields the lines all along their length, not only in three zones. Check: a 50 mm stone at 25 m/s (kick-up at 90 km/h, 0.2 kg) carries ½ × 0.2 × 25² ≈ 63 J, well inside the 2 mm wall dent limit; a slow rock contact at 2 kN over 100 mm span gives a bending stress of about 42 MPa against 160 MPa yield. Brake lines are never more exposed than today. Benchmark: GMC describes the Hummer EV chassis as surrounding and isolating the battery, drive unit and body from terrain, which is the same principle of a closed protective structure.

title: Rock slider with co-extruded TPV step tread replaces separate running board on off-road pack
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Gives the off-road rock slider a flat top with a co-extruded TPV tread so it serves as the entry step, and deletes the road running board (moulded board, two cast brackets, end caps) that off-road customers otherwise also get. Baseline: the off-road pack fits a rock slider (round tube) below the sill, and because the slider makes the sill harder to step over, the pack also keeps the standard running board above it: a PP-GF30 moulded board with an aluminium extrusion core, two cast brackets and end caps (about €62 per pair). Proposal: the slider uses a flat-topped S700MC rectangular hollow section (this assumes the slider is mounted on the sill jacking nodes at a 560 mm span; savings are not additive with that idea) with a 4 mm TPV tread (Santoprene-type, Shore A 80) co-extruded onto a snap-on 6063 carrier along the top face. The running board is deleted on the off-road pack. Why it works: one part does both jobs; the slider is already at step height (420 mm above ground on off-road height). Load check: step load 150 kg person dynamic ×2 = 2.9 kN at mid-span between jacking nodes (560 mm) gives 0.4 kN·m, small next to the 2.4 kN·m high-centred design case (half BEV GVW, 17 kN). The tread is sacrificial and clips off if torn by rocks; the steel slider strength is untouched. Benchmark: GMC offers Hummer EV dealer rock sliders with integrated steps alongside its dual-section-tube factory sliders, which shows that slider-plus-step is accepted in the segment.

title: Prop-shaft centre-bearing guard formed as a flange of the tunnel cross-brace
description: [MHEV] Extends the existing pressed tunnel cross-brace below the MHEV prop-shaft centre bearing into a U-shaped guard, deleting the separate off-road centre-bearing guard and its four bolts while keeping the same strike protection. Baseline: the MHEV rear prop shaft (two-piece, Ø80 mm tube) has a rubber-mounted centre bearing at the tunnel mid-point. The tunnel is closed underneath by a 2 mm CR420LA cross-brace for torsion stiffness. The off-road pack adds a 3 mm S355MC U-guard (1.6 kg) bolted on four M8 bolts under the bearing because the bearing hangs 25 mm below the brace and is the lowest point at the breakover line. Proposal: the cross-brace blank becomes 160 mm wider and is drawn into a U about 42 mm deep under the bearing (25 mm bearing drop + 15 mm whirl clearance + gauge), in 2.5 mm CR500Y780T-DP (EN 10338) for all MHEV cars. The separate guard is deleted. Why it works: the brace already spans the tunnel and is bolted on six M10s, so a guard formed in it has a shorter, stiffer load path than a bolted-on one. Strength check, OEM breakover rock-ride case (assumed): 0.5 × mid-car mass 3,200 × 9.81 ≈ 16 kN static ride-over; plastic bending capacity per mm σy t²/4 for DP780 (500 MPa) at 2.5 mm = 781 N·mm/mm versus S355 at 3 mm = 799 N·mm/mm, within 2%, while the U-form adds section depth. Bearing clearance to guard kept at 15 mm for shaft whirl. Benchmark: the Bronco Raptor skid plates cover the driveline continuously from front bumper to transfer case, a precedent for treating driveline guards as part of the structure.

title: MHEV 48 V belt starter-generator shielded by a formed lip on the sump skid
description: [MHEV] Deletes the separate splash and strike shield of the low-mounted 48 V belt starter-generator by forming an up-turned lip on the front sump skid plate that the off-road pack already carries, and on road cars by a cheaper PP undertray pocket. Baseline: the 48 V belt starter-generator (BSG, 15 kW) sits low on the front left of the 3.0 L I6. Every MHEV carries a 1.5 mm stamped aluminium shield (0.8 kg, 3 bolts) against stones, spray and off-road strike, and off-road cars also carry the 5 mm 5083 sump skid below it. Proposal: on off-road cars the sump skid gets a 70 mm formed up-turn lip along its left edge that covers the BSG from below and in front; the separate shield is deleted. On road cars the PP-T20 undertray gets a moulded pocket and splash lip in the same area (the road car only needs spray and stone protection, not strike). Why it works: on off-road cars the skid already takes the strike; the lip only needs to stop side-on stones and spray. Check: stone kick-up 0.2 kg at 25 m/s ≈ 63 J, trivial for 5 mm 5083. On road cars the BSG sits 290 mm above ground, behind the bumper, so only spray and gravel (≈ 5-10 J) matter, which 3 mm PP-T20 meets. IP: the BSG is IP6K9K already, so splash is a durability not a sealing issue. Benchmark: Jeep lists five skid plates on the Wrangler Rubicon 4xe, showing hybrid off-roaders combine electrified parts with full skid coverage.

title: Stamped swage beads replace four welded stiffener ribs on the aluminium sump skid
description: [MHEV] Stiffens the 5 mm 5083 sump skid with press-formed swage beads instead of four MIG-welded 6082 angle ribs. Deletes the welding, the ribs and the post-weld straightening while keeping the same stiffness and dent energy. Baseline: the MHEV off-road sump skid (5 mm 5083-H111, 1,050 × 620 mm) has four 6082-T6 angle ribs (30 × 30 × 4 mm) MIG-welded across its back to keep it from oil-canning and to spread rock loads to the mounts. The welds soften the 5083 heat-affected zone (yield drops from about 125 to 115 MPa locally) and each plate needs straightening. Proposal: four longitudinal swage beads, 12 mm deep and 40 mm wide, are pressed in the same draw operation. Why it works: a bead of depth d raises local second moment strongly. Per 40 mm bead, I rises from 40 × 5³/12 = 417 mm⁴ to about 40 × 5 × (12/2)² ≈ 7,200 mm⁴, about 40% of a welded 30 × 30 × 4 angle (Ix ≈ 18,000 mm⁴ about its own centroid), and the beads stiffen fore-aft whereas the ribs ran across, so bead count and depth are set by CAE to match the baseline oil-canning and load-spreading stiffness. Energy check against the OEM front-drop case (assumed) 0.5 × 1,760 kg × 9.81 × 0.30 ≈ 2.6 kJ: the beads run fore-aft, the direction rocks slide, so they also act as glide runners; dent depth in CAE stays within the 30 mm sump clearance. No HAZ softening, so the parent 5083 strength is kept everywhere. Benchmark: Land Rover fits the Defender OCTA with an aluminium alloy front under-shield, a precedent for aluminium front protection in this segment.

title: Bare 5083-H111 marine-alloy skid plates delete powder coating on all plates
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Ships the aluminium skid plates bare in 5083-H111 marine alloy with a brushed finish instead of pre-treating and powder coating them. Deletes the coating line cost, and also the chip-repair warranty claims, because bare 5083 does not need paint to resist salt. Baseline: all off-road pack aluminium skid plates (front, transmission, BEV front-EDU; about 16 kg per car) are chromate-free pre-treated and black polyester powder coated at 80 µm. Rock contact strips the coating in weeks, and dealers see cosmetic claims for chipped plates. Proposal: plates ship in bare 5083-H111 with a scotch-brite brushed finish and a laser-etched logo. Why it works: 5083 (Al-4.5Mg) is a marine alloy whose natural oxide resists chloride corrosion without paint; with Mg ≤ 5% and H111 temper it is not prone to intergranular attack below 65 °C. Plate service temperature is below 60 °C except near the MHEV exhaust, where a 0.5 mm aluminised steel heat shield already sits between. Strike: coating carries no load, so the strike energy capacity (OEM front-drop 2.6 kJ case) is unchanged. Galvanic: steel bolts get zinc-flake coating and PA washers, as today. Benchmark: Land Rover fits the Defender OCTA with an aluminium alloy front under-shield in a graphite finish; a bare brushed finish is a cheaper styled alternative.

title: Fuel-tank guard extended over the EVAP canister, deleting its separate off-road shield
description: [MHEV] Extends the MHEV off-road fuel-tank guard blank by 180 mm so its formed side flange covers the underbody EVAP carbon canister next to the tank. Deletes the separate canister strike shield, its two brackets and four fasteners, with the canister kept behind the same 3 mm steel the tank gets. On the off-road pack it has its own 2 mm S355MC shield (1.2 kg) on two brackets and four M8 fasteners, because a cracked canister breaks the EVAP system and triggers a leak fault. title: Self-piercing clinch studs replace welded cage nuts at all skid-plate mounting points
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Uses M10 self-piercing clinch studs pressed into the subframe and body crossmember flanges instead of welded cage nuts at the skid-plate fixing points. Deletes the projection weld, the cage-nut cost and cross-threading rework, and lets the plate hang on studs while nuts are run down. Baseline: about 20 skid-plate and guard fixing points per off-road car use M10 cage nuts in welded retainers on the subframes and crossmembers. Cage nuts float to absorb tolerance, but corrosion and mud lock the cage, and about 2% of points cross-thread or spin, needing rework. Proposal: M10 class 10.9 self-piercing clinch studs (zinc-nickel, pressed into 3 mm S420MC flanges at the subframe supplier) with flanged nuts. Skid holes become ±2.5 mm slots for tolerance. The plate hangs on the studs during fitting. Why it works: clinch studs in 3 mm S420MC reach push-out about 8 kN and torque-out about 90 N·m, above the 55 N·m fitting torque. Strike check: skid loads are carried in shear and bearing at the plate, not in stud push-out. A 2.6 kJ front-drop case (assumed OEM case, 0.5 × 1,760 × 9.81 × 0.30) generates roughly 30 kN peak spread over eight points, about 3.8 kN per point, below the 8 kN push-out with margin 2.1; shear capacity of an M10 10.9 is about 45 kN. Benchmark: Lexus lists GX 550 dealer skid plates that install with no drilling on existing attachment mounts, showing the mount interface is designed for easy fitting.

title: Rock slider rolled from S700MC rectangular hollow section replaces 4 mm S355 round tube
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Makes the rock slider from a 2.5 mm S700MC roll-formed rectangular hollow section instead of a bent 4 mm S355 round tube with welded end plates. Higher strength and a better section keep the plastic moment above the full-GVW design load with about 17% less steel and no tube bending. Baseline: each off-road rock slider is a 60.3 × 4.0 mm S355J2H round tube (EN 10219), mandrel-bent at both ends, with welded end plates and mounting tabs, 9.6 kg per side. Proposal: a 70 × 50 × 2.5 mm S700MC (EN 10149-2) roll-formed and laser-welded rectangular hollow section, cut and laser-notched for the end kick-up, 8.0 kg per side including tabs. Why it works: plastic moment Mp = σy × Zp. Round tube Zp = (D³ − d³)/6 = (60.3³ − 52.3³)/6 ≈ 12.7 cm³, so Mp = 355 × 12.7 ≈ 4.5 kN·m. RHS 70 × 50 × 2.5 (70 mm tall) Zp = [50 × 70² − 45 × 65²]/4 ≈ 13.7 cm³, so Mp = 700 × 13.7 ≈ 9.6 kN·m; wall slenderness 70/2.5 = 28 and 50/2.5 = 20 sit at the EN 1993-1-1 class 2-3 boundary for S700, so take the elastic moment ≈ 8 kN·m as the usable figure. Design case: high-centred on a rock with half the BEV GVW on one slider, 0.5 × 3,450 × 9.81 ≈ 17 kN at mid-span between jacking nodes 560 mm apart: M = F·L/4 ≈ 2.4 kN·m. Margin rises from 1.9 (round tube) to over 3. The flat bottom also slides better on rock than a round tube. Benchmark: Tesla supplies coated-steel rock sliders in the Cybertruck Terrestrial Armor Package, showing that steel sliders remain the norm on heavy BEVs.

title: Bolted armour plate becomes a pack shear diaphragm, deleting two underbody X-braces
description: [800V BEV] Changes the 800V BEV armour joint from slotted, non-structural fixings to fitted bolts in reamed holes, so the plate works as a shear diaphragm between the pack frame rails. The extra torsional stiffness lets two bolted underbody X-braces be deleted, while armour gauge and strike protection stay as they are. Baseline: the 800V BEV pack carries a bolted 5083-H111 armour plate (4 mm road, 6 mm off-road) on 52 M8 bolts in slotted holes, so the plate carries no in-plane load. Two 2.5 mm S420MC X-braces (3.2 kg in all) bolt between the front subframe rear mounts and the pack front rail to reach the body torsion target. Proposal: 64 M8 10.9 bolts in reamed Ø8.4 H11 holes at 150 mm pitch on the pack perimeter rails. The plate becomes a shear panel and the X-braces are deleted. Gauge, crush gap and strike behaviour are unchanged. Why it works: a 4 mm aluminium plate of 1.9 × 1.4 m has in-plane shear stiffness G·t = 26 GPa × 4 mm ≈ 104 kN/mm per unit aspect, far more than two diagonal straps (E·A/L ≈ 210 GPa × 150 mm² / 900 mm ≈ 35 kN/mm each), so even with joint slip the diaphragm adds more torsion stiffness than the braces it replaces; CAE target is +9% body torsion versus the braced baseline. Bolt check: diaphragm shear flow under a 1 g twist case ≈ 60 N/mm × 150 mm = 9 kN per bolt, about twice the slip resistance of an M8 10.9 at 18 kN clamp (about 4-5 kN at a friction coefficient of about 0.25), so the joint works in bearing: holes must be true fitted (H7 reamed, ground-shank bolts) or the pitch halved, which is to be re-costed. Strike: OEM rock-drop (assumed) quarte

title: BEV armour fitted at the pack plant; pack and armour marry as one unit
description: [800V BEV] Moves armour fitting from an overhead final-line station after pack marriage to the pack plant, where the pack is upside down on a rotary fixture and a multi-spindle nutrunner runs all armour bolts downward in one cycle. Cuts labour, rework and an ergonomic risk station; the pack arrives armoured. Baseline: after the 800V pack is married to the body, an operator fits the 28-43 kg armour overhead with a lift assist and runs 52 M8 bolts one at a time, about 7 min per car, with around 1% cross-thread rework. Proposal: the pack plant fits the armour while the pack is inverted on its end-of-line rotary fixture, before EOL leak and isolation test. A 13-spindle nutrunner runs the 52 bolts in four indexes (about 2 min). The pack then ships and marries with armour fitted. Why it works: gravity helps instead of fighting, and the armour bolts are already accessible from below in the car, so service removal is unchanged. Pack mass rises from about 610 to 650 kg, inside the 750 kg rating of the pack AGV and marriage lifter. Strike performance is unchanged: same plate, same bolts, same torque (25 N·m + angle), against the OEM rock-drop (assumed) 862 kg × 9.81 × 0.25 m ≈ 2.1 kJ and GB 38031-2025 bottom impact. The EOL test now includes the armoured pack, so any bolt that pierces too deep would be caught by the leak test. Benchmark: GMC fits steel plates and shields around the Hummer EV battery pack as part of the factory build, a precedent for treating armour as part of the pack system.

title: Recycled PET foam crush pad replaces aluminium honeycomb behind the front armour band
description: [800V BEV] Replaces the 15 mm 3003 aluminium honeycomb crush pad bonded behind the off-road armour front band with a 15 mm closed-cell recycled PET foam pad of higher plateau stress. Energy absorbed within the same 15 mm gap rises slightly, the pad cannot trap water, and it costs about a third. Baseline: on the off-road pack, a 0.6 × 1.4 m band behind the armour front edge carries a 15 mm 3003 aluminium honeycomb pad (50 kg/m³, crush plateau about 1.0 MPa) bonded to the armour, to spread a rock-drop load before the armour reaches the pack bottom cover. Honeycomb cells fill with water in wading and corrode against the 5083. Proposal: a 15 mm recycled PET structural foam (about 100 kg/m³, compressive plateau about 1.3 MPa, closed-cell) bonded with the same PU adhesive. Why it works: usable crush energy per area = plateau stress × usable stroke. Honeycomb: 1.0 MPa × 12 mm (80% of 15 mm before densification) = 12 kJ/m²; PET foam: 1.3 MPa × 10.5 mm (70%) ≈ 13.7 kJ/m², about 14% more. On a 200 × 200 mm spread zone that is 0.48 kJ versus 0.55 kJ of the 2.1 kJ OEM rock-drop case (assumed quarter-GVW 862 kg × 9.81 × 0.25 m), the rest being taken by the armour plate as before. Closed cells take up under 3% water by volume, so the pad no longer holds water after a 900 mm wade. Mass rises 0.6 kg. Benchmark: Mercedes protects the G 580 EQ pack with a 26 mm plate in a material mix including carbon, showing that layered composite protection is used in the segment.

title: Self-draining armour gap deletes the perimeter sponge seal and drain plugs
description: [800V BEV] Removes the EPDM sponge seal around the armour perimeter and the eight rubber drain plugs that try to keep mud out of the 15 mm gap, and replaces them with twelve pierced drain slots and fore-aft channels so mud and water flush out by themselves. The armour, gap and pack seal are unchanged. Baseline: the 800V BEV armour has a 6.6 m EPDM sponge seal around its perimeter and eight push-in drain plugs. The seal never stays tight after rock contact, so off-road owners still pack mud into the gap, which adds up to 15 kg, holds salt water against the pack cover and needs dealer cleaning. Proposal: no perimeter seal. The armour gets twelve 20 × 60 mm pierced slots at the low points and two fore-aft rib channels on its inner face; the front edge is closed by the up-turned lip, the rear edge is open. Driving flushes the gap. Why it works: the pack bottom cover is already sealed to IP67/IP68 on its own flange, so the armour gap never had a sealing job. Wading head at 900 mm on the pack seal: ρgh = 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.9 ≈ 8.8 kPa, which the pack gasket holds whether or not the gap is wet. Strike: slots are in low-stress zones away from bolts; net section loss is 1.4% of plate area and dent energy is unchanged within CAE noise against the OEM rock-drop (assumed) 862 kg × 9.81 × 0.25 m ≈ 2.1 kJ. Air in the gap stays nearly still with the front lip closed, so thermal shielding is kept. Benchmark: Mercedes puts a 1 mm stone-chip layer on the outermost face of the G 580 EQ underbody plate, showing that the outer face, not a seal, is where abrasion is handled.

title: Rear-EDU HV cables threaded inside the rear subframe front tube, deleting two guards
description: [800V BEV] Routes the two 800V shielded cables from the pack rear to the rear EDU through a sleeve in the rear subframe front tube instead of under the floor behind the pack. title: Extruded multi-cell crush cans replace machined solid blocks at the armour front corners
description: [800V BEV] Replaces the two machined 6082 solid corner blocks at the off-road armour front corners with short 6063-T6 multi-cell extrusion crush cans. They are cheaper, lighter, and they cap the peak load into the pack frame during a corner strike, which the solid blocks pass straight through. Baseline: on the off-road pack, two solid 6082-T6 blocks (1.4 kg each, machined from bar) bolt between the armour front corners and the pack frame front corners to resist side-slope and corner strikes. A solid block is rigid, so the strike force reaches the pack frame almost undamped. Proposal: two 6063-T6 four-cell extrusions (90 × 70 mm, 2.0 mm walls, 120 mm long, 0.6 kg each), sawn and drilled, bolted in the same place. Why it works: a crush can absorbs energy at a set mean force. Corner case (assumed OEM): sliding off a rock at 5 km/h with about 15% of BEV GVW effective, 0.5 × 520 kg × 1.39² ≈ 0.5 kJ. A four-cell 6063-T6 section of this size has a mean crush force of about 40 kN, so it absorbs 0.6 kJ in 15 mm of fold, while peak force into the pack frame is limited to about 55 kN instead of 120 kN or more with a solid block. The pack frame corner is checked at 70 kN, so the can protects the pack better. Static ride-over loads (0.5 × GVW ≈ 17 kN) stay well under the 40 kN crush threshold, so the can does not fold in normal off-road use. Benchmark: BYD claims a five-layer protective structure for the off-road Bao 5 pack, showing that layered energy management around the pack is the direction of travel.

title: Still air under the BEV shield replaces the PET felt insulation mat
description: [800V BEV] Deletes the 4 mm PET felt insulation mat bonded under the BEV pack bottom cover. The 15 mm near-still air gap under the armour, with a low-emissivity bare aluminium inner face, gives more thermal resistance than the mat did, so hot-road and cold-soak heat flow into the pack is not increased. Baseline: all 800V BEVs have a 4 mm PET felt mat (2.66 m², λ ≈ 0.035 W/m·K) bonded to the pack bottom cover to cut radiant heat from hot roads and heat loss in cold soak, and the armour sits 15 mm below it. Proposal: delete the mat. The armour inner face is left bare and degreased (ε ≈ 0.1) and the gap is closed at the front by the armour lip so the air is nearly still. Why it works: thermal resistance per m². Felt: R = 0.004 / 0.035 ≈ 0.11 m²K/W. Still air gap of 15 mm: conduction R = 0.015 / 0.026 ≈ 0.58 m²K/W, reduced by convection (Nusselt about 1.5 for a horizontal gap heated from below) to about 0.39, in parallel with radiation, which with ε ≈ 0.1 on one face is about 0.6 W/m²K, giving an effective R of about 0.31 m²K/W, nearly three times the felt. The baseline already has the gap under the felt, so the honest comparison is felt + gap + coated armour face (ε ≈ 0.9, R ≈ 0.23 m²K/W) against gap + bare face (R ≈ 0.31 m²K/W): about 25% less heat flux on a 65 °C road, provided the bare face stays below ε ≈ 0.3 in service (CFD and a fouled-face test to confirm). Strike: the mat carried no strike role; armour and gap are unchanged against GB 38031-2025 and the OEM rock-drop (assumed) 862 kg × 9.81 × 0.25 m ≈ 2.1 kJ. Benchmark: Mercedes builds the G 580 EQ underbody protection

title: Rock-slider inboard flange shields the BEV pack side rail, deleting side armour strips
description: [800V BEV] Adds a welded inboard flange to the BEV off-road rock slider that reaches under the outer 40 mm of the pack side rail, so the slider protects both the sill and the pack edge. The two separate aluminium pack side-armour angle strips and their 28 fasteners are deleted. Baseline: on the BEV off-road pack, the pack side rails are protected from rocks that slip past the slider by two 3 mm 5083 angle strips (1.9 m, 3.0 kg each) bolted along the rail lower edge with 14 M8 bolts each. The rock slider (S700MC section) sits 60 mm outboard and 25 mm lower. Proposal: the BEV slider gets a 4 mm S700MC inboard flange (110 mm wide, 1.7 m, 5.9 kg per side) welded to its lower face, ending 40 mm under the pack rail with 20 mm vertical clearance. The side strips are deleted. MHEV sliders keep the plain section. Why it works: a rock reaching the pack edge must first pass under the slider, which now covers it. Load check: side-slope strike with half the BEV GVW on the flange tip, 0.5 × 3,450 × 9.81 ≈ 17 kN at 110 mm lever gives 1.9 kN·m per 1.7 m flange; the flange root plastic moment is σy t² b/4 = 700 × 16 × 1,700 / 4 ≈ 4.8 kN·m, margin about 2.5. Deflection under that load is under 6 mm, inside the 20 mm clearance, so the pack rail is never loaded by the slider. Mass rises about 5.8 kg per car versus the strips. Benchmark: Tesla supplies coated-steel rock sliders together with an aluminium underbody battery shield for the Cybertruck, which shows sliders and pack armour work as one system.

Validate the side-slope strike rig, slider full-GVW and jacking cases, side-pole UN R135 / FMVSS 214 / FMVSS 305 (flange must not push into the pack in a pole crash, check in CAE), UN R26 projections, and wading-depth validation. Engineering review (13 Oct 2026) — open point: The flange check spreads the 17 kN over the full 1.7 m flange length. A rock is a point load at the flange tip, and only a local width (about 2-3 times the 110 mm lever, roughly 300 mm) works in the yield line: Mp = 700 × 16 × 300 / 4 ≈ 0.84 kN·m, against 1.9 kN·m of demand. The flange yields locally, its deflection exceeds the 20 mm clearance, and the pack rail is loaded, which is the outcome the idea says cannot happen. The 1.9 kN·m flange torque into the slider and jacking nodes is also unchecked. Gussets at about 250-300 mm pitch or a thicker flange are needed, and must be re-costed.
