reviewOpenPoints: The flange check spreads the 17 kN over the full 1.7 m flange length. A rock is a point load at the flange tip, and only a local width (about 2-3 times the 110 mm lever, roughly 300 mm) works in the yield line: Mp = 700 × 16 × 300 / 4 ≈ 0.84 kN·m, against 1.9 kN·m of demand. The flange yields locally, its deflection exceeds the 20 mm clearance, and the pack rail is loaded, which is the outcome the idea says cannot happen. The 1.9 kN·m flange torque into the slider and jacking nodes is also unchecked. Gussets at about 250-300 mm pitch or a thicker flange are needed, and must be re-costed.

title: Moulded PA66-GF50 stand-off pucks with steel limiters replace machined aluminium spacer tubes
description: [800V BEV] Replaces the 52 machined 6061 spacer tubes and their separate EPDM isolation washers that hold the armour 15 mm off the pack frame with one-piece PA66-GF50 pucks over-moulded on a steel compression limiter. The puck sets the gap, isolates aluminium from steel bolts and costs about half. Baseline: each of the 52 armour bolts passes through a 6061-T6 spacer tube (Ø16 × 15 mm, machined from tube) plus an EPDM washer that separates the aluminium armour from the zinc-flake steel bolt and pack frame insert. Proposal: one PA66-GF50 puck (Ø28 × 15 mm) over-moulded on a 1.5 mm wall steel compression limiter (cold-headed, zinc-nickel), with a moulded shoulder that seats in the armour hole. Why it works: the steel limiter carries the bolt clamp: M8 10.9 at 25 N·m + angle ≈ 18 kN; limiter area π/4 × (11² − 8.4²) ≈ 40 mm² gives 450 MPa, under the limiter yield of 600 MPa, so the plastic sees no clamp and cannot creep. In a strike, load passes through the puck face in compression: the PA66-GF50 annulus of about 520 mm² at a compressive strength of about 200 MPa takes about 104 kN per point, far above the roughly 3-5 kN per bolt of the OEM rock-drop case (assumed 862 kg × 9.81 × 0.25 m ≈ 2.1 kJ shared over the plate). The plastic shoulder isolates the aluminium armour from the steel, so the EPDM washer is deleted. Benchmark: Mercedes fixes the G 580 EQ underbody plate to the frame with 50 bolts, showing that densely bolted armour is normal and that each fixing is worth optimising.

title: Co-laminated TPO film replaces sprayed PVC stone-chip coat on aluminium armour
description: [800V BEV] Replaces the 1.5 mm sprayed PVC stone-chip coat applied to the formed armour with a 0.8 mm TPO film laminated to the 5083 coil before blanking. The coil-applied layer is cheaper, cleaner and gives more even abrasion protection than a hand-masked spray. Baseline: the armour (4 mm road, 6 mm off-road) is sprayed after forming with 1.5 mm PVC plastisol stone-chip coat (about 3.4 kg on 2.66 m²), with masking at 52 bolt holes, oven cure at 140 °C, and touch-up. Proposal: a 0.8 mm TPO film with a PP-g-MA tie layer is laminated onto the outer face of the 5083 coil at the coil service centre (heated nip rolls), then the coil is blanked and formed with the film on. Bolt holes are cut through the film. Why it works: abrasion resistance comes from toughness, not thickness: TPO at 0.8 mm has a Taber abrasion loss below that of 1.5 mm PVC and stays ductile to −40 °C. Forming strain on the armour is under 8%, inside the film elongation of over 400%. The film carries no structural role; strike capacity (OEM rock-drop, assumed 862 kg × 9.81 × 0.25 m ≈ 2.1 kJ, and GB 38031-2025 bottom impact) is unchanged. Mass falls about 1.5 kg. Low friction of TPO also helps the plate slide over rock. Benchmark: Mercedes lists a 1 mm stone-chip protection layer as the outermost layer of the G 580 EQ underbody protection, the same function in a similar thickness.

title: Roll-formed CR1200 martensitic ramp-strike beam replaces machined 6082 extrusion ahead of cells
description: [800V BEV] Replaces the extruded 6082-T6 ramp-strike beam ahead of the cells that carries the armour front lip and takes ramp strikes with a roll-formed CR1200Y1500T-MS martensitic steel closed section of equal plastic moment. Material and processing cost fall, and the steel section resists local crushing from rocks better. Baseline: the ramp-strike beam across the front of the cell space is a 6082-T6 two-cell extrusion (100 × 60 mm, 3 mm walls, 1.4 m, 4.6 kg), drilled and machined for the armour lip and pack mounts. It takes ramp strikes from rocks met at the armour front edge and transfers them to the pack frame. Proposal: a roll-formed and laser-welded CR1200Y1500T-MS (EN 10338) closed section (90 × 60 mm, 1.4 mm wall, 1.4 m, 4.6 kg), with weld nuts for the armour lip. Why it works: equal plastic moment with a cheaper material. Mp = σy × Zp. Extrusion (two flanges, three webs): Zp ≈ 37 cm³ × 260 MPa ≈ 9.7 kN·m. title: Armour blanked from continuous-cast 5083 coil instead of laser-cut from DC-cast plate
description: [800V BEV] Buys the 4 mm and 6 mm 5083 armour as continuous-cast, hot-rolled coil-plate and blanks it on a blanking line, instead of buying DC-cast hot-rolled plate and laser-cutting each blank. Material price and cutting time both fall, with the same alloy, temper and minimum properties. Baseline: armour blanks (1.95 × 1.45 m) are laser-cut one by one from DC-cast, hot-rolled 5083-H111 plate sheets, about 6 min per blank, with 18% skeleton scrap. Proposal: 5083-H111 continuous-cast (twin-belt or twin-roll) coil-plate in 4 and 6 mm, uncoiled, levelled and blanked on a 1,000 t blanking line with a nested die, with 9% scrap. Bolt holes are punched in the forming die. Why it works: continuous-cast 5083 coil is a cheaper route (one casting step straight to strip) and reaches EN 485-2 minimum properties for H111 (Rp0.2 ≥ 125 MPa, Rm ≥ 275 MPa, A ≥ 15% at 6 mm) when specified with a homogenising anneal. The strike criterion depends on those minimum properties and gauge, which are unchanged, so the OEM rock-drop case (assumed quarter-GVW 862 kg × 9.81 × 0.25 m ≈ 2.1 kJ) and GB 38031-2025 bottom impact give the same result. Tighter thickness tolerance on coil (±0.15 versus ±0.25 mm) lets the gauge be specified at nominal with less over-thickness. Benchmark: Tesla uses an aluminium underbody battery shield on the Cybertruck, showing large aluminium armour plates are a volume part where the material route matters.

title: Winch-ready front end: rail-tip weld nuts and fascia knock-out replace dealer cradle adaptors
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Builds winch provisions into every car: four M12 weld nuts on the steel rail-tip flange plates and a moulded knock-out fairlead aperture in the lower fascia. costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Scope: winch kit 6% of fleet; provisions on all cars. Fleet averages below. Winch cradle 6 mm → 4 mm S420MC (€85 → €40 on 6%), fleet avg: €5.1 − €2.4 = €2.7. Four weld nuts, plugs and fascia knock-out (€1.10 on all cars): €0 − €1.1 = €-1.1. Winch-configuration crash validation amortised (€200K over 350,000): €0 − €0.6 = €-0.6. ideaData.riskNotes: Winch mass (about 35 kg) ahead of the front axle changes front crash and pedestrian performance for winch cars; the winch configuration must be crash-validated. Validate UN R94/R137, Euro NCAP MPDB and full-width with winch fitted, UN R127/GTR 9 lower leg, approach angle, cradle at 80 kN static and off-axis pulls, wading-depth validation (winch motor), and UN R10 EMC of the winch. Engineering review (13 Oct 2026) — open point: The winch-mount check treats the M12 bolts as being in shear, but the bolts go into weld nuts on the forward-facing rail-tip flange plates, so a forward line pull puts them in TENSION. With the cradle hanging below the crash cans, the load is also offset, which bends the flange plates. At 40 kN per rail on two projection-welded M12 nuts (about 20 kN each, plus prying), weld-nut pull-off and flange-plate bending govern, and neither is checked. The cradle also drops from 6 mm to 4 mm S420MC with no strength figure. This is recovery hardware, so the same 80 kN capability must be shown for the 4 mm cradle and the weld-nut joint. Engineering review (13 Oct 2026) — open point: EUR 5.40 of the EUR 10.33 net is dealer or PDI fitting labour at EUR 60 an hour. If dealers fit the kit and the customer pays for fitting in the accessory price, that is a dealer or customer saving, not an OEM one. The basis must say who carries the fitting cost. Only PDI labour paid by the OEM counts.

title: 48 V MHEV winch drive deletes the 12 V auxiliary battery and heavy cabling
description: [MHEV] Specifies the MHEV winch with a 48 V motor fed from the existing 48 V battery through a fused contactor. Current falls by a factor of four, so the 35 mm² 12 V cables shrink to 16 mm², and the auxiliary 12 V battery and isolator that a 12 V winch needs on a luxury car are deleted. Baseline: the MHEV winch option (6% take × 60% MHEV = 3.6% of fleet) uses a 12 V series-wound winch motor of about 5.5 kW electrical. At 12 V it draws about 460 A, so the kit adds a 70 Ah AGM auxiliary battery with a smart isolator (€180) to protect the main 12 V battery and starting, plus two 4.5 m runs of 35 mm² cable (€48) and a 12 V solenoid pack (€35). Proposal: a 48 V permanent-magnet winch motor of the same 5.5 kW (115 A) on a 16 mm² fused feed from the 48 V battery through a sealed 48 V contactor (€40). The auxiliary battery and isolator are deleted. Why it works: I²R loss scales with current squared. 35 mm² over a 9 m loop: R = 0.0172 × 9 / 35 ≈ 4.4 mΩ, loss at 460 A ≈ 0.93 kW. 16 mm²: R ≈ 9.7 mΩ, loss at 115 A ≈ 0.13 kW, so more power reaches the drum. Energy: a 60 s full-load pull uses 5.5 kW × 60 s ≈ 92 Wh; the 1 kWh 48 V battery covers it and the 15 kW belt starter-generator recharges it with the engine running. Load-holding does not depend on electrics: the winch keeps its automatic mechanical load brake and manual free-spool clutch, and a hardwired isolator stops it. Line pull and rope are unchanged, so recovery capability is the same. Benchmark: INEOS offers a removable winch rated at 3.5 tonnes and a 5.5-tonne winch system for the Grenadier, showing winch options are a core

title: BEV front recovery eyes anchored on the front subframe towers, not the crash cans
description: [800V BEV] Moves the 800V BEV front recovery and towing-eye anchors from steel sleeves inside the aluminium crash cans to two forged brackets bolted to the steel front subframe towers. Deletes the can reinforcement sleeves, the threaded bosses and the off-road backing plates, and lets the crash cans be pure energy absorbers. Baseline: BEV front recovery is anchored in the 6008-T7 crash cans: each can has a pressed steel reinforcement sleeve and a machined threaded boss (€9 per side) for the screw-in towing eye, and off-road cars add backing plates for their fixed eyes (€4 per side). The sleeves stiffen the cans and must be tuned out in crash CAE. Proposal: two forged S355 brackets (€5.20 each) bolt by two M14 10.9 bolts each to the front faces of the hydroformed S420MC front subframe towers, 120 mm below and behind the cans. Each bracket has a threaded bore for the road screw-in eye and a through-bolt seat for the off-road fixed eye. Why it works: the subframe is the stiffest steel structure at the front and does not need to crush. Load check at the recovery design load of 85 kN, applied 30° off-axis in plan and 15° downward: axial ≈ 85 × cos30 × cos15 ≈ 71 kN, lateral ≈ 42 kN, vertical ≈ 22 kN. Two M14 10.9 bolts give about 2 × 60 kN in shear and 2 × 92 kN proof in tension, margin about 1.6 on combined load. The EU towing-device requirement (half of GVW, 0.5 × 3,450 × 9.81 ≈ 17 kN) is far exceeded. Benchmark: Land Rover shows the Defender OCTA front and rear recovery points exposed in a Phosphor Bronze finish, treating them as visible structural hardware.

title: Towbar, socket and rear beam delivered as one sequenced rear-end module
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Moves towbar fitting off the final line: the rear-end module supplier, who already builds the rear beam and fascia, bolts the towbar crossmember, neck mechanism and socket at bench height and delivers the tow or non-tow module in sequence. The final-line towbar station, its lift aid and its rework are deleted. Baseline: the tow pack (55%) is fitted at a dedicated final-line station after the rear fascia: an operator lifts the 14 kg towbar crossmember with a lift aid, bolts it to the rail-end nut plates (six M12), routes the socket pigtail and fits the socket, then refits the fascia lower section. About 4.5 min per tow car, with about 1.5% rework from fascia fitment. Proposal: the rear-end module supplier builds the beam, crash cans, towbar crossmember and socket into one module, torques the towbar bolts on a fixture with the same torque-angle spec, and sequences tow and non-tow modules to the line. The line fits the module to the rails as it already does for the beam. Why it works: all towbar loads still pass through the same bolts into the same nut plates. Rear recovery ratings (2.5 × GVW ≈ 85 kN) are unchanged. Module weight rises by 14 kg, inside the 40 kg capacity of the rear-module manipulator. title: Trailer circuits in the body harness plus a socket pigtail replace the tow harness
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Puts the thirteen trailer circuits into the rear body harness of every car, ending at a sealed 13-way inline connector behind the rear beam. Tow cars plug in a 0.6 m socket pigtail instead of having a separate 2.8 m tow harness routed through the body side at the final line. Baseline: tow-pack cars (55%) get a separate 2.8 m trailer harness (€38) laid at the final line from the rear zone module, through the D-pillar and under the boot floor to the socket, about 5 min of work with interior trim removal. Proposal: the rear body harness on all cars carries the trailer circuits (mixed 0.75-2.5 mm², about 0.35 kg copper, €4.50) to a sealed 13-way inline connector (€1.80) clipped to the rear beam. Tow cars add a 0.6 m socket pigtail (€9), fitted in 0.5 min from below. Why it works: the trailer feeds already come from the rear zone module, so the body harness passes them anyway; the separate harness only repeats the route. Load check: ISO 11446 pins 9 and 10 carry up to 15 A each; 2.5 mm² at 2.2 m keeps volt drop under 0.25 V. The towing load path and recovery points are not touched. Wading: the inline connector is sealed to IP6K7 and sits 520 mm above ground, below the 900 mm wade line, so it must be rated for immersion (ISO 20653 IPX7 at 1 m). Benchmark: Rivian places the R1S 7-pin connector behind a removable rear-bumper panel next to its integrated receiver, a factory-integrated towing interface.

title: Rear recovery bracket on towbar nut plates replaces welded rear towing-eye boss
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the welded rear towing-eye boss and its rail reinforcement from every body. Non-tow cars bolt a 10 mm S690QL rear recovery bracket to the towbar nut plates that every rail end already has; tow cars get a forged recovery loop on the towbar crossmember. Both are rated to the same 85 kN. Baseline: every car has a welded rear towing-eye boss with a 3 mm S420MC reinforcement in the right rear rail (€9, plus a €1.20 weld operation), rated to 2.0 × GVW. Every rail end also carries M12 nut plates for the towbar crossmember. Proposal: no boss. Non-tow cars (45%) get a laser-cut 10 mm S690QL bracket (€6.50) bolted by four M12 10.9 bolts to the nut plates, with a threaded bore for the screw-in eye. Tow cars (55%) get a forged loop on the towbar crossmember (€4.50). Why it works: the nut plates are designed for towing loads and sit at the rail end, the right place for a recovery anchor. Load check at 85 kN, 30° off-axis in plan and 15° vertical: four M12 10.9 bolts give about 4 × 45 kN in shear and 4 × 59 kN proof in tension, margin over 2. The bracket eye section, 10 mm × (80 − 33) mm = 470 mm² at 690 MPa yield, holds 324 kN. The rear rating rises from 2.0 to 2.5 × GVW. Benchmark: INEOS fits the Grenadier with towing eyes on all four corners usable for recovery, the four-corner principle this keeps.

title: One-piece cast G20Mn5 receiver head replaces six-part welded US hitch receiver
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces the US hitch receiver head, made from a 2-inch tube, collar plate, pin bushes, two safety-chain loops and a socket bracket welded together, with one quenched-and-tempered G20Mn5 steel casting welded to the crossmember by a single seam. Weld length and parts fall, strength is held. Baseline: the US tow pack (13.75% of fleet) receiver head is six parts: 50.8 × 50.8 × 6.3 mm S355J2H tube, collar plate, two pin bushes, two forged safety-chain loops and a socket bracket, joined by about 1.1 m of MAG weld (€34 parts + €9 welding). Proposal: one sand-cast G20Mn5+QT (EN 10340) head with integral loops, pin bosses and socket mount, machined for the 5/8 inch pin bore and receiver bore, welded to the crossmember tube by one circumferential seam (€26 + €5 machining + €2 weld). Why it works: G20Mn5+QT has Re ≥ 300 MPa and good weldability with Charpy ≥ 27 J at −40 °C. Load check: SAE J684 static tests for a 3,500 kg (7,700 lb) gross trailer weight and 350 kg tongue weight; the governing longitudinal tension of about 1.5 × GTW × g ≈ 51 kN acts on a receiver wall section of about 1,100 mm², 46 MPa, far below yield; safety-chain loops must each hold the GTW, 34 kN, over a 300 mm² section, 113 MPa. Fewer welds also mean fewer fatigue initiation sites at the receiver mouth. Benchmark: Tesla lists the Cybertruck at up to 11,000 lb towing, showing receiver hardware in this market is sized well above our rating.

title: Winch control folded into the front zone module with a hardwired stop and contactor
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the winch kit stand-alone control box by letting the front zone module drive a sealed winch contactor and read the remote. The safety functions stay hardware: a hardwired stop in the remote loop, a manual isolator and the mechanical load brake, so stopping the winch never depends on software. Baseline: the winch kit (6% of fleet) carries a stand-alone control box with its own contactor pack, logic board and wired-remote socket (€70), a wired remote (€25) and an in-cab isolator switch (€12). Proposal: a sealed IP67 reversing contactor (€35) on the cradle, coil-driven by two spare low-side outputs of the front zone module (€4 of hardware variant), which also reads the wired remote buttons and shows rope-out and motor temperature on the screen. The wired remote and in-cab isolator are kept. Why it works: the zone module already has spare outputs and a sealed front connector; the logic board in the box duplicates it. Fail-safe: the remote stop button is wired in series with the contactor coils, so releasing or pressing stop drops the coils in hardware even if the zone module hangs; the manual isolator cuts winch power; the winch mechanical load brake holds the load with no power. Load check: rated line pull 53.4 kN (12,000 lb winch); the brake holds 1.25 × line pull by specification, ≈ 67 kN. Recovery strength is unchanged because rope, drum, cradle and eyes are unchanged. Benchmark: Jeep lists a winch-capable steel front bumper on the Wrangler Rubicon 20th Anniversary edition, showing factory winch integration in the segment.

title: Caravan feed pins powered from the DC-DC, deleting the tow-pack 12 V battery upgrade
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Feeds the 13-pin permanent and charging pins (9 and 10) through an e-fuse channel from the DC-DC converter that powers the 12 V net on both powertrains, and keeps the standard 12 V battery. The tow-pack battery upgrade and its heavier tray are deleted. Baseline: the tow pack (55%) upgrades the 12 V AGM battery from 70 to 95 Ah (+€38, plus a larger tray €2) so the caravan fridge and charge feeds on ISO 11446 pins 9 and 10 cannot flatten it. Proposal: the standard battery stays. Pins 9 and 10 are fed by a 20 A e-fuse channel in the rear zone module, supplied by the 12 V DC-DC (800V-to-12 V on the BEV, 48-to-12 V on the MHEV, both rated about 3 kW). Pin 10 is live only with the drive system on; pin 9 is cut by the battery manager at 75% state of charge when parked. Why it works: while driving the DC-DC, not the battery, supplies the trailer. Load check: two 15 A feeds at 13.8 V ≈ 0.41 kW plus the 1.2 kW base load is well inside 3 kW. Parked, pin 9 at a 5 A fridge-standby load for 8 h would take 40 Ah, which is what the larger battery was for; cutting at 75% state of charge leaves the 70 Ah battery able to start the vehicle (BEV wake-up or MHEV starting), but limits parked pin-9 supply to about 17.5 Ah (about 3.5 h at 5 A against about 8 h today), a capability loss for tow-pack customers unless the BEV keeps its DC-DC awake from the HV pack. Towing load path, brakes and recovery points are untouched. Benchmark: Toyota quotes 3,500 kg braked towing for the LandCruiser 300, the caravan-towing class this tow pack serves.

title: Swan-neck tow ball made from bent 25CrMo4 tube with friction-welded ball
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces the solid forged 42CrMo4 swan-neck tow-ball arm with a bent seamless 25CrMo4 tube with a friction-welded forged ball end, then quench and temper. The tube has a higher section modulus than the solid neck at 34% less steel, so UN R55 fatigue margin is kept and cost falls. Baseline: EU and rest-of-world tow cars (75% non-US × 55% = 41% of fleet) use a solid forged 42CrMo4+QT swan neck, Ø45 mm at the root, 3.8 kg, with the ISO 1103 50 mm ball forged in (€38 forging + €12 machining). Proposal: seamless 25CrMo4 tube Ø50 × 8 mm (EN 10297-1) CNC-bent, a short forged 50 mm ball end friction-welded on, then quench and temper to Rm ≈ 900 MPa and machine the ball. Why it works: bending fatigue at the neck root governs. UN R55 dynamic test at ±0.6 D = ±10.2 kN with a 250 mm lever gives M ≈ 2.55 kN·m amplitude. Solid Ø45: Z = π·45³/32 ≈ 8,950 mm³, 285 MPa. Tube Ø50 × 8: I = π/64 × (50⁴ − 34⁴) ≈ 241,000 mm⁴, Z ≈ 9,650 mm³, 264 MPa, about 7% lower stress with 34% less cross-section (1,055 against 1,590 mm²). The friction weld sits 60 mm from the ball centre where M ≈ 0.6 kN·m, so its stress is low. The D-value, 17.0 kN, and static vertical load are unchanged. Benchmark: Land Rover offers an electrically deployable tow bar rated up to 3,500 kg, a reminder that the neck is a precision safety part at this rating.

title: Towing eye and wheel-nut key stowed in a pocket of the EPP jack tray
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Adds a moulded pocket to the existing EPP jack tray for the screw-in towing eye and the locking wheel-nut key, deleting the separate PU foam insert and the cloth bag. The eye is easier to find in a recovery, and the part count in the boot falls. Baseline: every car carries the screw-in towing eye (forged 42CrMo4, used front or rear) in a cloth bag (€0.90) pushed into a separate PU foam insert (€2.10) in the spare-wheel or under-floor well, next to the EPP jack tray (EPP 45 g/l). Owners often cannot find it when they need a tow. Proposal: the EPP jack tray mould gets a shaped pocket for the eye and the wheel-nut key, with a printed recovery-point diagram on the lid label. The foam insert and bag are deleted. Why it works: the tray already exists on every car, and a pocket is a tool change, not a part. Load check: the towing eye is unchanged, so its towing-device rating (Reg. (EU) 1005/2010, about 0.5 × GVW ≈ 17 kN) is unchanged; the label states that the screw-in eye is for on-road towing only, not kinetic or winch recovery, which uses the rated fixed eyes. The 0.6 kg eye in an EPP pocket must not rattle or come loose; a 20 g sled check sets the retention force at 0.6 × 9.81 × 20 ≈ 120 N, held by the pocket undercut. Benchmark: INEOS fits the Grenadier with towing eyes on all four corners usable for recovery, so its owners need no loose eye; where a screw-in eye is kept, it should be easy to find.

title: One symmetric forged recovery eye for all four corners, rear rating raised to front
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces the separate front off-road fixed hook forging and the offset rear eye forging with one symmetric 42CrMo4 forging used at all four corners. One die set and part number instead of two, a higher volume price, and the rear eye itself is uprated to 2.5 × GVW (the rear corner rating rises only once the rear bracket, rail and nut plates are proven at 85 kN). Baseline: the off-road pack (35%) has two front fixed hooks (forged 42CrMo4+QT, €14 each, rated 2.5 × GVW) and two rear eyes of a different offset shape (€12 each, rated 2.0 × GVW) from separate forging dies. Proposal: one symmetric eye (forged 42CrMo4+QT, 0.9 kg) with a 30 mm radiused bore for shackles or soft shackles, bolted by two M14 10.9 bolts at all four corners; the offset at the rear is taken by the mounting bracket. Why it works: the eye shape is set by the shackle bore and bolt pattern, which can be common; only brackets differ. Load check at the higher rating, 2.5 × BEV GVW ≈ 85 kN: eye section beside the bore, 2 × 14 mm × 22 mm = 616 mm² at 42CrMo4+QT yield of 650 MPa, holds about 400 kN, margin over 4. Two M14 10.9 bolts in shear hold about 120 kN. The rear eyes are therefore stronger than today, never weaker. Price: one forging at four per car is cheaper per piece (€12.80) because die cost and setup spread over twice the volume. Benchmark: Land Rover gives the Defender OCTA front and rear recovery points the same Phosphor Bronze finish, treating them as one visible family of parts.

title: Grained lower-grille flaps replace painted clip-in recovery-eye covers
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the painted clip-in covers over the recovery and towing-eye apertures. Road cars get a living-hinge flap moulded in the grained, unpainted lower grille and diffuser; off-road cars show the eyes exposed through grained apertures, so no cover is needed at all. Baseline: every car has two painted clip-in covers (front and rear, €4.50 each, tethered) over the screw-in towing-eye apertures in the painted bumpers; off-road cars have two painted covers over the fixed front eyes as well, removed by the owner before recovery and often lost. Proposal: the apertures move into the grained PP-EPDM-T15 lower grille (front) and diffuser (rear). Road cars get a living-hinge flap moulded in that part, pushed open by the eye. Off-road cars have open, bezelled apertures with the eyes exposed. Why it works: the cover is cosmetic; the grained parts are unpainted, so a moulded flap costs almost nothing and cannot be lost. Recovery strength is untouched: eyes, brackets and the 85 kN rating are unchanged, and the open aperture clears a soft shackle and a 30° off-axis strap. Approach-angle line: the grille aperture sits behind the lowest point. Pedestrian: the flap sits in the lower-leg (flexPLI) zone but is soft unpainted PP with no hard point, so lower-leg performance is unchanged (to confirm in UN R127 / GTR 9 test). Benchmark: Land Rover leaves the Defender OCTA front and rear recovery points exposed in a Phosphor Bronze finish, showing that visible recovery hardware is a design feature.

title: Thread-rolled M24 shank on the screw-in towing eye replaces lathe-cut thread
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Rolls the M24 thread of the screw-in towing eye after quench and temper instead of hard-turning it on a lathe. Cycle time falls from about 70 s to 4 s, insert cost disappears, and the rolled thread has higher fatigue strength from compressive residual stress, so the eye is at least as strong. Baseline: every car carries a forged 42CrMo4+QT screw-in towing eye (0.6 kg) with an M24 × 3 thread hard-turned at about 32 HRC on a CNC lathe, about 70 s per part with carbide insert wear. Proposal: the thread is cold-rolled on a two-die thread-rolling machine after QT (4 s), with the blank diameter turned to the rolling pitch diameter in the same op as the collar. Why it works: rolling forms the thread instead of cutting it, so grain flow follows the flanks and the root carries compressive residual stress; rolled-after-heat-treat threads typically show 30-50% higher fatigue strength than cut threads, with the same stress area (353 mm²) and minor diameter. Load check, towing-device case plus a 30° side pull: axial 0.5 × GVW = 0.5 × 3,450 × 9.81 ≈ 17 kN gives 48 MPa on the stress area; the side component, 17 × sin30 ≈ 8.5 kN at a 40 mm lever, gives M ≈ 0.34 kN·m on the minor diameter (Z = π × 20.3³/32 ≈ 820 mm³), about 415 MPa, under the 650 MPa yield of 42CrMo4+QT. The rated off-road fixed eyes (85 kN) are separate and unchanged. Benchmark: INEOS fits the Grenadier with towing eyes on all four corners usable for recovery; where a screw-in eye is kept for road cars, its thread quality is what carries the load.

ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: wading is signed off on vehicles twice, at verification and production-prototype stage. Each loop uses about 14 prototypes for 40 trough runs at 0.5, 0.7 and 0.9 m and 3-10 km/h, and every leak found means a strip-down, a fix and a re-run. Each loop costs about €4.2M including prototype share and rebuilds. Proposal: build a smoothed-particle-hydrodynamics (SPH) bow-wave model of the full underbody and engine bay or frunk, correlated once against the existing trough with 12 level probes. The model maps the local water level and splash velocity at every component below the 1,050 mm dry line. Each component is then qualified on a plunge rig at 1.2 m head, and one vehicle loop is kept for final sign-off. Head-pressure check: rated depth 900 mm gives ρgh = 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.90 = 8.8 kPa at ground level. The bow wave at 7 km/h (1.94 m/s) adds about v²/2g = 0.19 m at the front face, so the dry line is set at 1,050 mm. The 1.2 m rig head (11.8 kPa) covers the worst static plus bow-wave case (0.90 + 0.19 = 1.09 m, 10.7 kPa) with a 1.1× margin, and the 0.9 m static head with 1.3×; because the crest exceeds the 150 mm allowance, front-face parts up to 1,100 mm stay in the immersion band. Why it works: most trough runs only find where water reaches, which the correlated model predicts. Sealing failures are component-level and repeat on a rig at a fraction of the cost. Benchmark: Land Rover quotes 900 mm for Range Rover only at Off-Road 2 height with a shallow entry, which shows that validated depth is a function of ride height and speed, exactly what the model sweeps.

ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Two plunge rigs (1.5 m tank, heated soak chamber) at the validation centre; no plant change. Prototype build plan loses one wading-only batch of about 14 cars. The SPH model is reused for every derivative and model-year change.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Every component below the dry line gets a modelled local water level and splash velocity in its specification, so suppliers design seals to a stated head rather than a generic IPX7 claim. Rig fixtures reuse the vehicle mounting brackets so orientation is representative.

Late-leak rework €1.0 → €0.4 = €0.6. Mid = 12.0 − 1.4 − 1.2 + 0.6 = €10.0. Net €8-€12 per vehicle (fleet average) × 50,000 vehicles/yr = €400K-€600K per year (engineering estimate; assumed mix MHEV 60% / 800V BEV 40%, off-road pack 30% take; tooling and validation amortised over 7 years = 350,000 vehicles where stated).

title: Cabin-floor harness pass-throughs below the dry line cut from eleven to four
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Re-routes the chassis harness branches so only four sealed pass-throughs sit below the 1,050 mm dry line instead of eleven. This deletes seven grommets, their installation and leak-test rework, at the cost of about 1.2 m of extra wire bundle. Baseline: the chassis harness enters the cabin through eleven grommeted holes below 1,050 mm. Four are in the front footwells at 250-400 mm, three under the rear seat, two at the tunnel and two at the A-pillar foot. Each is an EPDM grommet with tape wrap and a sealing audit, and each is a potential wading leak. Proposal: group the wheel-arch, seat, rear-axle and air-suspension branches into two 40-way sealed bulkhead connectors, one per side at the pillar foot, plus two large grommets for the 12 V supply and the 48 V or HV-interlock feeds. Seven holes are deleted from the floor panels. Head-pressure check: the lowest remaining pass-through sits at 400 mm. At 900 mm rated depth plus a 150 mm bow wave the head is 0.65 m, ρgh = 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.65 = 6.4 kPa. Bulkhead-connector interface seals are specified at ≥ 20 kPa contact pressure (3× margin) and tested at IPX7 after thermal shock. Footwell grommets that used to see 0.80 m (7.8 kPa) are deleted outright. Why it works: every hole below the waterline is a leak path and a manual operation. Fewer, better-sealed interfaces cut both. Benchmark: Rivian quotes up to 43.2 in (about 1,097 mm) fording for R1S, a depth that only works with a cabin sealed against leaks, which is the design intent here.

title: Ultrasonic seal-leak scan replaces the off-road pack's extended underbody flood test
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces the extra underbody flood-jet station, drying booth and wet-carpet rework run on off-road-pack bodies with a 70-second robotic ultrasonic scan of door, tailgate and floor seals on every car. The standard monsoon booth stays. Baseline: every car passes a standard 2-minute monsoon booth. Off-road-pack cars (30% take) also get a 4-minute underbody flood test with 2 bar jets aimed at door bottoms, sills and floor seams to simulate wading. Then they go through a drying booth, with carpet lifts on a 10% sample. About 3% of pack cars need wet-carpet rework at about €60. Proposal: a 40 kHz ultrasonic emitter is placed in the cabin and a robot-held microphone array scans the door, tailgate and floor seal lines and the grommets in 70 s. Gaps of 0.1 mm and above are detected and their position is logged to the build record. The extended flood test and drying booth are deleted. Head-pressure check: wading at 900 mm puts about 0.45 m of head on the door-bottom seal line (450 mm sill height), ρgh = 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.45 = 4.4 kPa. A 0.1 mm × 10 mm slot passes Q = Cd·A·√(2ΔP/ρ) = 0.6 × 1×10⁻⁶ × √8.8 = 1.8 mL/s, about 0.1 L/min, so the 0.1 mm threshold catches the gaps that would soak a carpet in a short wade; smaller gaps (a 0.05 mm slot still passes about 0.9 mL/s, 1.6 L in a 30-minute wade) and porous sealer are covered by the retained weekly flood audit. Why it works: leaks are geometry (gaps). Ultrasound finds gaps directly and gives their location, whereas flooding only shows the consequence. Benchmark: Rivian's lap-pool demonstration held water about a foot

title: One commonised sealed housing family for every chassis ECU below the dry line
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces five bespoke ECU housings (different die-castings, gaskets, screw patterns and immersion validation programmes) with two sizes of one laser-welded PBT-GF30 housing, cutting piece cost, gaskets and three validation programmes. Baseline: five chassis ECUs mount below 1,050 mm: air-suspension valve-block controller, rear-wheel-steer ECU, deployable side-step controller, CDC damper ECU and the wade-zone body node. Each has its own AlSi9Cu3 die-cast or PBT housing with formed gasket, 6-8 screws and an ePTFE vent, and each is validated to IP6K9K, IPX7 and thermal shock separately. On average 3.6 of them are fitted per car because of option mix. Proposal: two sizes (90 × 70 and 140 × 100 mm) of one PBT-GF30 housing, laser-transmission-welded (laser-transparent cover, absorbing base), with a common connector window, an adhesive ePTFE vent and the same mounting feet. One validation family test covers both sizes. Head-pressure check: the lowest node sits at 350 mm. At 900 mm plus a 150 mm bow wave the head is 0.70 m, ρgh = 6.9 kPa. A thermal-shock plunge from 85 °C to 15 °C would pull 101.3 × (1 − 288/358) = 19.8 kPa of vacuum in a sealed box. The 1 L/min vent equalises the 0.15 L free volume in seconds, and weld burst exceeds 200 kPa. Why it works: these ECUs carry similar boards and power levels, and the wading case dominates their housing design. One proven housing replaces five near-identical problems. Benchmark: Defender OCTA quotes 1,000 mm wading on air suspension, which puts every chassis node in this zone under the same immersion duty.

title: Sealed connector bay on the pack front replaces three immersion-rated 800V connector pairs
description: [800V BEV] Moves the pack's two EDU HV feeds and the auxiliary HV feed inside one FIPG-sealed bay cover. Bolted busbar lugs and overmoulded cable glands replace three immersion-rated 800V connector pairs, minus the cost of the bay cover and its interlock. Baseline: the 800V BEV pack front face carries three HV connector pairs (front EDU, rear EDU, auxiliary for e-compressor, PTC and OBC). Each is rated 250 A or 40 A at 800 V and sealed to IP6K9K plus IPX7/IPX8 at 1 m with thermal shock, at an average €30 per pair. Proposal: a vacuum-HPDC AlSi10MnMg bay cover sealed to the pack front flange with one FIPG silicone bead. Inside the bay, cables terminate on M8 bolted busbar lugs. Cables enter through overmoulded LSR cable glands (€11 each including lug). The cover's screws sit under the service-disconnect cover, so the HV string is mechanically broken before the bay can be opened, and isolation does not rely on software. Head-pressure check: the pack front sits at 330 mm. At 900 mm plus a 150 mm bow wave the head is 0.72 m, ρgh = 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.72 = 7.1 kPa. The bay shares the pack's ePTFE breathing so it sees no thermal-shock vacuum, and the FIPG bead is qualified to 30 kPa (4× margin). Why it works: an immersion-rated pluggable 800V connector pays for sealing, touch-safety and mating cycles. Inside a sealed bay, touch-safety and sealing are provided once by the cover. Benchmark: Mercedes attributes the G 580 EQ's 850 mm wading, 150 mm deeper than the petrol G, to the battery sitting in a protective casing; we extend that casing over the connectors.

ideaData.manufacturingImpact: New bay-cover HPDC die and an FIPG dispense step on the existing pack-lid robot. Cable harnesses become gland-and-lug assemblies. EDU-end connectors are unchanged. Pack EOL leak test covers the bay in the same cycle.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Lugs are captive in a PA66-GF30 carrier with torque-to-yield marking. Glands are keyed by diameter so cables cannot be swapped. The bay cover locates on two dowels and seals on a machined flange with one continuous bead path.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: High – three 800V connector pairs replaced by one sealed bay
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Per BEV: 3 HV connector pairs × €30 = €90 → 3 glands and lugs × €11 = €33. Bay cover −€14, FIPG and assembly −€3.3, interlock bracket −€3.0. Net per BEV = 90 − 33 − 14 − 3.3 − 3.0 = €36.7 × 40% BEV share = €14.7 fleet average. Net €12-€17 per vehicle (fleet average) × 50,000 vehicles/yr = €600K-€850K per year (engineering estimate; assumed mix MHEV 60% / 800V BEV 40%, off-road pack 30% take; tooling and validation amortised over 7 years = 350,000 vehicles where stated).

ideaData.riskNotes: Service time rises (remove cover, then lugs) and the FIPG must be re-dispensed after opening. Validate UN R100 (IPXXB inside the bay, isolation, post-immersion), FMVSS 305 post-crash isolation, UN R94/R95 and R137 pack-front intrusion, ISO 20653 IPX7/IPX8, OEM wading-depth validation at 900 mm, and the mechanical service-disconnect interlock on the cover screws. Engineering review (13 Oct 2026) — open point: Each 800V feed has two conductors (DC+ and DC-), each shielded. Three feeds need six lugs and six single-core glands (or three two-core glands with six lugs), each with 360-degree shield termination for UN R10, but the bridge prices three glands at €11. The proposed cost is understated by roughly €30 per BEV (about €12 fleet), which could halve the saving. Re-cost before release.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: Mercedes G 580 EQ (2025) — 850 mm wading, 150 mm deeper than the petrol G, attributed by Mercedes to the battery sitting in a protective casing. How this differs: We extend the sealed casing over the pack-front HV interfaces, so three immersion-rated 800V connector pairs become lugs inside one sealed bay.

title: Dry-line zoning drops immersion tests and seal grade for parts above 1,050 mm
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Removes the blanket 1 m immersion test and the class-3 immersion seal grade from electrical parts that sit entirely above 1,200 mm (the 1,050 mm wade-plus-bow-wave line plus a 150 mm IPX7 band). They keep IP6K9K spray and ISO 16750 splash tests; safety-critical parts are excluded and keep full immersion qualification. Baseline: the exterior and engine-bay electrical specification applies IP6K9K plus IPX7 immersion and splash thermal shock to every part regardless of height. About 38 part numbers sit entirely above 1,200 mm, the top of the retained IPX7 band: cowl and scuttle sensors, upper engine-bay or frunk modules, roof antennas, mirror electronics, upper lamps and the high-mounted camera. Each costs about €10k per validation lot (6 samples, 30 min at 1 m, pre- and post-electrical), and 14 of them use immersion-grade connector seals. Proposal: dry-line zoning at 1,050 mm (900 mm rated depth + 150 mm bow wave) in the specification and the PLM part attributes. Parts wholly above the line keep IP6K9K high-pressure spray, IPX5 and ISO 16750-4 splash but no immersion leg. Parts within 1,050-1,200 mm keep IPX7. title: One hot-soak plunge test replaces separate IPX7, IPX8 and thermal-shock legs
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Combines three component qualification legs (IPX7 immersion, OEM IPX8 at 1.2 m and splash thermal shock) into one hot-soak-then-plunge leg on one sample set for about 60 below-dry-line part numbers. This saves samples, chamber time and programme time. Baseline: each below-dry-line component runs three separate legs, each with 6 fresh samples and its own chamber booking. They are IPX7 (1 m, 30 min), the OEM IPX8 wading leg (1.2 m, 2 h) and ISO 16750-4 splash thermal shock (ice water on a part at maximum temperature). About 60 part numbers per programme; cost about €10k per part per leg (about €30k per part, €1.8M per programme) across samples, chambers and reports. Proposal: one combined leg. The part is soaked at its rated maximum temperature (85 °C chassis, 105 °C EDU-adjacent), then plunged within 10 s into 0 °C water at 1.2 m head for 2 h, energised and monitored, then given a post-test dielectric and function check. One sample set of 6. Head-pressure check: rated 900 mm wading gives ρgh = 8.8 kPa. The 1.2 m plunge applies 11.8 kPa. Thermal-shock vacuum for 85 → 0 °C is 101.3 × (1 − 273/358) = 24 kPa in a sealed part. The combined leg applies both at once, the real wading sequence, so it is more severe than any single legacy leg. Why it works: in a real wade, heat and head arrive together. Separate legs triple the samples and miss the interaction (a hot seal is softest exactly when vacuum pulls hardest). title: One-piece EPDM bellows with moulded clamp rings joins snorkel to airbox
description: [MHEV] Replaces three hose sections, two PP adaptors, four worm-drive clamps and the wing grommet on the factory-fit snorkel path with one moulded EPDM bellows that carries two PA66 snap clamp rings and a wing seal lip, cutting parts and five minutes of assembly. Baseline: on the MHEV off-road pack with factory snorkel (30% of MHEV, 9% of fleet), the snorkel joins the airbox through three EPDM hose sections, two PP-T20 adaptors, four worm-drive clamps and a separate wing grommet. This costs €18.4 plus 7 minutes of assembly. Proposal: one compression-moulded EPDM 70 ShA bellows with two convolutions for body tolerance and, where the airbox is engine-mounted, engine-roll movement (±12 mm), two integrated PA66-GF30 snap clamp rings with a positive click and a moulded wing seal lip, at €9.8 and 2.5 minutes. Head-pressure check: the lowest joint sits at 820 mm. At 900 mm plus a 150 mm bow wave the outside head is 0.23 m, ρgh = 2.3 kPa. Inside, the intake depression at 3.0 L I6 full load (0.33 kg/s through filter and snorkel) is about −3.5 kPa. So the joint sees 5.8 kPa pulling water inward, the governing case. title: EVAP canister fresh-air vent piped into the wheel-arch dry cavity, deleting the dust box
description: [MHEV] Deletes the underbody EVAP dust box, its splash shield and the low canister-vent-valve bracket. A 6 mm PA12 vent tube runs up to a foam-capped outlet in the rear quarter cavity above the dry line, and the vent valve moves up with it. Baseline: on the MHEV, the EVAP canister sits near the tank at about 350 mm. Its fresh-air port runs through the canister vent valve (CVV, used for leak diagnosis) to a labyrinth dust box with a drain and a splash shield at 380 mm. In a wade, water pushed into the dust box reaches the CVV and the carbon bed, causing OBD leak-check faults and canister damage. The dust box, shield and bracket cost €7.8. Proposal: route a 6 mm PA12 vent tube, 1.6 m long, up the rear wheelhouse to a foam-filter cap in the quarter cavity behind the wheel-arch liner at 1,100 mm. The CVV moves to a small bracket at the same height. Head-pressure check: at the old dust-box height the outside head was 0.90 + 0.15 − 0.38 = 0.67 m, ρgh = 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.67 = 6.6 kPa pushing water into an open vent. At 1,100 mm the outlet is 50 mm above the bow-wave line, so the static head is zero. The tube is a closed pipe, and its low-point joints at the canister are sealed quick connectors rated 50 kPa. Why it works: a vent only needs to breathe air. Putting the opening where water cannot reach removes the labyrinth that only exists to fight water. Benchmark: Land Rover quotes 900 mm wading for Range Rover, a depth that puts any underbody vent opening deep below the surface.

title: Rolling-diaphragm volume compensator on the MHEV front axle replaces its raised vent line
description: [MHEV] Seals the MHEV front differential with an FKM rolling diaphragm in the cover that absorbs thermal and oil volume change. This deletes the 1.4 m raised vent line, its axle-to-body flex section, clips and body bracket. Baseline: the MHEV front differential breathes through a 1.4 m PA12 vent line rising to 1,100 mm, with a flexible section for axle movement, five clips, a body bracket and an end cap. Total €6.9 plus 1.5 minutes. Proposal: the diff cover carries a 75 mm FKM rolling diaphragm with 0.30 L swept volume, vented on its outer side through a protected, self-draining labyrinth (it floods in a wade, but water there only meets the diaphragm, never the oil). The oil side is fully sealed, so no water path exists. Volume check: 1.3 L oil and 0.55 L air at 95 °C cooled to 15 °C by a wade. Air contraction 0.55 × (1 − 288/368) = 0.12 L and oil contraction 1.3 × 7×10⁻⁴ × 80 = 0.07 L total 0.19 L, inside the 0.30 L stroke. Without the diaphragm a sealed diff would pull 101.3 × (1 − 288/368) = 22 kPa of vacuum. With it the internal pressure stays within ±1 kPa. Head-pressure check: the diff centre sits at 330 mm. At 900 mm plus a 150 mm bow wave the outside head is 0.72 m, ρgh = 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.72 = 7.1 kPa, against shaft-seal ratings of 50 kPa. Why it works: a breather line exists only to relieve thermal vacuum. Absorb the volume change and the line, and its route up the body, has no job. Benchmark: Bronco is quoted at 33.5 in fording with Sasquatch and 31.5 in without, showing that fording depth is tied to package hardware heights such as vents.

title: Slotted aero undertrays sized for bow-wave and trapped-air loads delete the off-road variant
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces the road and off-road-pack aero undertray variants with one 2.2 mm PP-T20 panel. Vent slots at its high points release trapped air before it can lift the panel, so the thicker off-road panel, its twelve extra fasteners and two straps are deleted. Baseline: road cars use 2.0 mm PP-T20 aero undertrays (front 1.2 m², two mid 0.8 m²) with 22 fasteners. The off-road pack (30% take) has a 2.5 mm variant with 34 fasteners and two retaining straps, added after trough trials tore panels. These are aero panels, not the steel or aluminium skid plates, which are unchanged. Proposal: one 2.2 mm PP-T20 panel for all cars. It has eight 30 × 8 mm vent slots at the high points of each air pocket and cross-ribs between fasteners, held by 24 fasteners. Load check: a 15 mm air pocket under the 1.2 m² front panel traps 18 L, giving buoyant uplift of 18 × 9.81 = 177 N when submerged. The slots vent it within 2 s, and two drain holes at each panel's low points shed the same 18 L of water left standing on top of the panel on exit. Flow drag at 7 km/h is ½ρv² = ½ × 1,000 × 1.94² = 1.9 kPa on the 0.03 m² leading edge, 57 N. With 24 fasteners each sees under 15 N, against a 180 N pull-out rating. ideaData.title: Slotted aero undertrays sized for bow-wave and trapped-air loads delete the off-road variant
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: road cars use 2.0 mm PP-T20 aero undertrays (front 1.2 m², two mid 0.8 m²) with 22 fasteners. The off-road pack (30% take) has a 2.5 mm variant with 34 fasteners and two retaining straps, added after trough trials tore panels. These are aero panels, not the steel or aluminium skid plates, which are unchanged. Proposal: one 2.2 mm PP-T20 panel for all cars. It has eight 30 × 8 mm vent slots at the high points of each air pocket and cross-ribs between fasteners, held by 24 fasteners. Load check: a 15 mm air pocket under the 1.2 m² front panel traps 18 L, giving buoyant uplift of 18 × 9.81 = 177 N when submerged. The slots vent it within 2 s, and two drain holes at each panel's low points shed the same 18 L of water left standing on top of the panel on exit. Flow drag at 7 km/h is ½ρv² = ½ × 1,000 × 1.94² = 1.9 kPa on the 0.03 m² leading edge, 57 N. With 24 fasteners each sees under 15 N, against a 180 N pull-out rating. Head-pressure check: the panel sits at 300 mm, so ρgh under 900 mm wading is 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.6 = 5.9 kPa. It acts equally on both faces once the slots vent, so the net load is zero. Why it works: the torn panels were caused by trapped-air buoyancy, not water pressure. Vent the air and a thin panel survives. Benchmark: Defender OCTA's 1,000 mm wading rating puts every underbody aero panel deep in the water column.

ideaData.dfmDfa: Slots are moulded with a downward-facing lip so splash at speed does not enter. Fastener positions are common to both former variants so the body needs no new holes.

title: Rear EDU park-lock actuator moved inside the oil-wet housing, deleting its seal and connector
description: [800V BEV] Runs the rear EDU park-lock BLDC actuator inside the gearbox oil chamber and feeds it through spare pins of the existing EDU signal connector. This deletes the external actuator housing seal, its own sealed connector pair and pigtail. Baseline: the rear EDU park pawl is driven by an external BLDC actuator bolted to the housing at about 380 mm. It has an O-ring shaft seal, an AlSi9Cu3 actuator housing, its own sealed 6-way connector pair and a 0.4 m pigtail, and it breathes to avoid thermal-shock vacuum. Proposal: the motor and worm stage sit inside the gearbox oil chamber, as electric oil pumps do in many transmissions. They have an encapsulated stator, ATF-compatible enamel and a magnet trap at the sump. Leads exit through four spare pins of the EDU's existing sealed signal connector, which suits an actuator with an on-board driver (supply, ground, command, position feedback); that driver must then be qualified in hot ATF. The pawl, its spring and its defaults are unchanged, and the EPB remains the redundant secure. Head-pressure check: at 380 mm the head is 0.90 + 0.15 − 0.38 = 0.67 m, ρgh = 6.6 kPa. A 90 → 15 °C wade on the old sealed actuator would pull 101.3 × (1 − 288/363) = 21 kPa of vacuum. Inside the vented EDU the actuator sees neither, so one water boundary and one connector are removed. Why it works: the actuator only had a housing seal because it lived outside the oil. Inside, it shares the EDU's existing proven boundary. title: Conformal pack lid cuts free-air volume so one breathing vent replaces two
description: [800V BEV] Draws the pack lid closer to the module tops, cutting the pack's free-air volume from about 120 L to 72 L. The thermal-breathing flow in a wade then halves, so one ePTFE equalisation vent replaces two, and one vent, its boss and its fitting are deleted. Baseline: the 800V pack has about 120 L of free air between a flat lid and the module tops and corners. It breathes through two ePTFE equalisation vents (plus the separate burst disc). In a wade, lid and tray are quenched and the internal air cools by about 10 K in 5 min. The required vent flow is V·ΔT/(T·t) = 120 × 10/(318 × 5) = 0.75 L/min, more than one 1.0 L/min-at-7 kPa vent can pass at a low pressure difference. Proposal: a lid formed conformal to the module tops (draw depth +18 mm in two pockets) cuts the free volume to 72 L. Flow becomes 0.45 L/min, which one vent passes at about 3 kPa. The burst disc and its sizing are unchanged. Head-pressure check: the vent sits on the lid top at about 500 mm. At 900 mm plus a 150 mm bow wave it is 0.55 m under water, ρgh = 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.55 = 5.4 kPa. The ePTFE water-entry pressure is ≥ 60 kPa. The 3 kPa breathing vacuum adds to the 5.4 kPa head, 8.4 kPa across the membrane, still a 7× margin. Why it works: vent count is set by how much air must move, and air that is not there does not need to breathe. Benchmark: Mercedes credits the G 580 EQ's 850 mm wading to the battery in a protective casing; casing volume management is part of that.

title: 800V EDU HV header sealed by one LSR radial seal, not gasket and O-rings
description: [800V BEV] Replaces the HV header's flat FKM gasket, two cable O-rings, two of its four screws and the spot-face machining with one overmoulded liquid-silicone radial seal entering a machined bore. Seal parts and machining fall on both EDUs. Baseline: each EDU's 800V DC header (PA66-GF30) seals to the housing with a flat FKM gasket, held by four M6 screws on a spot-faced land. Two O-rings seal the cable boots, and the header is rated IP6K9K plus IPX7 with thermal shock. Proposal: a 2K header with a liquid-silicone (LSR 50 ShA) radial seal overmoulded on a 62 mm spigot, pushed into a machined bore and held by two screws plus an anti-rotation lug. Cable seals are overmoulded single-wire LSR. Head-pressure check: the EDU headers sit at 450 mm. At 900 mm plus a 150 mm bow wave the head is 0.60 m, ρgh = 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.60 = 5.9 kPa. The EDU is vented, so no thermal-shock vacuum acts across the header. A radial seal at 20-25% squeeze gives about 1.5 MPa contact pressure, far above 5.9 kPa, and, unlike a flat gasket, it does not depend on screw preload or face flatness. Why it works: radial seals tolerate housing distortion and screw relaxation that flat gaskets do not, so screws are reduced to retention duty. Benchmark: Jeep states that the Wrangler 4xe's HV electronics and the battery-to-motor wiring are sealed and waterproof for 30 in fording, and each EDU header is one of those boundaries.

title: Low-pressure hot-melt moulding seals wade-zone harness breakouts instead of tape and heat-shrink
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces adhesive-lined heat-shrink, PVC tape and sealant on 24 chassis-harness breakouts and splices below the dry line with automated polyamide low-pressure moulding, cutting labour and sealing-defect rework. Baseline: the chassis harness has 18 breakouts and 6 splices below 1,050 mm (wheel arches, rear axle, side steps, towbar). Each is sealed by hand with adhesive-lined heat-shrink, PVC tape and a sealant spot, at about €0.72 each including labour. About 0.4% of harnesses fail the wading audit at a breakout. Proposal: polyamide hot-melt low-pressure moulding (about 25 bar, 200 °C, 25 s cycle) at the harness supplier forms a bonded, sealed boot over each breakout and splice in one shot, at €0.48 each. Head-pressure check: the lowest breakouts sit at 300 mm. At 900 mm plus a 150 mm bow wave the head is 0.75 m, ρgh = 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.75 = 7.4 kPa. The moulded polyamide bonds to the PVC insulation with ≥ 1.5 N/mm peel (XLPE and PP-insulated cables need plasma pre-treatment or a polyolefin-adhesion grade to reach that), and the boot is qualified at 50 kPa after thermal cycling, a 6× margin. Why it works: hand-taped seals vary with the operator. A moulded boot is repeatable, inspectable by vision and bonds instead of clamping. Benchmark: Range Rover Electric is quoted with the same 900 mm wading as the combustion Range Rover, so a shared platform harness must seal to that depth on both powertrains.

The moulded polyamide bonds to the PVC insulation with ≥ 1.5 N/mm peel (XLPE and PP-insulated cables need plasma pre-treatment or a polyolefin-adhesion grade to reach that), and the boot is qualified at 50 kPa after thermal cycling, a 6× margin. Why it works: hand-taped seals vary with the operator. A moulded boot is repeatable, inspectable by vision and bonds instead of clamping. Benchmark: Range Rover Electric is quoted with the same 900 mm wading as the combustion Range Rover, so a shared platform harness must seal to that depth on both powertrains.

title: Airbox lower shell with moulded swirl vanes and drain replaces the separate water separator
description: [MHEV] Moulds tangential swirl vanes and a drain into the MHEV airbox lower shell on every car. The separate in-line water separator, its two clamps and its fitting, used only on the off-road pack, are deleted. Baseline: the MHEV off-road pack (30% of MHEV) adds a separate PP in-line water separator with vanes and a drain valve between the high intake and the airbox, at €11.5 plus two clamps (€1.4) and 2.5 minutes of fitting. Road MHEVs have none. Proposal: the PP-T20 airbox lower shell on all MHEVs gets a tangential inlet, six moulded swirl vanes ahead of the filter and a TPV flap drain at the low point. The shell costs €1.8 more. Separation check: inlet flow at 0.33 kg/s is about 0.27 m³/s through a 0.018 m² inlet, 15 m/s. Vanes turn the flow 90° on a 60 mm radius, giving centrifugal acceleration v²/r = 15²/0.06 = 3,750 m/s², over 380 g. Spray droplets of 100 µm and above reach the wall in under 10 mm of travel. The added pressure loss is about 0.4 kPa at full load. Head-pressure check: the drain sits at 780 mm. At 900 mm plus a 150 mm bow wave it is 0.27 m under water outside, ρgh = 2.6 kPa, while intake depression inside is −3.5 kPa. The TPV flap is held shut by the 6.1 kPa net difference and opens only when the engine is off, so the lower shell needs a sump below the filter sized for the water separated during the longest wade. Why it works: separation needs a turn and a drain, which the airbox can provide in its own wall. Benchmark: Grenadier's 800 mm wading is quoted with or without its raised air intake, showing the standard intake height already carries the rating,

title: 13-pin tow socket with overmoulded harness tail deletes its in-line connector and boot
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Overmoulds the trailer harness tail directly into the rear of the 13-pin socket. The submerged in-line 13-way sealed connector pair, the rear rubber boot and the contact-grease operation are deleted on tow-pack cars. Baseline: the ISO 11446 13-pin socket on tow-pack cars (40% take) sits at 480 mm on the towbar bracket. It has a flip lid, a rubber rear boot, a sealed in-line 13-way connector pair behind the bumper and contact grease, about €6.6 per car. In a wade both the socket face and the in-line connector are under water. Proposal: the socket body is moulded with its harness tail overmoulded at the rear (PA66-GF30 body, TPE overmould to IP6K9K/IPX7 at the rear). The socket face is drained downward with tin-plated contacts and the flip lid kept. The in-line connector and boot are deleted. Head-pressure check: at 480 mm under 900 mm wading plus a 150 mm bow wave the head is 0.57 m, ρgh = 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.57 = 5.6 kPa. The rear overmould is qualified at 30 kPa, a 5× margin. The front face is allowed to flood and drain, as today, so its contacts see the same exposure as before. Why it works: the in-line connector existed only for assembly convenience. Overmoulding removes the second submerged interface. Benchmark: Grenadier is quoted at 800 mm wading, a depth that submerges any rear-bumper tow electrics.

title: Snorkel ram head injection-moulded in PP-T20 with louvre labyrinth replaces rotomoulded head and cap
description: [MHEV] Replaces the rotomoulded HDPE snorkel head, separate PA6 rain cap, screws and mesh with two vibration-welded PP-T20 injection shells. A 180° louvre labyrinth and snap-in mesh are moulded in, cutting piece cost and one fitting operation. Baseline: the MHEV factory snorkel (9% of fleet) ends in a 3.5 mm rotomoulded HDPE ram head (€24) with a separate PA6 rain cap (€4.5), three screws and a stainless mesh (€1.6) and 1.5 minutes of fitting. Proposal: two PP-T20 injection-moulded shells, vibration-welded, with a 180° louvre labyrinth that turns the incoming air twice before the snorkel tube, plus a snap-in PA mesh, total €16.5 including weld. Separation check: head inlet area 0.018 m² at 0.27 m³/s gives 15 m/s. Two 180° turns on a 30 mm radius give centrifugal acceleration v²/r = 15²/0.03 = 7,500 m/s². Rain and spray droplets of 200 µm and above reach the louvre walls and drain through two 4 mm slots at the lowest louvre. Pressure loss is 0.25 kPa, the same as the baseline cap. The head sits at about 1,750 mm, above any wade or bow wave, so sealing is a rain and spray duty, not immersion: the tube joint below the head at 1,500 mm sits above the 1,050 mm bow-wave line, so ρgh = 0. Why it works: rotomoulding suits low volumes and thick walls, but at 4,500 heads a year an injection tool pays back and moulds the separation geometry the cap was added for. Benchmark: Grenadier Trialmaster editions list a snorkel among their equipment, alongside the 800 mm wading rating.

title: Laser-welded aluminium inverter cover replaces the gasket and eighteen screws on each EDU
description: [800V BEV] Replaces each EDU's die-cast inverter cover, formed gasket, 18 screws and 18 tapped holes with a 1.5 mm 5754 aluminium cover laser-seam-welded to a vacuum-HPDC flange. This cuts parts, machining and torque operations, minus the weld process and a warranty-exchange allowance. Baseline: each 800V EDU inverter is closed by a 2.5 mm AlSi10Mg HPDC cover with a formed silicone gasket, 18 M5 screws into 18 tapped holes, and an ePTFE vent. Proposal: a 1.5 mm 5754-O stamped cover laser-seam-welded with 4047 filler wire (fillet, 2.5 kW fibre laser, 45 s) to a flange on a vacuum-HPDC AlSi10MnMg housing with gas content below 5 mL/100 g to avoid weld porosity. The vent stays. Head-pressure check: the inverter sits at 500 mm. At 900 mm plus a 150 mm bow wave the head is 0.55 m, ρgh = 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.55 = 5.4 kPa. The vent equalises internal pressure, but if blocked by silt an 85 → 15 °C quench would pull 101.3 × (1 − 288/358) = 19.8 kPa. The welded seam bursts above 300 kPa, so either case has more than a 15× margin. A gasket under screw relaxation was the weakest point of the baseline. Why it works: a weld cannot relax, creep or be mis-torqued, and the cover becomes a stamping instead of a casting. Benchmark: Tesla tells Cybertruck owners Wade Mode allows about 31 in, and that water damage is not covered by warranty, a sign of how much the EDU and pack sealing must be trusted.

title: Frunk-tub drains with floating-ball checks stop wading backflow and delete drain hoses
description: [800V BEV] Moulds two floating-ball check drains into the frunk tub floor. They let rainwater out and seal by buoyancy when wading water rises from below, deleting the drain hoses, clamps and separate rubber valves. Baseline: the 800V BEV frunk tub (PP-T20) has two floor drains with EPDM duckbills on 0.6 m hoses run to below the tub skirt, plus clamps, at €4.4 plus a minute of fitting. In wading the frunk floor at 620 mm is below the water surface, and duckbills can weep at the near-zero pressure differences of slow water rise. Proposal: two drains moulded into the tub floor, each with an 18 mm PP ball (density 0.90) in a cage below a 14 mm TPV seat. Rainwater drains past the ball. Rising water floats the ball onto the seat. Head-pressure check: frunk floor at 620 mm under 900 mm wading plus a 150 mm bow wave gives 0.43 m, ρgh = 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.43 = 4.2 kPa (4.4 kPa design, 0.45 m). Sealing force = ΔP × seat area = 4.4 kPa × 1.54×10⁻⁴ m² = 0.68 N plus net buoyancy of 3 mN, pressing a smooth ball on a 70 ShA TPV seat. The leak target is under 1 mL/min, and the seal tightens as the head rises. Why it works: a ball check seals from the first millimetre of rise by buoyancy, then pressure takes over. It needs no hose to put the outlet somewhere else. Benchmark: Rivian quotes up to 43.2 in fording for the R1S, a depth that puts any front storage floor well below the surface.

title: Bead-stiffened 1.2 mm pack lid replaces 1.5 mm flat lid at equal seal hold
description: [800V BEV] Cuts the 800V pack lid from 1.5 mm flat DC04 to 1.2 mm DX54 with a diagonal bead pattern. The beads keep flange rotation and seal unloading under wading load, saving 5.7 kg of steel per pack, less a bead-forming stage. Baseline: a flat 1.5 mm DC04 steel lid over 2.4 m² (28.3 kg) with an FIPG perimeter seal. Under the external wading load the flat panel bows inward, rotates the flange and unloads the seal between bolts. Thickness was set to limit that. Proposal: 1.2 mm DX54 galvanised steel with 6 mm deep diagonal beads at 150 mm pitch and a 20 mm stiffening rib inboard of the flange. The bead section raises local bending stiffness by about 3.5×, more than offsetting the t³ loss of (1.2/1.5)³ = 0.51. Head-pressure check: the lid top sits at 450 mm. At 900 mm plus a 150 mm bow wave the head is 0.60 m, ρgh = 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.60 = 5.9 kPa. A 45 → 15 °C thermal-shock vacuum adds up to 9.6 kPa transiently if the vent lags, total 15.5 kPa × 2.4 m² = 37 kN external. FE shows flange rotation of 0.21° (baseline 0.28°) and minimum seal compression of 31% (baseline 29%). The mica fire sheet under the lid is unchanged. Why it works: stiffness comes from shape, not thickness, and the seal cares about flange rotation, which the inboard rib controls. Benchmark: Mercedes credits the G 580 EQ's 850 mm wading to the battery in a protective casing, so the lid's sealing under water load is the core of the rating.

title: Overmoulded TPV grommets seal pack coolant pipes through the tray wall, deleting bulkhead fittings
description: [800V BEV] Replaces the two machined aluminium bulkhead fittings (each with two FKM O-rings and a nut), and the machined tray bosses, that take the coolant pipes through the pack wall. Continuous aluminium pipes pass through punched holes sealed by TPV grommets overmoulded on the pipe. Baseline: the pack coolant inlet and outlet cross the tray wall through two machined 6061 bulkhead fittings, each with an O-ring to the tray, an O-ring to the pipe and a lock nut (€7.8 each), set in machined tray bosses (€2.2). That is two sealing joints per pipe below the waterline. Proposal: the 3003 aluminium coolant pipe runs continuously from the cold-plate manifold to the external quick connector. A TPV 70 ShA grommet with a double lip and a snap-lock flange is overmoulded on the pipe at the pipe supplier and pressed into a punched 32 mm hole in the tray wall. The coolant joint is now a continuous pipe, and the grommet only seals the enclosure. Head-pressure check: the tray wall at the pipe sits at 250 mm. title: Localised wicking barriers at ECU entries replace water-blocked cable on wade-zone branches
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Uses standard FLRY cable on the wade-zone chassis branches. A gel-filled solder-sleeve wicking barrier sits only where each branch enters a sealed ECU or sensor, replacing longitudinally water-tight (strand-filled) cable over the full 22 m of branch length. Baseline: wheel-arch, rear-steer, side-step and air-supply branches use longitudinally water-tight (LWT) cable with filled strands over their full 22 m, about €0.35/m premium (€7.7 per car). If water enters at a damaged sheath or a connector, it can wick along the strands into an ECU, driven by head and thermal-shock vacuum. Proposal: standard FLRY-B cable, plus a gel-filled blocking sleeve (strands gel-blocked over 15 mm without solder, on a clamped section so no flexing reaches it) at the 14 points where a branch enters a sealed ECU or sensor connector. Each costs €0.31 including 0.2 minutes at the harness supplier. Head-pressure check: the lowest connectors sit at 300 mm. At 900 mm plus a 150 mm bow wave the head is 0.75 m, ρgh = 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.75 = 7.4 kPa. A sealed, unvented ECU at 85 → 15 °C would add 19.8 kPa of vacuum. Bulk flow along the strands needs a pressure difference, which exists across the ECU boundary (capillary wicking also creeps slowly without one), so a barrier at that boundary, rated 50 kPa, stops it with a 1.8× margin on the combined 27.2 kPa. Why it works: wicking only harms the ECU at the end of the wire. Block it there, once, instead of along every metre. Benchmark: Defender OCTA quotes 1,000 mm wading, which puts these whole branches under water.

title: Closed-end rivet nuts in the floor below the wade line delete post-paint sealer dabs
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Specifies closed-end (blind) rivet nuts for the 26 floor and sill fixings below 600 mm, set before paint. The post-paint sealer dab on each open-end rivnut, its operation and the wading-leak rework they cause are deleted. Baseline: 26 open-end M6 rivet nuts in the floor pan and inner sill below 600 mm carry harness clips, heat shields and trim. Each is sealed after paint with a PVC sealer dab (€0.09 material + 0.15 min at €0.95), and about 0.3% of cars show a cabin leak traced to a missed dab. Proposal: closed-end steel rivet nuts with a sealed dome and a pre-applied under-head sealing ring (€0.11 more each, to be confirmed with the ring), set at body-in-white before e-coat, so neither the thread nor the hole interface is open to the outside. Head-pressure check: the floor sits at 300 mm. At 900 mm plus a 150 mm bow wave the head is 0.75 m, ρgh = 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.75 = 7.4 kPa. Through an unsealed M6 rivnut thread clearance of about 0.05 mm² this passes Q = 0.6 × 5×10⁻⁸ × √(2 × 7,400/1,000) = 0.12 mL/s, enough to wet a carpet in a long wade. A closed end has no path. Why it works: the sealing is built into the fastener, so there is nothing to forget. Benchmark: Rivian's lap-pool demonstration held water about a foot above the bottom of the door well, which puts floor fixings well under water.

title: One-piece roof drain tubes delete the mid-pillar joint below the wade line
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Fits each of the four panoramic-roof drain tubes as one piece from the roof frame to the sill outlet. This deletes the barbed joint and clamp at about 650 mm in each pillar, which wading water reaches, and the joining operation. Baseline: the four panoramic-roof drains run in two segments each. The roof-module tube joins a pre-installed pillar tube at about 650 mm in the A- and C-pillars through a barbed connector and a clamp. During a wade, water rises inside the drain from its sill outlet at 300 mm to the outside level, so the joint sits under water inside the pillar. A loose joint wets the headliner, carpet or footwell electronics. Proposal: one-piece EPDM/PVC drain tubes fitted with the roof module, pushed down each pillar on a pre-installed pull cord to a moulded sill-outlet grommet. Head-pressure check: water inside the tube rises to the outside level, 900 mm plus a 150 mm bow wave = 1,050 mm. At the old joint height of 650 mm that is 0.40 m, ρgh = 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.40 = 3.9 kPa on a clamp joint. The tube top at the roof frame is about 1,750 mm, so the water cannot overflow the tray, and with no joint below it the tube is a closed pipe. Why it works: the joint existed only for build sequence, and a pull-through tube removes the only submerged joint in the drain path. Benchmark: Land Rover's 900 mm Range Rover rating puts the lower pillar of any panoramic-roof drain below the water surface.

title: One camera module family serves all four surround positions and the hitch view
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Collapses four surround-camera housings and the separate hitch camera into one module (same housing, optics and board) located by position-coded bracket adapters and pin-coded ID. This cuts variant tooling and validation and buys at five times the volume. Baseline: four surround-view part numbers: front (heater, washer interface), left and right mirror (different housing and connector angle) and rear, all 3 MP, 190° FoV at about €38 each. The tow and off-road pack (40% take) adds a 1.3 MP hitch camera from another supplier at €31. Each variant has its own tooling, optics validation and service part. Proposal: one module (190° lens, same imager, heater pad, sealed header) at about €36.4, about 230,000 units a year. A position-coded PA6-GF30 bracket adapter (€0.45) sets the mounting angle, and two coded header pins tell the surround-view ECU which position it is in. The hitch view uses the same module on a 60° down-tilt adapter. Geometry check: the hitch target at 1.0 m behind and 0.5 m below the camera sits at 27° below horizontal, well inside the 190° lens's coverage. The ball and coupler fill about 120 px at 3 MP, enough for the coupling guide lines. Head-pressure check: the lowest position (front, 600 mm) sees 0.90 + 0.15 − 0.60 = 0.45 m of wading head, ρgh = 4.4 kPa. All positions are sealed to the worst case, so one IPX7/IPX8 validation covers all. Why it works: surround cameras differ mainly in how they are mounted, not what they are. Move the difference into a cheap bracket and the expensive part becomes one. Benchmark: GMC's Hummer EV UltraVision ad

title: Ultrasonic lens-vibration cleaning replaces the front camera washer on road trims
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Fits road trims (70%) with a piezo ring bonded to the front camera cover glass that sheds water droplets and de-ices by vibration. Their front-camera washer jet, line, check valve, pump port and PTC heater are deleted; the off-road pack keeps its washer for mud. Baseline: every car's front surround camera has a washer jet (€2.4), a 2.6 m line with fittings (€1.9), a check valve (€0.6), a share of a pump outlet and solenoid (€1.6), a PTC lens heater (€2.2) and fitting (€1.0), total €9.7. Proposal: road trims (70%) use a piezoelectric ring transducer bonded to the cover glass, driven at about 40 kHz for droplet removal and at a higher-loss mode for de-icing (heating). Ring plus driver cost €6.2. Off-road pack cars keep the washer jet, because dried clay needs fluid. Physics check: a 3 mm water drop on glass has a capillary holding force of about 2πrγ = 2π × 1.5×10⁻³ × 0.072 = 0.7 mN. Surface accelerations above about 10⁴ m/s² at resonance overcome it, and the drop atomises or runs off. De-icing at 1.5 W melts a 0.5 mm ice film (lens area 4 cm², about 0.18 g) in about 40 s at −10 °C. Head-pressure check: no fluid path into the camera. The piezo is bonded inside the sealed housing, so wading at 600 mm mounting height (0.45 m head, ρgh = 4.4 kPa) sees the same sealed module. Why it works: on road cars the front camera mostly faces rain, spray and frost, which vibration clears, and only off-road mud needs fluid. title: 850 nm LED rings on RGB-IR cameras replace the pack's white night-illumination lamps
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Lights the camera's own field with invisible 850 nm LEDs on the camera board for night trail view and transparent-bonnet use, on RGB-IR imagers. The off-road pack's four white night-illumination lamps, their brackets and harness are deleted; mirror puddle lamps stay. Baseline: the off-road pack (30% take) adds four white LED night-illumination lamps (two in the front bumper, two under the sills, €14 each plus €6 brackets and harness) so the surround and transparent-bonnet views work at night on unlit trails. Proposal: all 360° cameras move to RGB-IR imagers (+€1.5 each). Pack cameras get a four-LED 850 nm ring (1.2 W, €3.2 per camera, a board population option) that lights 3-4 m around each camera. The ISP fuses IR luminance with residual colour. Physics check: four 850 nm LEDs at 300 mW each with a 120° lens give about 0.1 W/m² at 3 m, about 25 lux-equivalent on silicon after quantum-efficiency correction (about 35% QE at 850 nm on an RGB-IR sensor), enough for 10 dB SNR at the 360° camera frame rate. White night lamps at 3 m give 10-15 lux and dazzle the camera with hot spots at the lamp. Head-pressure check: the LEDs sit inside the sealed camera window, so the camera's existing IPX7 rating covers them (front position 0.45 m head, ρgh = 4.4 kPa). The four deleted lamps were themselves sealing liabilities below the sill. Why it works: the camera needs light it can see, not light the driver sees, and lighting from the camera makes the illumination coaxial, with no shadows cast toward the lens. Physics check: four 850 nm LEDs at 300 mW each with a 120° lens give about 0.1 W/m² at 3 m, about 25 lux-equivalent on silicon after quantum-efficiency correction (about 35% QE at 850 nm on an RGB-IR sensor), enough for 10 dB SNR at the 360° camera frame rate. White night lamps at 3 m give 10-15 lux and dazzle the camera with hot spots at the lamp. Head-pressure check: the LEDs sit inside the sealed camera window, so the camera's existing IPX7 rating covers them (front position 0.45 m head, ρgh = 4.4 kPa). The four deleted lamps were themselves sealing liabilities below the sill. Why it works: the camera needs light it can see, not light the driver sees, and lighting from the camera makes the illumination coaxial, with no shadows cast toward the lens. Benchmark: Land Rover's ClearSight Ground View creates a virtual transparent bonnet, which is only useful at night if the terrain under the bonnet is lit for the camera.

The off-road pack's four white night-illumination lamps, their brackets and harness are deleted; mirror puddle lamps stay.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Four lamp positions, brackets and two harness branches leave the pack build. Camera boards add an optional LED ring population. No new GA operation. The IR ring option is set by the camera pin code at end of line.
ideaData.dfmDfa: The LED ring is on the camera board behind a separate IR-transparent window segment with a light-block baffle, so IR does not flare into the lens. It is selected by the same pin coding that identifies the camera position.

Net €7-€10 per vehicle (fleet average) × 50,000 vehicles/yr = €350K-€500K per year (engineering estimate; assumed mix MHEV 60% / 800V BEV 40%, off-road pack 30% take; tooling and validation amortised over 7 years = 350,000 vehicles where stated).
