title: Rendered mud and water occlusion replaces two physical mud-rig validation loops
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Validates surround-view stitching and lens-occlusion detection on recorded drives with physics-rendered droplets, mud splats and silt film. Two of the three physical mud-rig and field-trip validation loops are deleted, and one is kept for correlation and regulation. Baseline: the off-road vision function is validated in three loops of mud-spray rig hours (about 420 h per loop) plus two remote off-road field trips per loop, about €0.9M per loop. They check that stitching, the transparent-bonnet history and the 'clean camera' prompt work with real soiling. Proposal: physics-based occlusion rendering (a ray-traced model of the fisheye lens and cover glass, with droplet, mud and silt deposits from measured soiling maps) applied to 2,000 h of recorded off-road drives, run in software-in-the-loop. One physical loop is kept to correlate the renderer and for regulatory tests. Correlation check: the renderer must match measured MTF loss and veiling glare within 10% for 1-3 mm drops and 0.2-1 mm mud films at five illumination levels. Exposure check: off-road soiling on the front camera at 600 mm is dominated by tyre spray. At 15 km/h a tyre throws water at about the 4.2 m/s tread speed, giving deposition rates the soiling map captures by CFD. Head-pressure check: the cameras are sealed to the worst position, the front camera at 0.45 m head (ρgh = 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.45 = 4.4 kPa), which is still proven physically in the kept loop. Why it works: most rig hours test perception, not hardware, and recorded drives with rendered soiling cover far more scenarios per euro. Ben

title: Rear surround camera moved inside the rear-screen wiper sweep, deleting its washer jet
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Mounts the rear surround camera inside the tailgate glass, in a clear frit-free zone that the rear wiper sweeps and the screen heater warms. Its external housing seal, washer jet, line through the tailgate, check valve and lens heater are deleted. Baseline: the rear surround camera sits in the tailgate finisher at about 1,000 mm. It has a sealed external housing and bezel, a washer jet fed through the tailgate hinge grommet with a check valve, and a lens heater, about €12.1 per car. The rear wake soils it heavily off-road. Proposal: the camera is bonded on a bracket inside the rear screen at the top of the wiper sweep, behind a 60 × 40 mm clear zone with no privacy tint, no frit and the heater wires routed around it. A flocked anti-reflection hood stops cabin reflections. Geometry check: from 1,550 mm height through a 55° raked screen, a 190° lens tilted 35° down sees the ground from 0.25 m behind the bumper. The bumper occludes the first 0.25 m, which the rear parking sensors cover. UN R158 and FMVSS 111 test objects at 0.3-6 m stay in view. Head-pressure check: the camera is inside the cabin at 1,550 mm, above any wade or bow wave, so ρgh = 0. The sealed external housing and its bezel, a known water-ingress point, no longer exist. Why it works: the rear screen is already wiped, washed and heated, so the camera borrows all three. Benchmark: a Land Rover bulletin for the Defender L663 covers a rear camera washer jet dripping from a faulty one-way valve in its feed pipe, the hardware this idea deletes.

title: Stepper-driven rotary distributor valve replaces three camera-wash solenoid valves
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Routes camera-wash fluid on the off-road pack through one stepper-driven ceramic-disc rotary distributor with four outlets. It replaces three solenoid valves, two of their three driver channels and two harness branches. Baseline: the off-road pack (30% take) washes the front, rear and hitch cameras through three 12 V solenoid valves (€3.4 each) at the reservoir. Each needs its own driver channel in the body controller (€0.9) and a two-wire branch (€1.1), €16.2 per car. Proposal: one rotary distributor (€8.9) with a ceramic disc on a stepper motor, four outlets (one spare) and a LIN-controlled driver (€1.2) on one branch (€1.1). The pump runs and the disc indexes to the outlet needed. Flow check: the disc port is 2.0 mm, giving 1.2 L/min at 2.5 bar, the same as a solenoid. Indexing between outlets takes 120 ms, so a front-then-rear wash sequence costs 0.1 s. Ceramic discs tolerate the grit that sticks solenoid plungers. Head-pressure check: the distributor sits on the reservoir at 500 mm. Wading puts 0.55 m of head outside it (ρgh = 5.4 kPa), while internally it holds 2.5 bar, a 46× ratio. The disc seal is pressed by a spring at about 0.4 MPa, so it does not open in a wade. Why it works: only one camera is washed at a time, so one valve that chooses is enough. Benchmark: the Hummer EV gives the driver a wash function for its underbody cameras, a multi-outlet cleaning duty like this one.

title: Dual-imager rear camera in the tailgate finisher absorbs the separate hitch camera
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Fits tow-pack cars with a rear camera module that carries a second, narrow down-looking imager behind the same window and serialiser. The separate hitch camera, its bracket, coax run and fitting are deleted. Baseline: the tow and off-road pack (40% take) adds a separate hitch camera (€31) in the lower tailgate with a bracket (€1.8), a 2.2 m coax run (€4.1) and 1.5 minutes of fitting, besides the 190° rear surround camera in the tailgate finisher. Proposal: on tow cars the rear module's board is populated with a second 1.3 MP imager behind a 60° lens tilted 55° down, sharing the housing, window, heater and a dual-input serialiser (two sensors aggregated on one GMSL2 link), at a €14 premium. Geometry check: the finisher camera at 1,000 mm and the ball at 450 mm height, 0.35 m behind the bumper face, puts the ball about 57° below horizontal (atan 0.55/0.35). The 60° lens tilted 55° covers 25-85°, which includes the ball and 0.6 m of drawbar, at 2.3 px/mm on the ball, enough for coupling guidance. Head-pressure check: the finisher at 1,000 mm is in the bow-wave band at 0.05 m head (ρgh = 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.05 = 0.5 kPa) and sealed like the base module. The deleted hitch camera at 600 mm was 0.45 m under in a wade (ρgh = 4.4 kPa), a sealing point removed. Why it works: both views look backwards from nearly the same place, so one housing and one link can carry both. Benchmark: GMC notes that some Hummer EV UltraVision views are unavailable in CrabWalk and that the system is not compatible with all trailers, which shows how trailer and hitch views shape camera arch

title: Laser-welded camera module back-filled with dry nitrogen deletes its vent and stops post-wade fogging
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Seals each surround camera hermetically by laser welding and back-fills it with dry nitrogen. The ePTFE vent, the internal anti-fog coat, the desiccant sachet and the screwed rear cover with gasket are deleted, and so is the fogging caused by the camera breathing moist air after a cold wade. Baseline: each surround camera (4.3 per car including hitch) has a screwed rear cover with gasket (€0.9), an ePTFE vent (€0.55), an internal anti-fog coating (€0.4) and a desiccant sachet (€0.3). After a wade, the warm camera (30 °C) is quenched in 10 °C water and breathes moist air through the vent. The lens fogs internally for 10-30 minutes, a known off-road complaint, and water ingress into camera housings has led to recalls in the segment. Proposal: a laser-transmission-welded PBT-GF30 rear cover, back-filled with dry nitrogen (dew point −40 °C) through a fill port sealed by a laser-welded plug, then helium leak-tested, at €0.8 per camera. Pressure check: sealed at 20 °C (293 K), internal pressure swings to 1.29 bar at 105 °C and 0.80 bar at −40 °C, so ±29 kPa acts on the 22 mm window and welded cover, stresses under 2 MPa. Head-pressure check: the front camera at 600 mm under 900 mm wading plus a 150 mm bow wave sees 0.45 m, ρgh = 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.45 = 4.4 kPa, against weld burst above 300 kPa. With no vent, there is no path for moisture to enter. Why it works: fogging needs water vapour inside, and a hermetic dry-gas fill keeps it out for life. Benchmark: a JLR recall for Range Rover and Range Rover Sport covers water ingress into the rear surround camera housing

Validate ISO 20653 IP6K9K/IPX7/IPX8, thermal shock −40/+105 °C, UN R158 and FMVSS 111 image quality after wading, and OEM wading-depth validation at 900 mm. Engineering review (13 Oct 2026) — open point: PBT-GF30 is not a moisture barrier. Water vapour permeates a laser-welded polymer housing over the years, far faster than nitrogen escapes, so with the desiccant and anti-fog coat deleted the camera picks up humidity again and fogs late in life. How this differs: We remove the moisture path entirely by making the camera hermetic and dry-gas filled, instead of a vented housing that breathes in a wade.

title: Reversing washer pump drains camera lines after each wash, deleting heated nozzles and lines
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] On the cold-climate and off-road pack, runs the camera-wash pump briefly in reverse after each wash so the camera lines and nozzles hold no fluid to freeze. The heated nozzles, the heated line segments, their relay and harness, and the line check valves are deleted. Baseline: the cold-climate and off-road pack (30% take) fits heated camera nozzles (2 × €2.6), heated line segments with a co-extruded resistance wire (€3.2), a relay and harness (€1.8) and two check valves (€1.2) that hold the lines full, about €11.4 per car. Check valves in camera washer feeds are a known failure point. Proposal: a bidirectional pump (€1.9 premium, often shared with the screen pump) runs 2.5 s in reverse after each camera wash, pulling the 44 mL in the 4 mm × 3.5 m camera lines back to the reservoir. Nozzles have no check valve, so air enters as fluid leaves. Freeze check: a dry 4 mm PA12 line has no fluid to freeze. The film left is about 0.05 mm, below any blockage risk. The next wash refills the line in 44 mL ÷ 1.2 L/min = 2.2 s, an acceptable delay for camera cleaning, which is not a screen-visibility function. Head-pressure check: an empty line at a nozzle in a wade (front at 600 mm, 0.45 m head, ρgh = 4.4 kPa) admits water to the nozzle, which is drained back the same way. No camera interior is exposed, since the nozzle is outside the sealed camera. Why it works: a line that is empty cannot freeze, so heating it is not needed. Benchmark: a Land Rover bulletin for the Defender L663 traced dripping headlamp and rear-camera washer jets to a faulty one-way valve in the jet

title: Front zone controller drives radar-radome heater and camera-wash pump, deleting the cleaning relay box
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Moves the radar-radome heater, the high-pressure camera-wash pump and the cleaning sequencing on the off-road and cold pack onto three smart high-side channels of the existing front zone controller. The separate sensor-cleaning and heating relay box, its bracket and its harness branch are deleted. Baseline: the off-road and cold pack (30% take) fits a separate sensor-cleaning and heating module in the front bumper (€18). It switches the 60 W radar-radome heater, the camera-wash pump and the wash sequence, with its own bracket (€0.9) and harness branch (€1.8). Proposal: the existing front zone controller drives the three loads from three smart high-side switches (PROFET-type, €4.1 including board area), with the sequencing in zone software and a €0.6 re-route of the branches. Load check: the radome heater draws 60 W ÷ 13.5 V = 4.4 A, the pump 3.5 A for under 2 s, and the third channel is spare. Each smart switch is rated 10 A with diagnostic feedback (open load, over-current), which the relay box lacked. Head-pressure check: the zone controller sits above the dry line at 1,050 mm (ρgh = 0). The deleted relay box at 550 mm was 0.50 m under water in a wade (4.9 kPa), a sealed enclosure that no longer exists. Why it works: the zone controller already has the power, the network and the location, and a box that only switches three loads repeats it. Benchmark: GMC's Hummer EV adds a wash function for its underbody cameras, showing that off-road cleaning adds switched loads that need a home.

title: Camera lens heaters powered over the video coax, deleting separate heater wires
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Feeds the front and rear camera lens heaters from the power-over-coax supply already on the video link, switched by the camera's serialiser GPIO. The separate two-wire heater branches, fuses, connector pins and body-controller heater outputs are deleted. Baseline: the front and rear surround cameras have 1.5 W lens heaters on a separate two-wire 12 V branch from the body controller (4 m of wire, a fuse, two connector pins at each end, about €2.6 per camera) and a body-controller output (€0.7). Proposal: the surround-view ECU's power-over-coax supply rises from about 2 W to 4 W per channel (12 V at up to 330 mA, within GMSL2 power-over-coax practice). The camera board switches its heater through a FET (€0.15) from a serialiser GPIO commanded by the ECU, with an upgraded inductor filter (€0.5) at the ECU end. Power check: camera electronics need 1.4 W and the heater 1.5 W, total 2.9 W, within the 4 W budget. Coax DC loss over 6 m of 50 Ω FAKRA-class cable at 0.24 A is under 0.2 W. Heater duty is only below +5 °C or after a wash. Head-pressure check: one fewer connector interface at each camera reduces the sealed paths. At the front camera (600 mm) wading puts 0.45 m on it, ρgh = 4.4 kPa, and the camera's single sealed coax header is rated far above. Why it works: the coax already brings power to the camera, so a bigger share of it can run the heater. Benchmark: Tesla's parts catalogue lists a heating element in the Cybertruck front camera, the duty this supplies without extra wires.

title: Surround cameras right-sized from 3 MP to 2 MP after a ground-resolution check
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Moves all surround and hitch cameras from 3 MP to 2 MP imagers, with a small lens sharpness upgrade so the edges of the field hold resolution. Imager cost and ECU frame memory fall, because the bird's-eye and ground views never display more than 2 MP of detail. Baseline: all surround cameras (4.3 per car) use 3 MP (2,048 × 1,536) imagers at about €9.2. Proposal: 2 MP (1,920 × 1,080) imagers at about €6.4, with an upgraded lens (€0.4 more) to hold edge MTF, plus re-tuned stitching. Resolution check: with an equidistant fisheye, 1,920 px across 190° is 0.10°/px horizontally. At 2 m from the camera that gives 2 × tan(0.10°) × 1,000 = 3.5 mm per pixel, against a 10-20 mm per pixel need for obstacle and kerb display. The bird's-eye view is rendered at 1,280 × 720 per quadrant and the transparent bonnet at 1,280 × 800, so 3 MP detail is discarded. Vertical resolution falls from 1,536 to 1,080 lines, but the ground view samples below the horizon only, where 2 MP still gives 4.8 mm per pixel at 2 m. Head-pressure check: imager change only, so the sealing is unchanged (front camera at 600 mm, 0.45 m head, ρgh = 4.4 kPa). Why it works: resolution should match what the display and functions use, not the sensor catalogue. Benchmark: Toyota's Land Cruiser Multi-Terrain Monitor gives an immediate view of the area around the vehicle, a display-resolution function rather than a measurement function.

title: Snap-in hard-coated PC dome shield lets the off-road front camera use a standard window
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Protects the off-road pack's front camera with a replaceable 2 mm hard-coated polycarbonate dome shield in its bracket. The ruggedised sapphire cover window and the separate stone guard are deleted. Baseline: the off-road pack (30% take) front camera is a ruggedised variant with a sapphire cover window (€6.8 premium) and a separate steel stone-guard bar (€2.1) against rock and branch strikes on trails. Proposal: the standard camera module with a snap-in 2 mm polycarbonate dome shield (polysiloxane hard-coated outside, anti-reflection coated inside, €1.6) held in the camera bracket with a €0.4 bracket change. The shield is replaceable by the dealer in a minute. Strike check: a 10 g stone at 15 m/s (trail speed plus tyre throw) carries ½mv² = ½ × 0.01 × 15² = 1.1 J. Two-millimetre PC survives over 5 J dart impact without penetration, a 4.5× margin, and a crack in the shield leaves the camera intact. Hard coat holds haze below 2% after 1,000 Taber cycles. Optical check: a dome centred on the entrance pupil keeps the 190° field undistorted, with under 2% MTF loss at mid-field. Head-pressure check: the shield is not a seal, since the camera behind it stays sealed (0.45 m wading head at 600 mm, ρgh = 4.4 kPa). The dome has two 3 mm drain notches so water and silt do not pool. Why it works: the camera needs protecting from impact, and a cheap sacrificial shield does that better than an expensive hard window. Benchmark: GMC covers the Hummer EV's underbody cameras with a clear lens protector, the same sacrificial-shield principle.

title: Push-fit connectors and PA12 tube replace barbed joints and EPDM hose on camera-wash lines
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces the 4.5 m of EPDM hose and the six barb-and-clip joints on the camera-wash lines with PA12 tube and push-fit washer connectors. This cuts material, joint labour and the leak rework that loose barbs cause. Baseline: camera-wash lines total 4.5 m of 4 mm EPDM hose (€0.90/m) with six barbed joints closed by spring clips (€0.20 each), at about 0.5 minutes each. About 0.3% of joints leak or come off and need rework at €40. Proposal: 4 mm PA12 tube (€0.45/m) and push-fit washer connectors (€0.42 each, 0.1 minutes) with an internal O-ring and a visible latch. Pressure check: the washer pump delivers 2.5 bar, and push-fit connectors are rated 6 bar burst at 80 °C, a 2.4× margin over the 2.5 bar working pressure (confirm against the pump dead-head pressure and the usual 3× burst rule), against barbed hose joints that rely on clip tension. Head-pressure check: the lowest joint sits at the front fascia at 550 mm. At 900 mm plus a 150 mm bow wave it is 0.50 m under water, ρgh = 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.50 = 4.9 kPa outside, negligible against the internal rating, and the O-ring seals in both directions. Why it works: barbed hose joints are cheap parts but expensive operations, and push-fit joints make the operation quick and verifiable. Benchmark: a Land Rover bulletin for the Defender L663 covers dripping headlamp and rear-camera washer jets traced to a valve in the jet feed pipe, showing that camera-wash plumbing joints and valves drive field faults.

title: Moulded drip lip above each side camera replaces its hydrophobic lens coating
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Moulds a 2 mm drip lip with side channels into the mirror moulding above each side surround camera, so sheet water from the mirror and door glass leaves before it reaches the lens. The hydrophobic lens coating used to fight run-off droplets is deleted. Baseline: rain, wash and post-wade water runs off the mirror and door glass as a sheet and drips across the side surround camera lens, leaving droplets in the view. The lens carries a hydrophobic coating (€1.1 per camera) to shed them faster, plus a slightly longer camera-wash cycle where fitted. Proposal: a 2 mm drip lip with 1.5 mm side channels moulded into the mirror base or cap moulding 6 mm above the camera window. Sheet water is lifted off at the lip and channelled to the sides, so it never reaches the lens. The tool insert costs about €0.1 per part. Flow check: a falling water sheet detaches at a sharp edge when its Weber number is above about 1. For a 0.5 mm sheet at 0.3 m/s, We = ρv²t/γ = 1,000 × 0.09 × 0.0005/0.072 = 0.6 on a rounded edge, but a 90° lip with a 0.3 mm radius forces detachment (the Coandă effect breaks down), confirmed in a spray booth. Head-pressure check: the lip is not a seal. The camera behind it is sealed for its 1,000 mm position at 0.05 m bow-wave head (ρgh = 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.05 = 0.5 kPa). Why it works: it is cheaper to keep water off the lens than to make the lens shed it. Benchmark: Toyota's Land Cruiser Multi-Terrain Monitor gives a camera view of the area around the vehicle, which depends on the side cameras seeing through run-off water.

title: Camera snaps into a moulded fascia bayonet boss, deleting its bracket and screws
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Moulds a keyed bayonet boss into the front fascia and the tailgate finisher, so the surround camera twists in and locks. The separate glass-filled bracket, its two screws, the heat-staking step and most of the fitting time are deleted at each position. Baseline: the front and rear surround cameras each mount through a PA6-GF30 bracket (€1.4) screwed with two screws (€0.12 each pair) to a heat-staked boss on the fascia or finisher (€0.3), taking 0.8 minutes. Proposal: a bayonet boss moulded into the PP-EPDM-T20 fascia and the finisher, with three lugs, an anti-rotation key and a snap detent. The camera twists 30° to lock in 0.25 minutes. Aim check: surround stitching needs ±0.5° camera aim. The bayonet boss locates on its own datum face, so its angle depends on local moulding tolerance (±0.2°) and fascia mounting (±0.2°), not a bracket stack (±0.4°), giving ±0.3° total. Thermal growth of the PP fascia (CTE 60 ppm/K) over the 40 mm boss is 0.1 mm across −40/+85 °C, a negligible angle change. Retention: the boss holds 150 N pull-out and 2 N·m twist, above a 1.1 J stone strike's impulse. Head-pressure check: the camera's sealing is at its own header, so the boss is not a seal. The front position at 600 mm sees 0.45 m of wading head (ρgh = 4.4 kPa) on the sealed camera. Why it works: the fascia is already a precise moulding, so it can hold the camera directly. Benchmark: Mercedes shows the G 580 EQ's transparent bonnet with its 360-degree camera, a function whose stitching quality depends on camera aim holding over life.

title: Camera housing carries its coax header directly, deleting the pigtail and in-line joint
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Moulds a sealed coax header into each surround camera housing, so the harness plugs straight into the camera. The 150 mm overmoulded pigtail and one connector half (with its sealed joint) are deleted at every camera. Baseline: each surround and hitch camera (4.3 per car) has a 150 mm overmoulded coax pigtail (€1.6) ending in an in-line sealed FAKRA or HFM connector half (€1.4) that mates with the harness. The camera thus has two sealed interfaces: the pigtail exit and the in-line joint. Proposal: the camera housing carries a sealed coax header (€0.9 premium) and the harness connector mates directly, with the harness lengthened by 0.15 m (€0.13 per camera). Signal check: deleting one connector pair removes about 0.3 dB insertion loss and one impedance discontinuity at 3 GHz, improving GMSL2 link margin. title: Keyed fixed-aim camera-wash nozzle replaces the ball-joint nozzle and its aiming step
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces the adjustable ball-joint camera-wash nozzles with fixed-orifice nozzles located by two datum pins, so the jet lands on the lens without adjustment. The aiming operation, its gauge and the mis-aim rework are deleted. Baseline: camera-wash nozzles (2.3 per car on average across trims and packs) are ball-joint types (€1.25) aimed at end of line with a gauge pin (1.2 minutes each), and about 0.8% are found mis-aimed later and re-aimed (€25). Proposal: a fixed nozzle (€0.70) moulded in PA6-GF30 with the orifice angle built in, located by two datum pins in the camera bezel or fascia. Aim check: at a 40 mm throw the jet must hit within ±3 mm of the lens centre, which allows ±4.3°. The datum location holds the nozzle to ±0.8°, plus moulding tolerance on the orifice of ±0.5°, giving a root-sum-square ±0.94°, a 4.5× margin. Pressure check: the nozzle sees 2.5 bar internally. In a wade the front nozzle at 600 mm is 0.45 m under water, ρgh = 4.4 kPa outside, which does not move a pinned nozzle and cannot back-feed the camera, which is separately sealed. Why it works: a jet only needs adjusting when its mounting is imprecise, and a datum-pinned nozzle on a precise moulding makes aiming redundant. Benchmark: the Cybertruck front bumper camera has a dedicated washer jet, the class of nozzle this idea fixes in place.

title: Active-alignment adhesive bead doubles as the camera lens seal, deleting the front O-ring
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Uses the continuous, AOI-inspected active-alignment adhesive bead between lens barrel and housing as the front water seal. The front O-ring, the lens retaining ring and their assembly step are deleted on every surround camera. Baseline: each surround camera (4.3 per car) seals its lens barrel to the front housing with a silicone O-ring (€0.18) compressed by a threaded retaining ring (€0.35), assembled in a separate step (€0.25), in addition to the UV- and thermal-cure epoxy bead that fixes the lens after active alignment. Proposal: the active-alignment bead is dispensed as a continuous 360° ring with a 0.4 mm minimum bond width, inspected by automatic optical inspection for gaps (€0.12 more adhesive, €0.06 AOI). It becomes the seal, and the O-ring and retainer are deleted. Pressure check: epoxy shear strength of about 15 MPa over a 0.4 mm × 60 mm bond holds 360 N, far above a 30 kPa pressure difference on the 15 mm lens (5.3 N). Head-pressure check: the front camera at 600 mm under 900 mm wading plus a 150 mm bow wave is 0.45 m under water, ρgh = 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.45 = 4.4 kPa. If the camera is hermetic, the internal swing of up to ±29 kPa also acts, so the bead is qualified to 50 kPa after 1,000 thermal cycles from −40 to +105 °C. Why it works: the adhesive is already continuous around the lens, so specifying and inspecting it as a seal removes a duplicated function. Benchmark: a JLR recall for Range Rover and Range Rover Sport covers water ingress into the rear surround camera housing or bezel, so the front seal of a camera is a field-critical interface.

title: High-mounted BEV cooling pack lets one cut-back front chin serve all BEVs
description: [800V BEV] Deletes the BEV off-road lower-fascia variant, its tool and its extra stone guard, and simplifies the lower grille insert on every BEV. The only added cost is longer coolant hoses and a revised carrier bracket for the raised cooling pack. Baseline: the 800V BEV inherits the MHEV front-end layout. Its cooling pack (LT radiator plus heat-pump outdoor heat exchanger) sits low behind a deep lower grille, so the fascia lower edge must reach 400 mm above ground at ride height. The BEV off-road pack (30% of BEVs, BEVs 40% of the fleet, so 12% of all cars) therefore carries its own cut-back lower fascia, a reshaped lower grille and a stainless stone guard. Proposal: because the BEV rejects about 25 kW at its design point instead of the MHEV's 110 kW, its cooling pack is about 40% smaller in face area. Mount it 120 mm higher across the frunk nose behind the upper grille, close the lower aperture, and cut the chin back on every BEV to a lower edge of 450 mm. Back-of-envelope: with the chin edge 830 mm ahead of the front tyre contact point, approach rises from atan(400/830) = 25.7° to atan(450/830) = 28.5°, about +2.8° before the +40 mm air-suspension off-road height is added. Why it works: on a BEV the lower grille exists only to feed a pack that no longer needs that face area, so the off-road chin becomes the standard chin and the variant disappears. The closed lower aperture also cuts cooling drag. The aPLI lower load path is kept by a stiffener rib behind the closed aperture at about 380 mm, so cutting the chin back does not remove lower-leg support. Benchmark: the Rivi

title: One body-side hole pattern serves road and off-road cladding, deleting pierce units and plugs
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the body-shop pierce units, robot program variants and wax-sealing steps that make the 14 extra off-road cladding holes. The off-road cladding instead carries six extra moulded bosses that pick up the common hole pattern. Baseline: the off-road wheel-arch and sill cladding (25% take) is wider and taller than the road cladding and needs 14 extra fixing holes in the BIW arch flanges and sill outer. These are pierced only on pack cars by six servo pierce heads on body-shop robots. That brings a robot-program variant, missed-hole rework and extra cavity-wax sealing. Proposal: design both cladding families around one common 22-point hole pattern. The road cladding uses all 22 holes. The off-road cladding uses the same positions, and its extra width is carried by six internal moulded bosses and ribs on the cladding itself, so no new body holes are needed. Back-of-envelope: each off-road cladding fixing must hold a 300 N branch or rock pull-off. The pull is shared by the nearest fixings: about five today, about three with the common pattern. title: Robots press-fit arch and sill cladding with force-signature check instead of manual fitting
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Cuts eight manual fitters to two loaders across both shifts, and the force-displacement check removes most of the warranty claims for cladding lost off-road. The robot capex is shown under investment and is not amortised in the bridge. Baseline: four arch claddings and two sill claddings are fitted by hand at two stations with two operators per side per shift (8 FTE over two shifts). Clip seating is checked by eye, and about 0.4% of off-road-driven cars lose or loosen a cladding in the field, often after branch or rock contact on a half-seated clip. Proposal: two six-axis robots with compliant vacuum-and-roller end effectors press each cladding along a programmed path over its clip line. The robot records a force-displacement trace at every clip, and a seated clip shows a snap peak of 120-180 N followed by a drop. A missing peak stops the car at the station. One operator per shift loads parts into a presentation rack. Back-of-envelope: 8 FTE × €55k = €440k per year, or €8.8 per car at 50,000 cars. Two FTE stay, so €6.6 per car is saved. Warranty: 0.4% × €180 per claim = €0.72 per car, falling to about €0.15. Why it works: the cladding is retained only as well as its worst clip, and only a measured snap proves the clip is seated. Benchmark: the HUMMER EV SUV quotes 34.4° breakover in Extract Mode with rock sliders available, showing how much sill-level contact these vehicles are expected to take.

title: One body wheel-arch opening sized for the off-road tyre deletes the arch-flange trim variant
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the body-shop laser-trim cell and roller-hem path variant that open up the rear wheel-arch flange on off-road pack bodies. Every body gets the larger opening, and road cars hide the extra gap behind a slightly deeper inner lip on the road cladding. Baseline: the off-road pack's 275/60 R20 all-terrain tyre (838 mm, about 33 inches, radius 419 mm against 395 mm for the road tyre) needs about 38 mm more radial clearance at the outer shoulder of the rear arch flange at full bump and articulation. Pack bodies therefore have their rear quarter arch flange trimmed in a separate laser-trim cell (about €1.1M) and roller-hemmed on a variant robot path, then re-sealed. Proposal: every body gets the larger arch opening, made in the main side-panel die line, so the trim cell and hem variant are deleted. On road cars the road cladding carries a deeper inner lip, sized to the final opening, that covers the larger flange gap. Why it works: the arch opening is pressed in a die that every body passes through, so making it the larger size costs nothing per car, while the variant needs a whole cell. title: Rear arch eyebrow and sill cladding moulded as one PP part per side
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes a joint per side: two tools, the lap-joint clips and foam, and one fitting operation. The rock-catching step at the arch-to-sill joint goes too, so breakover contacts slide off instead of snagging. Baseline: each side has a separate rear arch eyebrow (0.9 m) and sill cladding (2.0 m), joined by a lap joint with three clips and a foam pad. Four tools serve the two sides. The lap joint leaves a 4 mm forward-facing step, which is the first thing to snag on a rock or log during breakover and the most common cladding warranty item on off-road-driven cars. Proposal: one 2.6 m PP-EPDM-T20 moulding per side, 2.8 mm wall, on a 2,300 t press, with the sill lower edge raised 10 mm and chamfered at 30° through the arch transition so that a rock sliding along the sill is deflected. Back-of-envelope: thermal expansion over 2.6 m is 2.6 m × 80 × 10⁻⁶/K × 100 K = 21 mm, so the part has one fixed point at mid-door and slotted fixings either side, as long sills already do. Breakover: if the sill is the limiting contact, raising it by 10 mm on a 3,000 mm wheelbase gives about +0.7°; if the underbody centreline limits, the gain is only reduced snagging. Why it works: the joint has no function except to suit smaller tools; removing it removes a snag point and a part. Benchmark: the Land Cruiser 250 quotes 22° ramp breakover, showing that breakover is a published specification in this segment and that the sill line is where it is won or lost.

title: Lower-leg stiffener and approach-angle chin merged into one PP-LGF30 blade
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the steel lower-leg stiffener bar, its two brackets and the lower EPP block. One ribbed PP-LGF30 blade does both the pedestrian lower-load-path job and the chin structure, and it sits higher and further back. Baseline: the front lower has a painted PP chin cover, a separate 1.2 mm DC04 steel lower-leg stiffener bar at 360 mm on two brackets, and an EPP 30 g/l lower absorber. The steel bar is the lowest hard point and limits approach angle. Proposal: one PP-LGF30 ribbed blade (3.5 mm walls, 30 mm rib depth, E ≈ 6.5 GPa), bolted with four M6 bolts to the front-end carrier lower beam. It is the chin's structural lower and the lower-leg stiffener at once, sitting 15 mm higher and 10 mm further back. The rib pattern is tuned in CAE so that the lower load path reaches about 4-5 kN at 25 mm deflection, the stiffness target that keeps aPLI knee bending and tibia moments in range. Back-of-envelope: lifting the lowest hard point by 15 mm at 830 mm ahead of the tyre contact gives about +1.0° approach. A ramp contact at 5 km/h by a 3,000 kg car is absorbed by the suspension, not the chin. The blade sees the same 1.5 kN quasi-static push the steel bar was designed for. Why it works: the stiffener only needs stiffness at one height. A ribbed long-glass blade gives that at lower mass and becomes the chin structure as well. title: Clip-on 25 mm flare lips cover off-road tyres, deleting a full wide-cladding set
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the complete four-arch wide-cladding set and its four tools. The off-road pack reuses the road cladding plus four small flare lips from one family tool, which also removes four part numbers from the line. Baseline: the off-road pack fits 275/60 R20 all-terrain tyres on a wheel with 20 mm less offset (ET), so the tyre tread and sidewall bulge stand about 25 mm further out. EU 2021/535 wheel-guard coverage (30° ahead and 50° behind the wheel centre) then needs a complete wide arch-cladding set: four tools (€1.6M) and parts €18 dearer than the road set. Proposal: keep the road cladding on every car and add four PP-EPDM-T20 flare lips, 25 mm deep, moulded in one four-cavity family tool (€0.35M). They hook into a moulded dovetail on the road cladding's outer edge and take three screws each. Back-of-envelope: the tyre's outer face moves out by 20 mm offset + 5 mm bulge at 2.4 bar = 25 mm, which the lip covers with the same 30°/50° coverage as the road car. A branch hit on the lip at 10 km/h of about 30 J is reacted by the dovetail over 300 mm of length. Why it works: only the outer edge of the cladding changes between the two tyre packages, so only the edge needs to be a variant. Benchmark: the Ford Bronco Raptor runs 37-inch tyres with 47.2° approach, an example of the large-tyre off-road packages whose arch coverage this solves.

title: Arch cladding ends tuck under the bumper fascia, deleting four end brackets
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the four separate end brackets, their eight screws and the fitting time. The fascia corner's moulded return lip traps the cladding end, and that lip resists pull-out better than the bracket did when a branch or rock catches the cladding edge. Baseline: each arch cladding's bumper-side end is held by a separate PP-GF30 bracket screwed to the fender liner flange with two screws. When a branch or rock catches that edge off-road, the bracket pulls out first and the cladding flaps. Each bracket, its screws and 25 s of fitting cost about €1.4. Proposal: mould a 12 mm return lip into the front and rear fascia corners (a slide change in the fascia tool, about €120k). The cladding end slides under the lip in a tongue-and-groove, with a TPE wiper on the tongue to absorb tolerance. Back-of-envelope: a 0.9 m cladding fixed at its centre grows 0.45 m × 80 × 10⁻⁶/K × 100 K = 3.6 mm at each end over the -30 to +70 °C range. The groove allows ±4 mm, so the end floats without buckling. A branch pulling the edge outward at 250 N is reacted by the fascia lip over 80 mm of engagement instead of two screws. Why it works: the fascia is already there and is stiffer than a small bracket, so letting it hold the cladding end deletes a part and improves retention. Benchmark: the Defender OCTA quotes 40° approach and 42° departure, which puts the bumper corners and cladding ends in play on steep off-road obstacles.

title: Rear arch cladding extended into the stone-fan zone, deleting applied anti-chip film
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the TPU paint-protection film applied behind the rear wheels on off-road pack cars, and the labour to apply it. The rear arch cladding carries an 80 mm extension that covers the measured chip zone instead. Baseline: on the off-road pack (25% take), all-terrain tyres throw gravel at the rear quarter behind the rear arch. The car therefore gets a 0.2 mm TPU paint-protection film of about 0.35 m² per side, applied by hand in final assembly (€24 per car including labour and scrap). Proposal: extend the rear arch cladding by 80 mm rearward and upward over the chip zone measured in a gravel-throw test. This works only if the measured zone is a strip of about 0.08 m² per side next to the arch; the 0.35 m² film is assumed oversized, and the extension grows if the map shows more. The cladding is PP-EPDM-T20 mould-in-colour, so a stone that chips paint does nothing to it. Back-of-envelope: a 10 g stone thrown at 15 m/s carries ½ × 0.01 × 15² = 1.1 J. Automotive paint chips at about 0.3 J, while 2.8 mm PP-EPDM-T20 takes more than 5 J at -30 °C in falling-dart impact (ISO 6603-2) without cracking, and is rated by SAE J400 gravelometer for chipping. Why it works: the chip zone is small and predictable, so a few centimetres more cladding covers it permanently, while film needs labour, can lift at the edges and yellows with age. Benchmark: the Ford Bronco Raptor runs 37-inch tyres, the kind of large off-road tyre that throws stones onto the rear body sides.

title: Chin and lower grille moulded as one part on the off-road MHEV fascia
description: [MHEV] Deletes the separate PC/ABS lower grille insert, its eight clips and its fitting on off-road MHEVs. The honeycomb is moulded into the mould-in-colour chin, which also removes a joint where mud and stones lodged. Baseline: the off-road MHEV front lower (15% of fleet) is a PP-EPDM-T20 chin plus a separate black PC/ABS honeycomb lower-grille insert held by eight clips. The joint between them packs with mud and the clips break on stone strikes. Proposal: one PP-EPDM-T20 mould-in-colour chin with the honeycomb moulded in, using collapsible-core lifters in the tool, at the same open area. Back-of-envelope: the engine radiator needs the same grille open area (about 0.11 m², 55% of the aperture) for crawl and towing airflow, which the moulded honeycomb keeps with 2.5 mm ribs on a 14 mm cell. A 10 g stone at 15 m/s (1.1 J) hitting a 2.5 mm PP-EPDM rib is absorbed without fracture, whereas the PC/ABS insert cracked at clip bosses. Why it works: the insert exists only because the two materials differed; with the chin in mould-in-colour PP-EPDM, the grille can be the same part. Benchmark: the Land Cruiser 250 quotes 32° approach, which puts its front lower directly in contact with obstacles.

title: 2K TPV corner pads moulded onto bumper corners replace bolt-on corner guards
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes four bolt-on corner guards with their clips, screws and fitting time on off-road pack cars. A TPV scuff pad is co-injected onto the bumper-lower corners in the same tool, and the only added costs are the 2K premium and a rotary-platen tool upgrade. Baseline: the off-road pack (25% take) has four bolt-on EPDM/PP corner guards, two front and two rear, each with four clips and two screws, to take scrapes when the corners brush rocks or banks on tight trails. Proposal: co-inject a 4 mm TPV pad (Shore 80A, a Santoprene 101-80-type grade) onto the PP-EPDM-T20 bumper lower corners in a rotary-platen 2K tool. Only the off-road-pack lower tools get the rotary upgrade. The TPV bonds chemically to PP, so there is no fixing. Back-of-envelope: a corner scrape at 3 km/h with 300 N normal force, μ = 0.8 and 0.5 m of slide dissipates 0.8 × 300 × 0.5 = 120 J as friction. That is taken by surface abrasion of the TPV (abrasion loss below 150 mm³ per DIN ISO 4649), not by fracture of the bumper. A 4 mm pad survives about 20 such events before the PP shows. Why it works: the guard only needs a sacrificial soft surface, which 2K moulding puts exactly where needed with no fixings. Benchmark: the Defender OCTA quotes 40° approach and 42° departure in off-road configuration, so its bumper corners are exposed to the same banks and rocks.

title: Flexible TPV sill-to-pack closer replaces rigid PP closer, raising breakover clearance
description: [800V BEV] Deletes two injection-moulded rigid PP closers, their clips and tools. A cheaper TPV extrusion with an integral clip bead sits flush with the pack side rail instead of 15 mm below it, and flexes rather than cracks when a rock touches it. Baseline: on the BEV, a rigid PP-T20 aero closer (2 × 1.9 m) bridges the sill lower edge to the battery-pack side rail. It hangs 15 mm below the pack rail, so it is the breakover-limiting element at mid-wheelbase, and it cracks on rock contact. Proposal: an extruded TPV (Shore 70A) lip closer with an integral clip bead that snaps into a channel on the sill extrusion and sits flush with the pack side rail. It deflects on contact and springs back. Back-of-envelope: breakover ≈ 2·atan(2h/L). Raising the mid-wheelbase clearance h from 245 to 260 mm on a 3,000 mm wheelbase gives 2·atan(490/3,000) = 18.6° → 2·atan(520/3,000) = 19.7°, about +1.1°. Aero: the closer only has to seal the gap at speed, where the TPV lip is held by a 0.5 kPa pressure difference that it carries easily. The pack side rail now becomes the breakover contact, so it must carry a sliding rock contact at the off-road strike energy without denting toward the cells. A replaceable wear face on the rail, or the rock-slider inboard flange of orf-53f8130a77e7, takes that contact, and a rock-ramp strike test on the rail is part of sign-off. Why it works: the closer is aero trim, not structure, so it can be soft and flush. Benchmark: the G 580 EQ quotes 20.3° breakover, so breakover is a headline specification for electric off-roaders, where the pack sets the floor height.

title: Microcellular-foamed cladding and bumper lowers save 10% resin and 15% cycle
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Saves about 10% of the resin in every cladding and bumper-lower moulding, and about 15% of machine time through lower hold pressure and faster cooling. The added costs are supercritical-fluid dosing units at the supplier and a licence fee. Baseline: arch cladding, sill cladding and bumper lowers total about 9.5 kg of PP-EPDM-T20 per car, solid-moulded at 2.8 mm with a 55 s cycle. Proposal: physical microcellular foaming (supercritical N₂, MuCell-type process) at the same 2.8 mm wall, with about 10% density reduction. Hold pressure falls, so sink marks over ribs disappear and the cycle drops about 15%. Back-of-envelope: resin saved 9.5 kg × 10% × €2.6/kg = €2.47. At €9 machine cost per set, 15% = €1.35, plus similar savings on the lowers, about €2.6 in total. Foaming lowers -30 °C impact strength by about 15%, so the stone and branch targets are checked again: a 2 J stone (SAE J400) and a 30 J branch hit are still met because the parts were designed with more than 30% margin. Protection equivalence is proven by test, not assumed. Why it works: cladding is stiffness-and-surface driven, not strength driven, and foaming keeps the bending stiffness almost unchanged (it scales with the cube of wall thickness, which stays the same). Benchmark: the Defender OCTA quotes 40° approach and 42° departure in off-road configuration, so its claddings take regular strikes, which is why impact margin is re-proven here.

title: Spring-hinged front plate holder folds on contact, deleting the relocated plate plinth
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the raised plate plinth, its brackets and the extra fascia drilling variant on off-road pack cars. EU-market cars instead carry a plate holder with a moulded leaf spring that lets the plate fold up on contact and return. Baseline: on the off-road pack's cut-back fascia, a 520 × 110 mm EU front plate would hang below the chin line and become the lowest point at the front. So pack cars get a separate raised plate plinth on two brackets plus an extra fascia drilling variant (€14 + €2). Proposal: one PP-T20 plate holder on all EU cars (70% of the fleet), mounted at the standard position. A moulded polypropylene living-hinge pivot along its top edge and a PP leaf spring hold it vertical. On contact with a rock or bank it folds up to 35° at about 150 N and springs back. Back-of-envelope: the plate's lower edge drops 110 mm below the hinge. Folding it 35° lifts the lower edge by 110 × (1 − cos 35°) = 20 mm and moves it 63 mm rearward, so it no longer sets the approach line. PP living hinges survive more than 10⁶ flexes, against perhaps a few hundred contacts in a car's life. Why it works: the plate only needs to be vertical when it is being read, not when the car is climbing. Benchmark: the Land Cruiser 250 quotes 32° approach, and a front plate in the wrong place can cost several degrees of that.

title: TPV anti-slip step pad co-moulded into the rear bumper top replaces stainless plate
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the bonded brushed-stainless step plate on the rear bumper top of off-road pack cars, with its adhesive tape and fitting. A textured TPV pad is co-injected into the rear fascia top surface instead, and it grips better in mud and feels cooler to the touch in the sun. Baseline: off-road pack cars (25% take) carry a 0.8 mm brushed 1.4016 stainless step plate (€18) bonded with acrylic foam tape (€2 including fitting) to the rear bumper top. Owners use it as a step to reach the roof rack and to protect the paint when loading. Proposal: the rear fascia tool for pack cars gets a rotary-platen 2K stage that co-injects a 3 mm textured TPV pad (Shore 70A) into a recessed zone on the bumper top. Back-of-envelope: a 120 kg person stepping up with a 2× dynamic factor puts 2.4 kN on a 100 × 150 mm footprint, which is carried through the fascia into the rear beam via four moulded ribs under the step zone, the same load path the stainless plate relied on. Grip: wet stainless with mud has μ ≈ 0.3, while textured TPV stays at about 0.6-0.7, which halves the slip risk when climbing. In 40 °C sun both surfaces can exceed 70 °C (black TPV absorbs more sunlight than brushed stainless), but TPV feels much cooler to the touch because of its low thermal effusivity. Why it works: the step needs grip and wear resistance, not metal, and a 2K pad delivers both without a bonded part. Benchmark: the Defender quotes a 300 kg static roof load for rooftop tents, which is why owners climb on the rear bumper.

title: One accessory T-slot interface takes crossbar, tent, awning and ladder clamps
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces four accessory foot families (crossbar feet, awning brackets, tent brackets, ladder hooks), each with its own tooling and validation, with one stamped T-nut and clamp interface into a slot extruded in the roof rail. The cost is a die change and a little more extrusion on every car. Baseline: the raised roof rail is a 6063-T6 hollow extrusion on every car. Each accessory clamps around the rail with its own model-specific foot: zinc die-cast crossbar feet, steel awning L-brackets, tent clamp plates and ladder top hooks. That is four foot families, each tooled, fit-checked and dynamic-load-tested separately. Proposal: add a 10 mm T-slot along the outer face of the existing rail. Every accessory then uses one stamped T-nut and one clamp foot that can sit anywhere along it. Back-of-envelope: a 165 kg dynamic roof load at a 3 g vertical pothole peak is 4.9 kN, or 1.2 kN per foot over four feet. The 2.5 mm 6063-T6 slot lips have a shear capacity of about 2 lips × 2.5 mm × 60 mm × 100 MPa = 30 kN per foot, a margin of about 25×. Lip bending, not shear, governs pull-out (about 10-15 kN per foot, still over 10× margin). Along the slot the 20 g City Crash load (about 3.7 kN per foot with 75 kg) needs a clamp preload of about 12 kN at μ = 0.3, or a positive stop in the slot. The rail-to-roof fixings, not the slot, still set the vehicle roof rating. Why it works: the accessories differ, but the interface they need is the same, so one slot replaces four families of feet. Benchmark: aftermarket platform racks for the Rivian R1S mount directly to the factory roof

title: Correlated roof-load model signs off body variants after one physical rig body
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Cuts dynamic and static roof-load sign-off from six physical prototype bodies to one fully instrumented worst-case body plus a cheap static proof on each of the others. The CAE correlation work is the added cost. Baseline: roof-load sign-off runs a physical test on every combination of three body styles and two roof types (steel or glass), six bodies in all. Each body gets a 300 kg static test and a dynamic proving-ground programme (pavé plus off-road track) with a loaded rack, at about €280k per body for the prototype and track time. Proposal: fully instrument one worst-case body (longest wheelbase, glass roof) with strain gauges at the rail feet, roof bows and pillars, and correlate a CAE model to it using measured road-load data from a virtual proving ground. Back-of-envelope: 300 kg static × 1.5 safety factor = 4.4 kN on four feet, which the rig applies in an hour. title: Expedition rear quarter panel with accessory grid replaces glass and clamp-on carrier
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the rear quarter glass and the clamp-on side gear-carrier bracket on expedition cars. A bonded composite panel with moulded-in M8 inserts goes into the same glass aperture with the same urethane bead, and accessories bolt straight to it. Baseline: expedition-oriented customers (about 8% take) fit a side gear carrier that clamps over the rear quarter glass, with brackets to the D-pillar and protective film on the glass. The glass stays underneath, and the bracket kit costs €45. Proposal: on the expedition pack, the fixed rear quarter glass is replaced by a body-colour SMC or PP-LGF30 panel bonded into the same aperture with the same PU urethane bead and primer process. It carries a grid of eight moulded-in M8 inserts for gear carriers, jerry-can holders or bags. Back-of-envelope: a 25 kg carrier load at a 3 g vertical peak is 735 N over eight inserts, about 92 N each, against a 3 kN insert pull-out. The panel takes the urethane bead like glass, but at 10-12 GPa against 70 GPa for glass it adds less shear stiffness, so the small loss in body torsion is checked in CAE. Rear vision is unaffected because UN R46 relies on the mirrors, and the quarter glass sits behind the second-row seats. Why it works: an expedition customer covers this glass anyway, so making it a structural accessory panel removes the glass and the bracket. Benchmark: the Defender offers an Expedition Roof Rack and quotes roof loads with it, an example of an OEM-engineered expedition accessory system.

title: Bolted flat-pack expedition rack from four extrusions replaces welded tubular platform
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Removes TIG welding, distortion straightening and post-weld powder coating from the expedition rack, and cuts its shipping volume about fivefold. Keeping the 6063-T6 profiles out of the heat-affected zone also saves 3 kg of aluminium. Baseline: the OEM expedition roof rack (10% take) is a TIG-welded 6061-T6 tubular frame with a perforated deck, powder coated after welding. It weighs 18 kg, needs straightening fixtures to correct weld distortion and ships fully built at 1.3 m³. Proposal: build the platform from four 6063-T6 extrusion profiles (side rails, T-slotted cross slats, a front fairing rail and a corner node), joined by M8 A4 stainless T-bolts into clinch nuts. The profiles are powder coated as straight lengths before assembly, and the rack ships flat-packed at about 0.25 m³. Back-of-envelope: TIG welding drops 6061-T6 to about 60% of its strength in the heat-affected zone, so the welded frame must be sized for the weakened joint. A bolted frame keeps full T6 strength and needs about 3 kg less metal for the same strength. Design load: 168 kg payload + 15 kg rack at 3 g = 5.4 kN, shared by four rail clamps at 1.35 kN each. Why it works: the welds were a manufacturing choice, not a structural need, and a bolted, slotted frame is also easier to repair and reconfigure. Benchmark: Land Rover quotes the Defender's 168 kg dynamic roof load with its Expedition Roof Rack, showing that an OEM-validated rack is part of the roof rating.

title: Sealed 12 V roof-rail port powers light bar, tent and awning
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the dealer-fit accessory power kit (fused relay, 7 m cable, grommet) and the water-leak warranty from drilled roof or door-seal cable routes. Off-road pack cars are pre-wired with a sealed connector in the roof-rail foot instead. Baseline: roof accessories (light bar, tent light, awning LED, about 15% of cars) get power through a dealer-fit kit costing the OEM €65: a fused relay off the 12 V battery and a cable routed through the door seal or a drilled roof grommet. The drilled routes cause water-leak warranty claims of about €4 per accessory car. Proposal: on off-road pack cars (25% take, which includes nearly all roof-accessory buyers), fit a sealed 2-pin connector (IP6K9K / IP67 to ISO 20653) in the rear roof-rail foot. It is fed by a 2.5 mm² circuit from a spare 20 A eFuse channel on the rear zone controller, through the existing C-pillar harness channel. Benchmark: the Defender quotes its dynamic roof load with an OEM Expedition Roof Rack, the factory roof-accessory system this port powers.

title: Two extruded load-space rails with sliding eyes replace fixed eyes and accessory rail kit
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces the four fixed lashing eyes and the separate expedition accessory rail kit with two extruded floor rails on the off-road pack, so fridge slides, drawers and nets bolt straight into the rails. The rails cost more than four eyes; the kit deletion pays for them. Baseline: every car has four fixed lashing eyes. Expedition customers (8% of the fleet, about one in three off-road pack buyers) add a €140 accessory rail kit with two rails, adapter plates and carpet cut-outs to mount a fridge slide or drawer system. Proposal: off-road pack cars get two 6063-T6 floor rails, 1.0 m long, bolted at four points into the existing lashing-eye nut plates, with four sliding eyes. Fridge slides, drawers and nets bolt straight into the rail slot. Back-of-envelope: a 40 kg fridge in a 20 g frontal crash puts 40 × 9.81 × 20 = 7.8 kN forward, shared by four rail anchors at about 2 kN each, against nut-plate anchors designed for the ISO 27955 lashing-point load. Each sliding eye is rated at 5 kN. Why it works: the expedition kit's rails are what the car needed in the first place; fitting them on the line removes the duplicate kit hardware and carpet cutting. Benchmark: aftermarket platform racks for the Rivian R1S mount directly to factory hard points, the same idea of an OEM interface that accessories bolt to.

title: Front crossbar with slide-in TPE fairing lip deletes the separate wind deflector
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the separate front wind deflector (fairing) and its brackets that roof-rack users fit against whistle. The front crossbar carries a TPE keder lip in an extruded channel instead, at a small premium on every crossbar set. Baseline: OEM crossbars (35% take) use an aerofoil 6063-T6 profile. Customers who carry a tent, box or basket often fit a separate front wind deflector (€38 plus two brackets at €3 each, 15% take) because loaded bars whistle and boom. Proposal: the front crossbar profile gets an extruded keyhole channel on its trailing upper edge, into which a TPE (Shore 80A) keder lip slides. The lip breaks up regular vortex shedding. Back-of-envelope: vortex-shedding frequency f = St·V/D = 0.2 × 30 m/s ÷ 0.03 m = 200 Hz, right in the band that reads as whistle in the cabin. A trailing lip trips the shear layer and spreads the shedding over a wide band, typically cutting the tone by 6-10 dB in wind-tunnel tests of loaded bars. The lip adds 60 g and no measurable roof load. Why it works: when the noise source is the front bar's wake, treating the bar itself removes the need for a separate fairing; boom from a tall tent or box is a separate case that may still need a deflector. Benchmark: the INEOS Grenadier's load-bar system is quoted at 150 kg dynamic and 420 kg static, a reminder that expedition bars run loaded and are therefore exposed to this noise.

title: 800V BEV camp mode powers fridge and tent from the HV pack
description: [800V BEV] Deletes the 12 V leisure battery, its battery-to-battery charger, isolator and harness from the BEV expedition pack. Camp loads run from the HV pack through the existing 800-12 V DC-DC with the contactors closed. Baseline: the BEV expedition pack (BEVs 40% × expedition 10% = 4% of fleet) copies the MHEV layout: a 50 Ah AGM leisure battery in the load space with a DC-DC battery-to-battery charger, isolator and harness (€185), for overnight loads. Typical camp loads are a fridge at 45 W average plus 15 W of lights, 0.72 kWh over 12 hours. Proposal: a camp mode keeps the HV contactors closed and runs the existing 3.5 kW 800-12 V DC-DC to supply the 12 V accessory circuits, with a pack SoC floor (default 20%) at which camp mode ends. Back-of-envelope: standby overhead (DC-DC no-load about 30 W, BMS and zone controller about 25 W) is 55 W × 12 h = 0.66 kWh, so 0.72 + 0.66 = 1.4 kWh per night, about 1.4% of a 100 kWh pack. Contactor economiser coils take 2-4 W. Insulation monitoring stays active throughout, and an insulation fault or crash signal opens the contactors through the hardware path, independent of the camp-mode software. The 12 V battery still keeps the car alive. Why it works: the BEV carries a 100 kWh battery, so a second 0.6 kWh battery is redundant. Benchmark: the Defender quotes a 300 kg static roof load for rooftop-tent use, the overnight camping that creates these loads.

title: Tailgate inner trim moulded with a MOLLE slot grid replaces the bolt-on gear panel
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the accessory aluminium MOLLE gear panel, its rivnut kit and the trim cut-out. On off-road pack cars the tailgate inner trim is moulded with a webbing-slot grid from a switchable tool insert, so pouches clip straight on. Baseline: the expedition accessory range offers a tailgate gear panel (10% take): a powder-coated 2 mm 5754 aluminium MOLLE panel (€52), bolted through eight rivnuts that the dealer sets in the tailgate inner (OEM-supplied rivnut kit €6), with a trim cut-out (€3). Proposal: the off-road pack's PP-T20 tailgate inner trim tool gets a switchable insert that moulds a grid of 25 × 40 mm slots on the standard 1-inch webbing pitch, backed by 3 mm ribs. Pouches, first-aid kits and recovery-strap bags clip straight on, with a 15 kg total rating. Back-of-envelope: in a tailgate slam the trim sees a peak of about 30 g for a few milliseconds; 15 kg × 9.81 × 30 = 4.4 kN; the clips near the grid carry most of it, so four screw fixings into the tailgate inner at the grid corners (about 1.1 kN each) take the slam load, and the twelve trim clips only hold the trim. In a frontal crash the gear is loaded forward into the load space, so it is limited to soft items, as stated in the owner's guide. Why it works: the trim is already a large moulding, and the slots cost only a tool insert, where the panel needed metal, coating and rivnuts. Benchmark: the INEOS Grenadier roof is rated 150 kg dynamic and 420 kg static, an expedition specification whose owners carry this kind of gear.

title: Moulded PA6-GF30 jerry-can cradles on the expedition rack replace welded stainless holders
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces the TIG-welded stainless jerry-can holders with injection-moulded PA6-GF30 cradles that have steel-insert feet into the rack T-slot, a webbing strap and the common accessory lock. Welding, polishing and the separate lock cylinder go. Baseline: expedition-rack buyers who carry water or fuel (5% of fleet, two holders each) get TIG-welded 1.4301 stainless cradles with cam straps and their own lock: €48 each. Proposal: an injection-moulded PA6-GF30 cradle (UV-stabilised black) with two moulded-in steel insert feet that clamp into the rack slats' T-slot, a polyester webbing strap with an over-centre buckle, and the keyed-alike accessory lock cylinder: €21 each. Back-of-envelope: a 20 L water can weighs about 24 kg filled. A 3 g vertical peak gives 0.7 kN, and the ISO 11154 City Crash case (about 20 g) gives 24 × 9.81 × 20 = 4.7 kN forward, reacted by the two steel feet in the T-slot at about 2.4 kN each, inside the slot's tens-of-kilonewton capacity. The cradle body only locates the can, and the strap and feet carry the crash load. Why it works: the holder's job is to locate and strap the can, which a moulding does without welding. Benchmark: the Defender's 168 kg dynamic roof load with its Expedition Roof Rack shows the payload budget that two filled cans (about 48 kg) take from.

title: One key code for crossbar, rack, tent-clamp and roof-step locks
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces up to nine differently keyed lock cylinders from several accessory suppliers with one keyed-alike cylinder family coded per vehicle. Cylinder volume rises enough to cut the piece price, and three spare key sets are deleted. Baseline: expedition accessories each have their own lock cylinder and key pair: crossbars (four cylinders), the rack (two), the roof-access step (one) and the tent clamps (two). They come from different suppliers, and owners end up with four key sets, which also brings replacement-key logistics. Proposal: one accessory cylinder family (ZAMAK 3 die-cast housing, brass wafers, stainless shutter) keyed alike per vehicle at the cylinder supplier from a VIN-linked code, used in every roof and expedition accessory. Back-of-envelope: total volume rises from four small families to one family of about 90,000 cylinders a year (crossbars 35% × 4, rack, step and tent clamps), which brings the piece price from about €4.2 to €2.6. A lock only has to resist casual theft: the target is 12 Nm of attack torque on the barrel without opening, which wafer cylinders of this size meet. Why it works: every accessory needs the same small lock, so buying one family keyed per car is cheaper and better for the owner. Benchmark: the INEOS Grenadier load-bar system is rated 150 kg dynamic and 420 kg static, the kind of loaded expedition roof whose accessories need locks.

title: Torque-limiting clamp knobs on crossbar feet replace the supplied torque wrench
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the click torque wrench and four Allen bolts from every crossbar kit. Ratchet knobs slip at the specified clamp torque, so under- and over-torque claims (bars shifting, paint damage) also fall. Baseline: crossbar kits (35% take) ship with a 6 Nm click torque wrench (€8.5) and four Allen clamp bolts (€1.2). Owners who skip the wrench under- or over-torque the clamp, giving bars that creep under dynamic roof load or crushed rail paint, about €2 per kit in warranty. Proposal: four PA6-GF30 knobs with an internal POM-pawl ratchet that slips at 6 ± 0.5 Nm, over captive M8 bolts. Back-of-envelope: clamp force F = T ÷ (0.2·d) = 6 ÷ (0.2 × 0.008) = 3.75 kN per foot. With a rubber pad (μ ≈ 0.3) the slip resistance is about 1.1 kN per foot, or 4.5 kN over four feet. A 165 kg dynamic load at 0.8 g longitudinal braking is 1.3 kN, so the margin is about 3.5×. The ISO 11154 City Crash (20 g) is carried by the foot hook, not by friction. Why it works: the clamp torque is the only adjustable thing, so building the limit into the knob makes the right torque the only possible torque. Benchmark: the Defender's 168 kg dynamic roof load depends on a correctly fitted Expedition Roof Rack, which is the point of making correct clamping automatic.

title: PA6-GF30 snap-in deck panels replace perforated aluminium sheet on the expedition rack
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces the laser-cut, riveted and powder-coated aluminium deck with four injection-moulded grid panels that snap into the slat T-slots. Rivets, cutting and coating go, and the rack gets 3.5 kg lighter, which goes back to roof payload. Baseline: the expedition rack deck is 2.0 mm 5754-H22 perforated sheet, laser-cut, fixed to the slats with 24 rivets and powder coated: €62 and 9 kg per rack. Proposal: four UV-stabilised black PA6-GF30 grid panels, 25 mm rib depth, that snap into the cross-slat T-slots with moulded hooks. Total 5.5 kg. Back-of-envelope: a 100 kg person standing on the deck puts about 1 kN on a 100 × 100 mm footprint. A rib grid of 25 mm × 2.5 mm ribs on a 50 mm pitch carries that at a bending stress of about 35 MPa over a slat pitch of about 110 mm (wider pitch needs deeper ribs), against 120 MPa conditioned strength for PA6-GF30, a factor of about 3.4. The 3.5 kg saved raises usable payload within the 168 kg-class dynamic rating by the same amount. Why it works: the deck spreads load and gives grip; it does not carry the rack's structural load, which the slats do, so a moulded grid is enough. Benchmark: the Defender quotes its dynamic roof load with an OEM Expedition Roof Rack, so rack mass counts directly against usable payload.

title: PTFE-lined extrusion runners replace ball-bearing slides on the expedition fridge slide
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces the pair of steel ball-bearing drawer slides under the expedition fridge slide with two 6063-T6 extrusions running on PTFE strips, with a stamped stainless crash lock. The part gets cheaper, lighter and more tolerant of dust and mud. Baseline: the OEM expedition fridge slide (6% take) uses two heavy-duty steel ball-bearing drawer slides, 1,000 mm and rated at 150 kg (€64 per pair). Off-road dust and sand wear the balls, and the slides get stiff within a season. Proposal: two 6063-T6 extrusions with a nested C-profile, running on bonded 1.5 mm glass-filled PTFE strips, plus a cold-headed 10 mm 1.4310 stainless lock pin at fully stowed and fully extended. Back-of-envelope: a 40 kg fridge with μ = 0.05 on PTFE needs only 40 × 9.81 × 0.05 = 20 N to pull out when clean, and about 40-80 N with dust (μ 0.1-0.2). In a 20 g frontal crash the stowed fridge loads the lock pin at 7.8 kN; a 10 mm pin in 1.4310 shears at about 0.6 × 1,000 MPa × 78 mm² = 47 kN, a factor of about 6. Sand between plain surfaces is pushed aside, whereas in a ball race it jams the balls. Why it works: the slide moves a few times a day at walking pace, so plain bearings are adequate and far more tolerant of grit. Benchmark: Rivian R1S aftermarket racks mount straight to factory hard points; we apply the same OEM-interface idea to the load-space fridge mount, which bolts into the load-space rails.

title: MIM 17-4PH sliding lashing eye replaces forged-and-machined 42CrMo4 eye
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces the forged, machined and plated 42CrMo4 sliding lashing eyes in the load-space rails with metal-injection-moulded 17-4PH eyes that come net shape and need no plating. Baseline: the sliding lashing eyes in the off-road-pack load-space rails (four per car) are hot-forged 42CrMo4, machined at the slide face and the eye bore, then zinc-nickel plated: €4.8 each. Proposal: metal-injection-moulded 17-4PH stainless, H1150 aged, net shape including the slide tongue and eye, with no machining or plating: €2.6 each at about 50,000 eyes (12,500 sets) a year. Back-of-envelope: each eye is rated at 5 kN to ISO 27955. The eye's minimum section of 2 × 6 × 8 mm = 96 mm² at a MIM 17-4PH H1150 UTS of about 860 MPa (90% of wrought) gives about 83 kN static, and even with a stress-concentration factor of 3 the eye stays elastic at 5 kN. The part weighs 38 g, inside the MIM sweet spot. Stainless also resists wet expedition gear without plating. Why it works: a small, complex steel part at automotive volume is exactly what MIM does cheaply. Benchmark: Rivian R1S racks bolt to factory hard points, and these rail eyes are the load-space equivalent of that OEM interface.

title: Awning brackets sliced from 6082-T6 extrusion replace powder-coated bent steel L-brackets
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces three laser-cut, bent and powder-coated 5 mm S355 L-brackets per awning with slices of an anodised 6082-T6 L-extrusion. Cutting, bending and coating become sawing and drilling, and each bracket saves 0.65 kg. Baseline: the OEM side awning (8% take) hangs from three 5 mm S355 L-brackets, laser-cut, press-brake bent and powder coated: €9.5 and 1.1 kg each. Proposal: a 6082-T6 L-profile extrusion with a stiffening fillet and a T-slot foot that matches the roof rail, sawn into 60 mm slices, CNC drilled and clear anodised: €5.2 and 0.45 kg each. Back-of-envelope: with the awning open, a 10 m/s gust gives q = ½ × 1.2 × 10² = 60 Pa on 6 m² = 360 N of uplift. The awning's centre of pressure sits about 1.25 m out, so about 450 Nm of root moment is shared by three brackets, 150 Nm each. A 60 mm-wide, 6 mm-thick 6082-T6 leg has a section modulus of 360 mm³, giving 150,000 ÷ 360 = 417 MPa without the fillet, so the extrusion uses an 8 mm leg (Z = 60 × 8² ÷ 6 = 640 mm³, 234 MPa) with a 10 mm root fillet that brings the peak to about 200 MPa against 260 MPa yield at the 10 m/s stow limit stated in the owner's guide; a 1.5× proof gust (about 12 m/s) needs a 10 mm leg. The closed awning adds only 25 kg to the dynamic roof load. Why it works: a constant-section bracket is an extrusion slice by nature, so it needs no bending tool and no coating line. Benchmark: the Defender quotes its dynamic roof load with an Expedition Roof Rack, the OEM roof system an awning is hung from.

title: Crawl heat balance lets the off-road MHEV keep the road cooling module
description: [MHEV] Deletes the off-road MHEV's uprated radiator core, larger shroud and uprated charge-air LT radiator, together with their tooling and variant logistics. A heat balance shows that low-range crawling rejects about one-seventh of the road design heat load. The tow pack keeps its own specification. Baseline: the off-road pack on the MHEV (25% of MHEVs, MHEVs 60% of fleet, so 15% of cars) gets a 34 mm radiator core instead of 27 mm, a larger shroud and an uprated charge-air LT radiator for 'desert crawl' at 45 °C. Proposal: off-road-pack MHEVs keep the road cooling module; tow-pack cars are unaffected. Back-of-envelope: crawling at 5 km/h up a 30% (16.7°) grade at 3,000 kg needs m·g·v·sinθ = 3,000 × 9.81 × 1.39 × 0.29 = 11.9 kW at the wheels. At low-load efficiency the engine rejects about 1.1-1.2× its brake power to coolant, roughly 14 kW. With the fan alone moving about 1.6 kg/s through the road core and an inlet temperature difference of 60 K (105 °C coolant, 45 °C air), a core effectiveness of 0.35 gives 0.35 × 1.6 × 1.005 × 60 ≈ 34 kW of capacity, more than twice what crawling needs. The road design point (sustained Vmax, or a 3,500 kg trailer at 12% grade) is about 110 kW, so rock crawling is not the sizing case. Soft-sand driving at 15-30 km/h (about 33 kW at the wheels) with condenser pre-heat (ΔT about 45 K, capacity about 26 kW fan-only plus ram air) is the case the deletion must pass, and it is the first point run in the climatic tunnel. Why it works: crawling is low power with low airflow, and the fan's airflow scales with the much smaller heat load. Benchmark:

title: 800V BEV keeps the road battery chiller off-road; trail pack losses are ~50 W
description: [800V BEV] Deletes the uprated chiller fitted to off-road-pack BEVs for crawling in heat, and the larger condenser core only if the cabin A/C pull-down at 45 °C crawl passes with the road condenser. The battery's I²R losses while crawling are tiny, and DC fast charging remains the sizing case, which the road system already meets. Baseline: the BEV off-road pack (12% of fleet) gets a 30% larger battery chiller, a deeper condenser core and a 'desert' fan calibration for slow trail driving at 45 °C ambient. Proposal: off-road BEVs keep the road chiller and condenser. Back-of-envelope: rock-walking at 20 kW from an 800 V pack draws 25 A. With a pack resistance of about 0.08 Ω, the I²R loss is 25² × 0.08 = 50 W. Ambient soak at 45 °C into a 30 °C pack, with UA ≈ 15 W/K, adds about 225 W. That is under 0.3 kW in total, against a road chiller sized at about 8 kW for 270 kW DC charging, which at 386 A dissipates about 12 kW in the pack. Drive-unit and inverter losses go to their own loop, not the battery chiller. The condenser is a separate case: it is sized by cabin A/C plus chiller plus compressor heat at fan-only airflow, so its deletion depends on the 45 °C crawl pull-down test, not on this balance. Why it works: cell heat scales with current squared, and walking-pace driving is very low current, so the chiller has more than twenty times the capacity it needs. Benchmark: the Jeep Wrangler 4xe battery uses a dedicated heater plus a chiller off the air-conditioning refrigerant, a conventional road-type battery thermal circuit on a vehicle sold for serious off-road use.

title: Steady-state descent heat balance keeps the off-road pack on road 4-piston calipers
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the off-road pack's 6-piston front caliper upgrade, its larger pads and its separate brake homologation. A steady-state disc heat balance shows that a long descent is limited by disc area and cooling, not by caliper size. The friction brakes are sized to do the whole job alone. Baseline: the off-road pack (25% take) gets 6-piston monobloc front calipers with larger pads instead of the road 4-piston calipers, on the same 380 mm discs, for long descents. Proposal: keep the road calipers and pads. Back-of-envelope (friction brakes alone, with no engine braking or regen credited): 3,100 kg GVW descending a 15% grade at a hill-descent speed of 6 km/h (1.67 m/s) needs m·g·v·sinθ = 3,100 × 9.81 × 1.67 × 0.148 = 7.5 kW, less 0.8 kW of rolling resistance, so 6.8 kW of braking. With a 60/40 split that is 2.0 kW per front disc. A 380 mm vented disc at 380 °C sheds about 1.1 kW by radiation (σεAT⁴, ε = 0.55, A = 0.20 m²) and about 2.4 kW by low-speed convection, about 3.5 kW in total, so the disc settles near 300 °C at 2 kW. On the 25-30% grades that hill-descent control is built for, the load is 3.5-4.1 kW per front disc and the disc settles near 380-420 °C: still below pad fade onset (about 550 °C), but the brake-fluid temperature at the caliper becomes the limit and must be measured. An emergency stop from 60 km/h at the bottom of the descent (432 kJ, 130 kJ per front disc) adds only about 20 K. A larger caliper does not cool the disc, so it does not change this balance. Back-of-envelope (friction brakes alone, with no engine braking or regen credited): 3,100 kg GVW descending a 15% grade at a hill-descent speed of 6 km/h (1.67 m/s) needs m·g·v·sinθ = 3,100 × 9.81 × 1.67 × 0.148 = 7.5 kW, less 0.8 kW of rolling resistance, so 6.8 kW of braking. With a 60/40 split that is 2.0 kW per front disc. A 380 mm vented disc at 380 °C sheds about 1.1 kW by radiation (σεAT⁴, ε = 0.55, A = 0.20 m²) and about 2.4 kW by low-speed convection, about 3.5 kW in total, so the disc settles near 300 °C at 2 kW. On the 25-30% grades that hill-descent control is built for, the load is 3.5-4.1 kW per front disc and the disc settles near 380-420 °C: still below pad fade onset (about 550 °C), but the brake-fluid temperature at the caliper becomes the limit and must be measured. An emergency stop from 60 km/h at the bottom of the descent (432 kJ, 130 kJ per front disc) adds only about 20 K. A larger caliper does not cool the disc, so it does not change this balance. Why it works: on a slow descent the brake is in steady state, where disc area and airflow set the temperature, not piston count. Benchmark: Land Cruiser 300 Crawl Control uses engine and brakes to hold slow off-road speeds, the kind of sustained brake duty this heat balance covers.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Deletes the off-road pack's 6-piston front caliper upgrade, its larger pads and its separate brake homologation. ideaData.manufacturingImpact: One front caliper and pad family for road and off-road cars. The 6-piston variant leaves the off-road pack (the tow pack keeps it if its own heat balance needs it). One brake homologation set fewer.
ideaData.dfmDfa: No packaging change. The wheel and knuckle are already common. Hill-descent control keeps its current ESC calibration. Caliper fixings, brake hoses and the bracket are already common, so the off-road build simply loses a part family.
