title: GPF heat shield extended as grass-ignition guard, deleting the off-road debris tray
description: [MHEV] Deletes the separate perforated stainless debris tray bolted under the gasoline particulate filter on off-road-pack MHEVs. The road double-skin heat shield is extended 60 mm each side and closed underneath, and it keeps the outer skin below grass-ignition temperature. Baseline: on MHEV crawls through dry grass, the underfloor GPF skin reaches about 550 °C. The off-road pack (15% of fleet) adds a perforated 0.8 mm 1.4301 stainless debris tray (€26 plus bolts and labour) under the GPF so that grass cannot pack against it. Proposal: extend the road double-skin heat shield (0.5 mm DX53+AS120 aluminised steel, 4 mm air gap) by 60 mm on each side and close it underneath, with 8 mm drain louvres facing rearward. Fit it to every MHEV so there is one shield part. Back-of-envelope: with ε ≈ 0.3 on the aluminised inner faces, a two-layer shield halves the radiant transfer of a single layer, so the outer skin settles at about 200-220 °C over a 550 °C GPF. That is below the 260-300 °C range at which dry grass ignites on hot surfaces, and is checked by thermography during a crawl. Packed grass insulates the skin and lets it run hotter than this, so the deletion is approved only after a packed dry-grass test held against the shield through a stationary GPF regeneration shows the skin staying below about 250 °C. Why it works: the hazard is hot metal touching grass, and a closed, cool outer skin removes it without a separate tray. Benchmark: the Lexus GX 550 Overtrail is an engine-powered off-road trim grade, the kind of vehicle whose underfloor exhaust meets dry vegetation.

title: Dust-shield scoop feeds disc vanes, deleting MHEV off-road brake-cooling ducts and hoses
description: [MHEV] Deletes the off-road MHEV's bumper-to-knuckle brake-cooling ducts, hoses and deflectors, which clog with mud. A formed scoop in the stamped dust shield feeds the disc's inner vane inlet, which pumps air through the disc as it turns. Baseline: the off-road MHEV (15% of fleet) has two front brake-cooling ducts from bumper inlets to the knuckles, with hoses and deflectors. Off-road they fill with mud, and at hill-descent speed they do nothing useful. Proposal: delete the ducts. A formed scoop louvre in the stamped 0.8 mm dust shield feeds the inner vane inlet of the vented disc, and the shield's lower 25% is cut away to leave a 15 mm stone-eject gap so that grit cannot be trapped. Back-of-envelope: at a 6 km/h descent the ram pressure at a duct inlet is ½ρv² = 0.5 × 1.2 × 1.67² ≈ 1.7 Pa, essentially nothing, whereas the disc's own vane pumping is driven by rotation and works at every speed. At 100 km/h the scoop delivers about 60% of the duct's flow, and the steady-state descent case (2 kW per front disc, see the brake heat balance) does not need ram air. Why it works: ducts help only at speed, and in mud they block; the vanes do the work at descent speeds. Benchmark: Land Cruiser 300 Crawl Control holds slow off-road speeds with engine and brakes, the low-speed brake duty where ram ducts give no benefit.

title: Snubber-captive cooling-module isolators pass washboard durability, deleting off-road retention straps
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the two steel retention straps, their upper brackets and bolts that the off-road pack adds to the cooling module. Isolators with a moulded-in PA66 snubber cup limit travel and resist pull-out, at a small premium on every car. Baseline: the cooling module (about 18 kg filled) hangs on four EPDM grommets. On washboard and corrugated tracks it sees 6 g vertical peaks at 8-15 Hz, which can pull a grommet out, so the off-road pack (25% take) adds two steel straps with upper brackets and four bolts (€21.5 fitted). Proposal: every car gets isolators with a moulded-in PA66 snubber cup that limits module travel to ±6 mm and raises pull-out resistance to 2.5 kN. Back-of-envelope: 18 kg × 6 g = 1.06 kN is shared by the two lower isolators, 0.53 kN each, so the pull-out margin is 4.7×. Travel limiting also keeps the radiator hoses inside their flex range. The module's first vertical mode stays above 25 Hz, clear of the 8-15 Hz washboard input. Why it works: the straps only stop the module jumping out of soft grommets, and a captive snubber does that inside the isolator. Benchmark: the Ford Bronco Raptor is a desert-running 37-inch-tyre package, the kind of duty that makes corrugation durability a cooling-pack issue.

title: Front-end carrier lower beam formed as radiator bash lip, deleting the bolted radiator guard
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the bolted aluminium radiator lower guard on off-road pack cars. An overmoulded DP600 steel insert in the front-end carrier's lower beam projects ahead of and below the radiator tank, and the insert is loaded only on pack cars, with no tool change. Baseline: the off-road pack (25% take) adds a bolted 2.0 mm 5754-H22 aluminium guard (€19, six bolts) under the cooling module, because on steep approaches the chin flexes and the radiator lower tank becomes the next hard point. Proposal: the PA6-GF30 front-end carrier's lower beam gets a 2 mm DP600 steel insert, overmoulded and formed as a lip that projects 25 mm ahead of and 20 mm below the lower tank. The insert is loaded into the tool only for pack carriers, so there is one tool and two part numbers. The guard specification is kept as the requirement: a 600 J rock-face strike and a 5 kN quasi-static push at the tank zone with no tank contact. Back-of-envelope: a 2 mm DP600 lip formed as a 40 mm C-section with a 25 mm return yields at about 7 kN at the tank centre, but 7 kN over 60 mm absorbs only about 420 J. The insert is therefore 2.5 mm DP600, whose collapse load of about 11 kN (t² scaling) gives a 2.2× margin on the 5 kN push and absorbs about 650 J over 60 mm of travel, inside the 85 mm clearance to the tank. Why it works: the carrier is already there and already holds the cooling module, so a steel lip in it protects the tank without a second part. Benchmark: the Defender OCTA quotes 40° approach in off-road configuration, which brings the front lower into contact on steep obstacles.

title: Mud-tolerant BEV grille-shutter blades with stall-current homing delete the position sensor
description: [800V BEV] Deletes the Hall position sensor and its harness branch from the BEV active grille shutter, and the off-road pack's mud deflector. Wider blade end clearance tolerates mud, the actuator homes by stall current, and a return spring opens the blades if power is lost. Baseline: the BEV active grille shutter has a LIN actuator with a separate Hall position sensor. Blade end clearance is 2 mm, so mud jams the blades, and the off-road pack (12% of fleet) adds a mud deflector ahead of the shutter (€6). Proposal: widen the blade end clearance to 4 mm, with flexible TPE tips that keep the aero seal, and home the actuator by detecting stall current at the closed and open stops. The sensor goes. A return spring biases the blades open when unpowered. Back-of-envelope: the drag benefit of a closed shutter is about ΔCd 0.010, and the 2 mm of extra gap costs about 0.001, which is 10% of the benefit. Stall detection needs a current rise of about 30% over running current within 50 ms, well within the actuator ASIC's resolution. A mud-jammed blade is detected as an early stall and reported, and the spring and thermal derate keep cooling safe. On the BEV there is no OBD emissions monitor tied to the shutter. Why it works: the sensor only confirms a position the motor can already infer from its current. Benchmark: the Mercedes G 580 EQ wades to 850 mm, 150 mm deeper than its combustion siblings, which shows how much water and mud an electric off-roader's front end must tolerate.

title: Phenolic caliper pistons cut brake-fluid heating on long descents and save cost
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces the chrome-plated steel front caliper pistons with glass-filled phenolic pistons that cost less, conduct about a hundred times less heat into the fluid and cannot corrode after wading. The boot is changed to suit. Baseline: the front 4-piston calipers use chrome-plated steel pistons (€3.2 each, eight per car). On a long descent the pad backing plate reaches about 350 °C, and the steel piston (k ≈ 45 W/m·K) carries that heat into the fluid. Proposal: glass-filled phenolic (PF-GF) pistons at €2.0 each, with a revised boot groove. Back-of-envelope: phenolic has k ≈ 0.5 W/m·K. In the series path backing plate → piston → fluid, the piston's resistance rises by about 90×, so the steady fluid temperature at the piston face falls from about 165 °C to about 120 °C at a 2 kW per disc descent. That moves the fluid clear of the DOT 4 wet boiling point (155 °C) after two years of moisture uptake. Phenolic does not rust, so pistons do not stick after wading and water crossings (900 mm wade: ρgh = 8.8 kPa on the boot, plus up to about 30 kPa of vacuum when air behind a 150 °C boot is quenched, so boot sealing is validated hot-into-water). The strength needed is in compression only (about 25 MPa at 100 bar line pressure), which PF-GF carries easily. Why it works: the piston should insulate the fluid, and phenolic is both a better insulator and cheaper than plated steel. Benchmark: the Mercedes G 580 EQ wades to 850 mm, the kind of water exposure that makes corrosion-free pistons valuable.

title: One copper-free pad compound for road and off-road pack, proven on long descents
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the off-road pack's separate high-temperature semi-metallic pad compound, its UN R90 approvals and its dyno programme. One copper-free low-steel compound, validated for descents, serves every car. Baseline: two front pad compounds. The road compound is an ECE low-steel pad. The off-road pack (25%) gets a high-temperature semi-metallic pad with more dust and noise, chosen for long descents. That means two part numbers per axle and two UN R90 approval and dyno programmes. Proposal: one copper-free (<0.5% Cu, meeting the Washington and California Better Brakes rules) ECE low-steel compound with a phenolic and cashew resin system, μ = 0.40 ± 0.05 up to 650 °C. Back-of-envelope: the steady-state descent case puts the disc at about 300 °C (2 kW per front disc at 6 km/h on 15%, friction brakes alone), so the pad interface runs at 300-350 °C (about 400-450 °C on 25-30% grades), inside the road compound's stable μ band with about 200-300 K of margin to fade onset. The R13-H Type-I fade series is the harder thermal case and is already met by the road pad. Why it works: the pad compound was over-specified for a descent that is mild in brake-temperature terms. Benchmark: Land Cruiser 300 Crawl Control holds slow speeds with the brakes, which is exactly the low-temperature, long-duration duty this compound is proven for.

title: Grooved one-piece front rotor replaces the off-road pack's pinned two-piece rotor
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces the off-road pack's two-piece front disc (iron ring, forged aluminium hat, 12 drive pins) with the road one-piece disc plus a machined thermal-choke groove at the hat-to-ring junction, which keeps hub-bearing temperature in limit. Baseline: the off-road pack (25%) uses two-piece front discs (GJL-250 HC ring on a forged 6061 hat with 12 drive pins, €82 each) so that descent heat does not reach the hub bearing and wheel. Road cars use one-piece discs. Proposal: the off-road pack uses the road one-piece disc in GJL-150 HC high-carbon iron, with a 3 mm-deep undercut groove machined at the hat-to-ring junction (€48). Back-of-envelope: the groove cuts the conductive section between ring and hat by about 35%, so with the ring at 300 °C after a long hill the bearing seat runs at about 110 °C, against about 95 °C with the two-piece disc and a 150 °C grease limit. The added unsprung mass is about 1.2 kg per front corner, an honest ride trade. High-carbon iron also resists the thermal cracking that comes from hot discs entering water on a wade. Why it works: the hub only needs heat flow choked, not stopped, and a groove does that in a single casting. Benchmark: the Defender 110 wades to 900 mm on air suspension, which makes hot rotors meeting cold water, and the cracking it causes, a real design case.

title: Non-handed pillar-vane front disc replaces the handed curved-vane pair
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces left and right curved-vane front discs with one pillar-vane disc for both sides. One casting core and one part number are deleted, wrong-hand fitting errors disappear, and the pillar vanes resist the thermal cracking caused by hot discs meeting water. Baseline: front discs have curved vanes, so they are handed: two castings, two core boxes and two part numbers. The line occasionally fits a disc on the wrong side, where it pumps air backwards. On off-road pack cars, hot discs plunged into water during crossings show thermal-crack warranty claims (about 0.5% × €400). Proposal: one non-handed pillar-vane disc (about 140 pillars in three staggered rows) in GJL-150 HC. Back-of-envelope: pillar vanes move about 10% less air than curved vanes at 100 km/h. That shortens the cooling time in the AMS stop series, but on a slow descent cooling is dominated by radiation and natural convection (the 6 km/h, 2 kW per disc heat balance), where vane pattern hardly matters. A hot disc at 300 °C entering 10 °C water sees a sharp surface temperature drop, and pillar vanes spread the resulting thermal stress through a grid of short ligaments instead of long radial vanes, which is why they are used on heavy-duty discs for crack resistance. Why it works: one design serves both sides and suits off-road duty better. Benchmark: the Defender OCTA wades to about 1,000 mm, so hot brakes meeting water is a design case in this segment.
